cards.front: Roughly how many species have been known and described so far, as per NCERT?
cards.back: About 1.7–1.8 million species.

cards.front: What term refers to the number and types of organisms present on earth?
cards.back: Biodiversity

cards.front: Why can local names of organisms not be used for scientific study?
cards.back: Local names vary from place to place, even within a country, causing confusion. A standardised name is needed so each organism is known by the same name worldwide.

cards.front: What is nomenclature?
cards.back: The process of giving a standardised (correct) name to an organism so that it is known by the same name all over the world.

cards.front: What must be done before an organism can be correctly named?
cards.back: It must be correctly described and identified, so we know what organism the name is attached to.
cards.hint: Order: identification, then nomenclature

cards.front: Which code gives the scientific names of plants?
cards.back: ICBN: International Code for Botanical Nomenclature.

cards.front: Which code governs the naming of animals?
cards.back: ICZN: International Code of Zoological Nomenclature.
cards.hint: Z = Zoological = animals

cards.front: Who proposed the system of binomial nomenclature?
cards.back: Carolus Linnaeus

cards.front: In binomial nomenclature, what are the two components of a scientific name?
cards.back: • First word: generic name (genus) • Second word: specific epithet

cards.front: In Mangifera indica, which word is the specific epithet?
cards.back: indica. Mangifera is the genus.

cards.front: In which language are biological names generally written?
cards.back: Latin (or Latinised), regardless of their origin.

cards.front: How are biological names written when printed vs handwritten?
cards.back: • Printed: in italics • Handwritten: the two words underlined separately
cards.hint: Trap: underline each word separately, not as one line

cards.front: Which part of a binomial starts with a capital letter?
cards.back: The genus name starts with a capital letter; the specific epithet starts with a small letter.

cards.front: In Mangifera indica Linn., what does 'Linn.' indicate?
cards.back: The author who first described the species (Linnaeus), written in abbreviated form after the specific epithet.

cards.front: Where is the author's name placed in a biological name, and how is it written?
cards.back: After the specific epithet, at the end of the name, in an abbreviated form.

cards.front: What is classification?
cards.back: The process by which anything is grouped into convenient categories based on some easily observable characters.

cards.front: What is a taxon? Give an example.
cards.back: A scientific term for a category at any level of classification, e.g. plants, animals, mammals, dogs are each taxa.

cards.front: What four processes are basic to taxonomy?
cards.back: • Characterisation • Identification • Classification • Nomenclature
cards.hint: C-I-C-N

cards.front: What forms the basis of modern taxonomic studies, as per NCERT?
cards.back: External and internal structure, structure of cell, development process and ecological information of organisms.

cards.front: From which Latin word is 'systematics' derived and what does it mean?
cards.back: systema, meaning the systematic arrangement of organisms.

cards.front: What title did Linnaeus give to his publication?
cards.back: Systema Naturae

cards.front: Systematics vs taxonomy: what additional aspect does systematics consider?
cards.back: Systematics also takes into account evolutionary relationships between organisms, besides identification, nomenclature and classification.

cards.front: What are taxonomic categories collectively called, since they show a ranked order?
cards.back: Taxonomic hierarchy. Each category is a rank, and together they form the hierarchy.

cards.front: Arrange in ascending order: Family, Species, Phylum, Order, Genus, Kingdom, Class.
cards.back: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum/Division → Kingdom
cards.hint: Some Good Fathers Organise Classes Properly Kindly

cards.front: As we go up the taxonomic hierarchy from species to kingdom, what happens to the number of common characters?
cards.back: Number of common characters decreases. Lower the taxon, more the characters shared by its members.
cards.hint: Trap: number of organisms increases, shared characters decrease

cards.front: What is the lowest taxonomic category?
cards.back: Species

cards.front: How do taxonomists distinguish one species from closely related species of the same genus?
cards.back: On the basis of distinct morphological differences.

cards.front: Name the three species of genus Panthera given in NCERT.
cards.back: • P. leo (lion) • P. tigris (tiger) • P. pardus (leopard)

cards.front: Give two species of genus Solanum cited in NCERT.
cards.back: • Solanum tuberosum (potato) • Solanum melongena (brinjal)

cards.front: What is a genus?
cards.back: A group of related species that have more characters in common than species of other genera.

cards.front: Besides Panthera, which genus (of cats) does NCERT place in family Felidae?
cards.back: Felis (cats)

cards.front: Which family includes the genera Panthera and Felis?
cards.back: Felidae

cards.front: Name three plant genera NCERT places in family Solanaceae.
cards.back: Solanum, Petunia, Datura

cards.front: Family Felidae is separated from Canidae; which animals belong to Canidae?
cards.back: Dogs (family Canidae)

cards.front: On which characters are plant families characterised?
cards.back: Both vegetative and reproductive features of plant species.

cards.front: Which order includes the plant families Convolvulaceae and Solanaceae, and on what basis?
cards.back: Order Polymoniales, mainly based on floral characters.

cards.front: Which order includes the families Felidae and Canidae?
cards.back: Order Carnivora

cards.front: Class Mammalia includes which two orders cited in NCERT, with examples?
cards.back: • Primata: monkey, gorilla, gibbon • Carnivora: tiger, cat, dog

cards.front: Fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals are grouped in phylum Chordata based on which features?
cards.back: Presence of notochord and dorsal hollow neural system.

cards.front: In plants, which category corresponds to 'phylum' of animals?
cards.back: Division

cards.front: Which is the highest taxonomic category in this hierarchy?
cards.back: Kingdom, e.g. Kingdom Plantae and Kingdom Animalia.

cards.front: Give the scientific name, family and order of man as per NCERT.
cards.back: Homo sapiens; family Hominidae; order Primata; class Mammalia; phylum Chordata.

cards.front: Give the family and order of housefly (Musca domestica).
cards.back: Family Muscidae; order Diptera; class Insecta; phylum Arthropoda.

cards.front: Give the family and order of mango (Mangifera indica).
cards.back: Family Anacardiaceae; order Sapindales; class Dicotyledonae; division Angiospermae.
cards.hint: Trap: mango is NOT in Solanaceae

cards.front: Give the family and order of wheat (Triticum aestivum).
cards.back: Family Poaceae; order Poales; class Monocotyledonae; division Angiospermae.

cards.front: Odd one out by class: Mango, Wheat, Potato, Brinjal?
cards.back: Wheat: it is a monocot (Monocotyledonae); the others are dicots.

cards.front: Insects are grouped together on the basis of which common feature mentioned in NCERT?
cards.back: Three pairs of jointed legs.

cards.front: Who made the earliest attempt at a scientific basis for classification?
cards.back: Aristotle

cards.front: How did Aristotle classify plants and animals?
cards.back: • Plants: trees, shrubs, herbs • Animals: those with red blood and those without

cards.front: Who proposed the Two Kingdom classification and what were the kingdoms?
cards.back: Linnaeus: Kingdom Plantae and Kingdom Animalia.

cards.front: Who proposed the Five Kingdom classification and in which year?
cards.back: R.H. Whittaker, 1969

cards.front: Name the five kingdoms of Whittaker.
cards.back: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia

cards.front: List the main criteria Whittaker used for five kingdom classification.
cards.back: • Cell structure • Body organisation • Mode of nutrition • Reproduction • Phylogenetic relationships

cards.front: Name the four shapes of bacteria.
cards.back: • Coccus (spherical) • Bacillus (rod) • Vibrium (comma) • Spirillum (spiral)

cards.front: Name the three groups of archaebacteria and their habitats.
cards.back: • Halophiles: extreme salty areas • Thermoacidophiles: hot springs • Methanogens: marshy areas

cards.front: Which bacteria in the gut of cows and buffaloes produce methane (biogas) from their dung?
cards.back: Methanogens (archaebacteria)
cards.hint: Trap: archaebacteria, NOT eubacteria

cards.front: Which chlorophyll do cyanobacteria have, similar to green plants?
cards.back: Chlorophyll a. They are photosynthetic autotrophs.

cards.front: In which specialised cells do some cyanobacteria fix nitrogen? Give two examples.
cards.back: Heterocysts, e.g. Nostoc and Anabaena.

cards.front: What do chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria oxidise to get energy?
cards.back: Inorganic substances such as nitrates, nitrites and ammonia; energy used for ATP production.

cards.front: Name four diseases caused by bacteria listed in NCERT.
cards.back: Cholera, typhoid, tetanus and citrus canker
cards.hint: Citrus canker is a plant disease

cards.front: How do bacteria mainly reproduce, and what do they form under unfavourable conditions?
cards.back: Mainly by fission; under unfavourable conditions they produce spores.

cards.front: Which organisms completely lack a cell wall and are the smallest living cells known?
cards.back: Mycoplasma. They can survive without oxygen and are pathogenic in animals and plants.

cards.front: Which two groups are included in chrysophytes?
cards.back: Diatoms and golden algae (desmids)

cards.front: What makes the cell walls of diatoms indestructible?
cards.back: They are embedded with silica; walls form two thin overlapping shells fitting like a soap box.

cards.front: What is diatomaceous earth and what is it used for?
cards.back: Accumulated diatom cell wall deposits. Used in polishing and filtration of oils and syrups.

cards.front: Which protists are called the chief producers in the oceans?
cards.back: Diatoms

cards.front: Describe the flagella of dinoflagellates.
cards.back: Two flagella: one lies longitudinally, the other transversely in a furrow between the wall plates.

cards.front: Which dinoflagellate causes red tides?
cards.back: Gonyaulax. Its toxins may even kill marine animals such as fishes.

cards.front: Instead of a cell wall, euglenoids have what?
cards.back: A protein-rich layer called pellicle, which makes the body flexible.

cards.front: How does Euglena nourish itself in light vs in darkness?
cards.back: • Sunlight: photosynthetic • Deprived of light: heterotrophic, preying on smaller organisms

cards.front: Slime moulds: mode of nutrition and the aggregate they form?
cards.back: Saprophytic protists; under suitable conditions form an aggregate called plasmodium, which can spread over several feet.

cards.front: Which protozoan causes sleeping sickness and to which group does it belong?
cards.back: Trypanosoma, a flagellated protozoan.

cards.front: Which protozoan group has a cavity (gullet) opening to the outside? Give an example.
cards.back: Ciliated protozoans, e.g. Paramoecium.

cards.front: Which protozoan group has an infectious spore-like stage? Give the key example.
cards.back: Sporozoans, e.g. Plasmodium (malarial parasite).

cards.front: Amoeboid protozoans: how do they capture prey? Name a parasitic example.
cards.back: With pseudopodia; parasitic example: Entamoeba.

cards.front: Which fungus causes white spots on mustard leaves?
cards.back: Albugo (a parasitic fungus)

cards.front: Which fungus causes wheat rust?
cards.back: Puccinia

cards.front: What are coenocytic hyphae?
cards.back: Continuous tubes filled with multinucleated cytoplasm, lacking septae.

cards.front: What are fungal cell walls made of?
cards.back: Chitin and polysaccharides.
cards.hint: Trap: NOT cellulose

cards.front: Name two symbiotic associations of fungi.
cards.back: • Lichens: with algae • Mycorrhiza: with roots of higher plants

cards.front: Give the sequence of steps in the sexual cycle of fungi.
cards.back: Plasmogamy (cytoplasm fusion) → karyogamy (nuclei fusion) → meiosis in zygote giving haploid spores.
cards.hint: P before K

cards.front: In which fungal classes does a dikaryotic (n + n) stage occur?
cards.back: Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes

cards.front: Phycomycetes: type of mycelium and asexual spores?
cards.back: Aseptate, coenocytic mycelium; asexual spores are zoospores (motile) or aplanospores (non-motile), formed endogenously in sporangium.

cards.front: Give three examples of Phycomycetes.
cards.back: Mucor, Rhizopus (bread mould), Albugo

cards.front: Ascomycetes are commonly called? Give one unicellular and one multicellular example.
cards.back: Sac-fungi. Unicellular: yeast (Saccharomyces); multicellular: Penicillium.

cards.front: Where are ascospores and conidia produced in Ascomycetes?
cards.back: • Conidia: exogenously, on special mycelium called conidiophores • Ascospores: endogenously in sac-like asci, arranged in ascocarps

cards.front: Which ascomycete is extensively used in biochemical and genetic work?
cards.back: Neurospora

cards.front: In Basidiomycetes, how does plasmogamy occur since sex organs are absent?
cards.back: By fusion of two vegetative or somatic cells of different strains or genotypes.

cards.front: How many basidiospores form on a basidium, and are they endogenous or exogenous?
cards.back: Four basidiospores, produced exogenously on the basidium.

cards.front: Give three examples of Basidiomycetes.
cards.back: Agaricus (mushroom), Ustilago (smut), Puccinia (rust)

cards.front: Why are Deuteromycetes called imperfect fungi?
cards.back: Only their asexual or vegetative phases are known; they reproduce only by conidia.

cards.front: Give three examples of Deuteromycetes.
cards.back: Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma

cards.front: Name two partially heterotrophic plants that are insectivorous, and one parasite.
cards.back: • Insectivorous: Bladderwort, Venus fly trap • Parasite: Cuscuta

cards.front: Who first recognised that the mosaic disease of tobacco is caused by microbes smaller than bacteria, and when?
cards.back: Dmitri Ivanowsky, 1892

cards.front: Who called the infectious fluid from infected tobacco 'Contagium vivum fluidum', and when?
cards.back: M.W. Beijerinek, 1898

cards.front: Who showed that viruses could be crystallised, and when?
cards.back: W.M. Stanley, 1935. The crystals consist largely of proteins.
cards.hint: Ivanowsky 1892 → Beijerinek 1898 → Stanley 1935

cards.front: What type of genetic material do plant viruses vs bacteriophages usually have?
cards.back: • Plant viruses: single-stranded RNA • Bacteriophages: usually double-stranded DNA

cards.front: Who discovered viroids, in which year, and which disease do they cause?
cards.back: T.O. Diener, 1971; potato spindle tuber disease.

cards.front: Viroid vs virus: key structural difference?
cards.back: A viroid is a free RNA that lacks the protein coat found in viruses.

cards.front: What are prions, and name the diseases they cause in cattle and humans?
cards.back: Abnormally folded proteins. Cattle: BSE (mad cow disease); humans: CJD (Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease).

cards.front: In lichens, what are the algal and fungal partners called?
cards.back: • Algal: phycobiont • Fungal: mycobiont
cards.hint: Phyco = algae, Myco = fungus

cards.front: Why are lichens good pollution indicators?
cards.back: They do not grow in polluted areas.

cards.front: What are algae?
cards.back: Simple, thalloid, chlorophyll-bearing, autotrophic and largely aquatic organisms.

cards.front: Apart from water, where else do algae occur, and with which animal are some associated?
cards.back: On moist stones, soils and wood; some live with fungi (lichen) and on animals, e.g. on sloth bear.

cards.front: Give one colonial and two filamentous algae.
cards.back: • Colonial: Volvox • Filamentous: Ulothrix, Spirogyra

cards.front: Which flagellated spores are formed in asexual reproduction of algae?
cards.back: Zoospores; on germination they give rise to new plants.

cards.front: Give an algal example of isogamy with non-flagellated (non-motile) gametes.
cards.back: Spirogyra: gametes similar in size but non-motile.

cards.front: Give an example of anisogamous reproduction in algae.
cards.back: Eudorina: gametes dissimilar in size.

cards.front: What is oogamy? Give two algal examples.
cards.back: Fusion of a large non-motile (static) female gamete with a smaller motile male gamete, e.g. Volvox, Fucus.

cards.front: What fraction of total CO<sub>2</sub> fixation on earth is carried out by algae?
cards.back: At least half of the total CO2 fixation, through photosynthesis.

cards.front: Name three marine algae used as food.
cards.back: Porphyra, Laminaria, Sargassum

cards.front: Which hydrocolloids are obtained from brown and red algae respectively?
cards.back: • Brown algae: algin • Red algae: carrageen

cards.front: Agar is obtained from which two algae? Give its uses.
cards.back: Gelidium and Gracilaria. Used to grow microbes and in preparing ice-creams and jellies.
cards.hint: Agar = red algae

cards.front: Which unicellular alga, rich in proteins, is used as food supplement even by space travellers?
cards.back: Chlorella

cards.front: Name the three main classes of algae.
cards.back: Chlorophyceae (green), Phaeophyceae (brown), Rhodophyceae (red)

cards.front: Which chlorophylls are present in Chlorophyceae?
cards.back: Chlorophyll a and b

cards.front: What are pyrenoids and in which algae are they found?
cards.back: Storage bodies in chloroplasts that store protein besides starch; found in green algae (Chlorophyceae).

cards.front: What is the cell wall composition of green algae?
cards.back: Inner layer of cellulose and outer layer of pectose.

cards.front: Give examples of Chlorophyceae.
cards.back: Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara

cards.front: Which pigments are found in brown algae, and which gives the brown colour?
cards.back: Chlorophyll a, c, carotenoids and xanthophylls; brown colour due to fucoxanthin.

cards.front: In what form is food stored in Phaeophyceae?
cards.back: As complex carbohydrates: laminarin or mannitol.

cards.front: Name the three parts of the plant body of brown algae.
cards.back: Holdfast (attachment), stipe (stalk), frond (leaf-like photosynthetic organ)

cards.front: Describe the zoospores of brown algae.
cards.back: Pear-shaped, with two unequal, laterally attached flagella.

cards.front: Give examples of Phaeophyceae.
cards.back: Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus

cards.front: Which pigment gives red algae their colour?
cards.back: r-phycoerythrin

cards.front: What is the stored food of red algae, and what does it resemble?
cards.back: Floridean starch, similar in structure to amylopectin and glycogen.

cards.front: Flagella in Chlorophyceae, Phaeophyceae and Rhodophyceae: compare.
cards.back: • Green: 2–8, equal, apical • Brown: 2, unequal, lateral • Red: absent

cards.front: Give examples of Rhodophyceae.
cards.back: Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium
cards.hint: Trap: Porphyra is red, not brown

cards.front: Why are bryophytes called amphibians of the plant kingdom?
cards.back: They live in soil but depend on water for sexual reproduction.

cards.front: Which generation forms the main plant body of bryophytes?
cards.back: The haploid gametophyte.
cards.hint: Trap: in pteridophytes it is the sporophyte

cards.front: In bryophytes, which structures anchor the plant instead of true roots?
cards.back: Rhizoids (unicellular or multicellular).

cards.front: Bryophytes: male and female sex organs and their products?
cards.back: • Antheridium: biflagellate antherozoids • Archegonium: flask-shaped, single egg

cards.front: Is the sporophyte of bryophytes free-living?
cards.back: No. It is attached to the photosynthetic gametophyte and derives nourishment from it.

cards.front: Why is Sphagnum moss economically important?
cards.back: It provides peat, used as fuel, and as packing material for trans-shipment of living material due to its water-holding capacity.

cards.front: Which organisms are the first to colonise rocks, along with lichens?
cards.back: Mosses. They decompose rocks, making the substrate suitable for higher plants.

cards.front: What are gemmae and where are they formed?
cards.back: Green, multicellular asexual buds formed in gemma cups on the thalli of liverworts.

cards.front: Give an example of a thalloid liverwort.
cards.back: Marchantia

cards.front: What are the three parts of a bryophyte sporophyte?
cards.back: Foot, seta, capsule

cards.front: What are the two stages of the moss gametophyte?
cards.back: • Protonema: creeping, green, branched, often filamentous; develops from spore • Leafy stage: develops from secondary protonema as a lateral bud

cards.front: Which stage of the moss bears the sex organs?
cards.back: The leafy stage (upright axes with spirally arranged leaves).
cards.hint: Trap: NOT the protonema

cards.front: Give three examples of mosses.
cards.back: Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum

cards.front: Which were the first terrestrial plants to possess vascular tissues?
cards.back: Pteridophytes (xylem and phloem)

cards.front: Microphylls vs macrophylls: give one example each in pteridophytes.
cards.back: • Microphylls (small): Selaginella • Macrophylls (large): ferns

cards.front: What are sporophylls and strobili?
cards.back: • Sporophylls: leaf-like appendages bearing sporangia • Strobili/cones: compact structures formed by sporophylls, e.g. Selaginella, Equisetum

cards.front: What is the gametophyte of pteridophytes called?
cards.back: Prothallus: small, multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic and thalloid.

cards.front: Name two heterosporous pteridophytes.
cards.back: Selaginella and Salvinia
cards.hint: Most pteridophytes are homosporous

cards.front: Which event in heterosporous pteridophytes is considered a precursor to the seed habit?
cards.back: Development of the zygote within the female gametophyte, which is retained on the parent sporophyte.

cards.front: Match the pteridophyte classes with an example each.
cards.back: • Psilopsida: Psilotum • Lycopsida: Selaginella, Lycopodium • Sphenopsida: Equisetum • Pteropsida: Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum

cards.front: Why are gymnosperms called naked-seeded plants?
cards.back: Their ovules are not enclosed by an ovary wall and stay exposed before and after fertilisation.

cards.front: Which gymnosperm is one of the tallest tree species?
cards.back: Giant redwood tree, Sequoia

cards.front: What are coralloid roots, and in which gymnosperm are they found?
cards.back: Small specialised roots associated with N2-fixing cyanobacteria; found in Cycas.
cards.hint: Pinus = mycorrhiza; Cycas = coralloid roots

cards.front: Which adaptations help conifer leaves withstand extreme conditions?
cards.back: Needle-like leaves (less surface area), thick cuticle and sunken stomata, which reduce water loss.

cards.front: Branched vs unbranched stem: Cycas, Pinus, Cedrus.
cards.back: • Unbranched: Cycas • Branched: Pinus, Cedrus

cards.front: Pinus vs Cycas: are male and female reproductive structures borne on the same or different trees?
cards.back: • Pinus: male and female cones on the same tree • Cycas: male cones and megasporophylls on different trees
cards.hint: Trap: Cycas has megasporophylls, not female cones

cards.front: In gymnosperms, the megaspore mother cell differentiates from which tissue?
cards.back: From one cell of the nucellus.

cards.front: In gymnosperms, how many archegonia does the female gametophyte bear?
cards.back: Two or more archegonia (female sex organs).

cards.front: What are the smallest and one of the tallest angiosperms named in NCERT?
cards.back: • Smallest: Wolffia • Tall: Eucalyptus (over 100 m)

cards.front: Which animals show the cellular level of organisation?
cards.back: Sponges (Porifera): cells arranged as loose aggregates.

cards.front: Organ level vs organ-system level: give the phylum showing organ level.
cards.back: Platyhelminthes show organ level; annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms and chordates show organ-system level.

cards.front: Which phyla show radial symmetry as per NCERT?
cards.back: Coelenterates, ctenophores and echinoderms (adult).
cards.hint: Trap: echinoderm larvae are bilateral

cards.front: What are diploblastic animals? Give an example.
cards.back: Animals with two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm, with undifferentiated mesoglea between them, e.g. coelenterates.

cards.front: Pseudocoelom: what is it and which group has it?
cards.back: A body cavity not lined by mesoderm; mesoderm is present as scattered pouches. Found in aschelminthes.

cards.front: What is metameric segmentation? Give an example.
cards.back: Serial repetition of body segments, external and internal, with repetition of some organs, e.g. earthworm.

cards.front: What is the notochord?
cards.back: A mesodermally derived rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development in some animals.

cards.front: Trace the path of water through a sponge's canal system.
cards.back: Ostia → spongocoel → osculum
cards.hint: In through Ostia, Out through Osculum

cards.front: Which cells line the spongocoel and canals in sponges?
cards.back: Choanocytes (collar cells)

cards.front: What forms the skeleton of sponges?
cards.back: Spicules or spongin fibres

cards.front: Sponges: hermaphrodite or not, type of fertilisation and development?
cards.back: Hermaphrodite; fertilisation internal; development indirect (larval stage).

cards.front: Which cells give Cnidaria its name, and what are their functions?
cards.back: Cnidoblasts/cnidocytes (stinging cells); used for anchorage, defence and capture of prey.

cards.front: In coelenterates, on which structure is the mouth located?
cards.back: On the hypostome; it opens into the gastro-vascular cavity.

cards.front: Polyp vs medusa: shape and example.
cards.back: • Polyp: sessile, cylindrical, e.g. Hydra, Adamsia • Medusa: umbrella-shaped, free-swimming, e.g. Aurelia

cards.front: What is metagenesis? Give an example.
cards.back: Alternation of generation between polyp (forms medusae asexually) and medusa (forms polyps sexually), e.g. Obelia.

cards.front: Match: Physalia, Pennatula, Gorgonia, Meandrina.
cards.back: • Physalia: Portuguese man-of-war • Pennatula: sea-pen • Gorgonia: sea-fan • Meandrina: brain coral

cards.front: How many rows of comb plates do ctenophores have, and what is their function?
cards.back: Eight external rows of ciliated comb plates, which help in locomotion.

cards.front: Which phenomenon is well-marked in ctenophores?
cards.back: Bioluminescence (property of a living organism to emit light).

cards.front: Which cells help in osmoregulation and excretion in Platyhelminthes?
cards.back: Flame cells

cards.front: Which flatworm shows high regeneration capacity?
cards.back: Planaria

cards.front: Give two parasitic Platyhelminthes with common names.
cards.back: • Taenia: tapeworm • Fasciola: liver fluke

cards.front: Aschelminthes: are sexes separate, and which sex is longer?
cards.back: Sexes separate (dioecious); females are often longer than males.

cards.front: Match: Ascaris, Wuchereria, Ancylostoma.
cards.back: • Ascaris: roundworm • Wuchereria: filaria worm • Ancylostoma: hookworm

cards.front: Which annelid has lateral appendages called parapodia, and what are they for?
cards.back: Nereis; parapodia help in swimming.

cards.front: Which organs perform osmoregulation and excretion in annelids?
cards.back: Nephridia
cards.hint: Trap: Malpighian tubules are in arthropods

cards.front: Odd one out by sexuality: Nereis, earthworm, leech?
cards.back: Nereis is dioecious; earthworms and leeches are monoecious.

cards.front: Which is the largest phylum of Animalia, and what share of named species does it include?
cards.back: Arthropoda; over two-thirds of all named species on earth.

cards.front: List the respiratory organs found in arthropods.
cards.back: Gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheal system

cards.front: Name the excretory organs and balancing organs of arthropods.
cards.back: • Excretion: Malpighian tubules • Balance: statocysts

cards.front: Match: Apis, Bombyx, Laccifer, Locusta, Limulus.
cards.back: • Apis: honey bee • Bombyx: silkworm • Laccifer: lac insect • Locusta: gregarious pest • Limulus: king crab, living fossil

cards.front: What is the radula, and in which phylum is it found?
cards.back: A file-like rasping organ in the mouth for feeding; found in molluscs.

cards.front: In molluscs, what are the functions of the feather-like gills in the mantle cavity?
cards.back: Respiratory and excretory functions.

cards.front: Match: Pila, Pinctada, Sepia, Loligo, Octopus.
cards.back: • Pila: apple snail • Pinctada: pearl oyster • Sepia: cuttlefish • Loligo: squid • Octopus: devil fish
cards.hint: Trap: cuttlefish and devil fish are NOT fishes

cards.front: Which system is the distinctive feature of echinoderms and what are its functions?
cards.back: Water vascular system: locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration.

cards.front: Which organ system is absent in echinoderms?
cards.back: Excretory system

cards.front: Match: Asterias, Echinus, Antedon, Cucumaria, Ophiura.
cards.back: • Asterias: star fish • Echinus: sea urchin • Antedon: sea lily • Cucumaria: sea cucumber • Ophiura: brittle star

cards.front: Name the three fundamental characters of chordates.
cards.back: • Notochord • Dorsal hollow nerve cord • Paired pharyngeal gill slits

cards.front: Chordates vs non-chordates: position of heart and nerve cord?
cards.back: • Chordates: heart ventral, nerve cord dorsal, hollow, single • Non-chordates: heart dorsal (if present), nerve cord ventral, solid, double

cards.front: Urochordata vs Cephalochordata: where is the notochord?
cards.back: • Urochordata: only in larval tail • Cephalochordata: from head to tail, persists throughout life

cards.front: Give three urochordates and one cephalochordate.
cards.back: • Urochordates: Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum • Cephalochordate: Branchiostoma (amphioxus or lancelet)

cards.front: Why are all vertebrates chordates but not all chordates vertebrates?
cards.back: In vertebrates the notochord is replaced by a vertebral column in the adult; other chordates lack a vertebral column.

cards.front: Cyclostomes: number of gill slits and nature of mouth?
cards.back: 6–15 pairs of gill slits; sucking, circular mouth without jaws.

cards.front: Cyclostomes: where do they spawn and what happens after spawning?
cards.back: Marine, but migrate to fresh water to spawn; adults die within a few days, and larvae return to the ocean after metamorphosis.

cards.front: Why must cartilaginous fishes swim constantly?
cards.back: They lack an air bladder, so they swim constantly to avoid sinking.

cards.front: Which cartilaginous fish has electric organs, and which has a poison sting?
cards.back: • Electric organs: Torpedo • Poison sting: Trygon

cards.front: In male cartilaginous fishes, which structures bear claspers?
cards.back: Pelvic fins

cards.front: Bony fishes: number of gill pairs and what covers them?
cards.back: Four pairs of gills, covered by an operculum on each side.
cards.hint: Cartilaginous fishes: no operculum

cards.front: Which amphibian is limbless?
cards.back: Ichthyophis

cards.front: Which reptile has a four-chambered heart?
cards.back: Crocodiles; other reptiles usually have a three-chambered heart.

cards.front: Match: Chelone, Testudo, Calotes, Hemidactylus.
cards.back: • Chelone: turtle • Testudo: tortoise • Calotes: garden lizard • Hemidactylus: wall lizard

cards.front: Name the three poisonous snakes given in NCERT.
cards.back: Naja (cobra), Bangarus (krait), Vipera (viper)

cards.front: Which is the only skin gland in birds?
cards.back: The oil gland at the base of the tail.

cards.front: What is the most unique mammalian characteristic?
cards.back: Presence of mammary glands (milk-producing).

cards.front: Which mammal is oviparous?
cards.back: Ornithorhynchus (platypus)

cards.front: From which part of the embryo does the primary root develop in most dicots?
cards.back: From the radicle; the primary root and its branches form the tap root system.

cards.front: Which type of root system is seen in monocots like wheat?
cards.back: Fibrous root system: the short-lived primary root is replaced by many roots arising from the base of the stem.

cards.front: What are adventitious roots? Give 3 examples of plants that have them.
cards.back: Roots arising from parts of the plant other than the radicle. • Grass • Monstera • Banyan tree

cards.front: Give 2 examples of tap roots and 1 example of adventitious roots swollen for food storage.
cards.back: • Tap roots: carrot, turnip • Adventitious roots: sweet potato
cards.hint: Trap: sweet potato is a root; potato is a stem.

cards.front: What are the hanging structures that support a banyan tree called?
cards.back: Prop roots: adventitious roots that grow down from branches to support the tree.

cards.front: Which roots arise from the lower nodes of maize and sugarcane stems?
cards.back: Stilt roots, which give mechanical support.
cards.hint: Maize and sugarcane stand on stilts.

cards.front: What are pneumatophores and which plant has them?
cards.back: Roots that grow vertically up out of the ground to get oxygen for respiration. Example: Rhizophora growing in swampy areas.

cards.front: From which part of the embryo does the stem develop?
cards.back: From the plumule. The stem bears nodes and internodes.
cards.hint: Radicle gives root, plumule gives shoot.

cards.front: Name 4 plants whose underground stems are modified to store food.
cards.back: • Potato • Ginger • Turmeric • Zaminkand • Colocasia
cards.hint: Potato has eyes (nodes with buds), so it is a stem.

cards.front: Stem tendrils develop from which buds? Give 2 examples.
cards.back: From axillary buds; slender and spirally coiled for climbing. • Cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon, grapevine
cards.hint: Trap: pea tendrils are modified leaves, not stem.

cards.front: Thorns of Citrus and Bougainvillea are modifications of what?
cards.back: Axillary buds of the stem, modified into woody, straight, pointed thorns that protect from browsing animals.
cards.hint: Thorn = stem; spine of cactus = leaf.

cards.front: In Opuntia and Euphorbia, which organ does photosynthesis?
cards.back: The stem: flattened in Opuntia, fleshy and cylindrical in Euphorbia; it contains chlorophyll and carries out photosynthesis.

cards.front: In which two plants does a slender lateral branch arch downward from the stem base and root on touching the ground?
cards.back: Mint and jasmine.

cards.front: Which aquatic plants have a lateral branch with short internodes, each node bearing a leaf rosette and a tuft of roots?
cards.back: Pistia and Eichhornia.

cards.front: In which plants do lateral branches grow horizontally under soil from the stem base and then emerge obliquely as leafy shoots?
cards.back: Banana, pineapple and Chrysanthemum.

cards.front: What is a pulvinus and in which plants is it found?
cards.back: A swollen leaf base, found in some leguminous plants.

cards.front: What is the key feature that tells a leaf from a leaflet of a compound leaf?
cards.back: A bud is present in the axil of the petiole of a leaf, but not in the axil of leaflets.

cards.front: Reticulate vs parallel venation: which plant group shows each?
cards.back: • Reticulate (network of veinlets): dicots • Parallel (veins run parallel): most monocots

cards.front: Give one example each of a pinnately compound and a palmately compound leaf.
cards.back: • Pinnately compound: neem • Palmately compound: silk cotton
cards.hint: Palm = leaflets from one point at petiole tip.

cards.front: Match phyllotaxy type to example: alternate, opposite, whorled.
cards.back: • Alternate: china rose, mustard, sunflower • Opposite: Calotropis, guava • Whorled: Alstonia
cards.hint: Whorled = more than 2 leaves per node.

cards.front: Name the leaf modification in pea, in cacti and in onion.
cards.back: • Pea: tendrils for climbing • Cacti: spines for defence • Onion, garlic: fleshy leaves storing food

cards.front: In Australian acacia, which part takes over photosynthesis?
cards.back: The petiole; it expands and turns green, as the leaves are small and short-lived.

cards.front: Racemose vs cymose inflorescence: key difference?
cards.back: • Racemose: main axis keeps growing; flowers lateral, in acropetal order • Cymose: main axis ends in a flower; flowers in basipetal order
cards.hint: Cymose: oldest flower at the tip.

cards.front: What is a perianth? Give an example.
cards.back: When calyx and corolla are not distinct, they are called perianth, as in lily.

cards.front: Give 3 examples of actinomorphic flowers.
cards.back: Mustard, datura, chilli: can be divided into two equal halves through any radial plane.

cards.front: Give 3 examples of zygomorphic flowers.
cards.back: Pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia: divisible into two similar halves in only one vertical plane.
cards.hint: Zygo = yoke: only one plane of symmetry.

cards.front: Which flower is given by NCERT as an example of an asymmetric flower?
cards.back: Canna: cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane.

cards.front: Hypogynous flower: ovary position and 3 examples?
cards.back: Gynoecium at the highest position; ovary superior. • Mustard, china rose, brinjal

cards.front: Give 3 examples of perigynous flowers. What is the ovary called?
cards.back: Plum, rose, peach; ovary is half inferior.
cards.hint: Rose-family fruits: plum, peach, rose.

cards.front: Give 3 examples of epigynous flowers.
cards.back: Guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower; ovary is inferior.

cards.front: Match aestivation to example: valvate, twisted, imbricate.
cards.back: • Valvate: Calotropis • Twisted: china rose, lady's finger, cotton • Imbricate: Cassia, gulmohur

cards.front: Name the petals of a vexillary (papilionaceous) corolla in pea.
cards.back: • Standard (vexillum): 1 largest • Wings (alae): 2 lateral • Keel (carina): 2 smallest, anterior, enclosing stamens and pistil

cards.front: Epipetalous vs epiphyllous stamens: give an example of each.
cards.back: • Epipetalous (attached to petals): brinjal • Epiphyllous (attached to perianth): lily

cards.front: Match stamen union to example: monoadelphous, diadelphous, polyadelphous.
cards.back: • Monoadelphous (one bundle): china rose • Diadelphous (two bundles): pea • Polyadelphous (many bundles): Citrus

cards.front: Apocarpous vs syncarpous gynoecium: give examples.
cards.back: • Apocarpous (free carpels): lotus, rose • Syncarpous (fused carpels): mustard, tomato

cards.front: Which placentation is seen in pea, and in china rose, tomato and lemon?
cards.back: • Pea: marginal • China rose, tomato, lemon: axile

cards.front: Which placentation is seen in mustard and Argemone? What becomes two-chambered in it?
cards.back: Parietal; the one-chambered ovary becomes two-chambered by a false septum.

cards.front: Free central vs basal placentation: give examples.
cards.back: • Free central (ovules on central axis, no septa): Dianthus, primrose • Basal (single ovule at base): sunflower, marigold

cards.front: What is a parthenocarpic fruit?
cards.back: A fruit formed without fertilisation of the ovary.

cards.front: Mango and coconut fruits are of which type, and from what kind of ovary?
cards.back: Drupe; develops from a monocarpellary superior ovary and is one-seeded.

cards.front: Mesocarp in mango vs coconut?
cards.back: • Mango: fleshy, edible mesocarp • Coconut: fibrous mesocarp

cards.front: Name the two layers of the seed coat in a dicot seed.
cards.back: Outer testa and inner tegmen.

cards.front: Give 1 example of an endospermic dicot seed and 3 of non-endospermic seeds.
cards.back: • Endospermic: castor • Non-endospermic: bean, gram, pea

cards.front: Monocot seeds are generally endospermic. Which is the NCERT exception?
cards.back: Orchids, whose seeds are non-endospermic.
cards.hint: Trap: castor is endospermic but is a dicot.

cards.front: In a maize grain, what is the aleurone layer?
cards.back: A proteinous layer separating the outer covering of the endosperm from the embryo.

cards.front: In a monocot seed, what are the scutellum, coleoptile and coleorhiza?
cards.back: • Scutellum: the single large shield-shaped cotyledon • Coleoptile: sheath over plumule • Coleorhiza: sheath over radicle
cards.hint: Rhiza = root.

cards.front: Fabaceae: androecium, ovary and placentation?
cards.back: • Stamens 10, diadelphous • Ovary superior, monocarpellary, unilocular • Marginal placentation
cards.hint: Diadelphous in pea: (9)+1 stamens.

cards.front: Fabaceae: name the fruit type and seed type.
cards.back: Fruit: legume; seed: one to many, non-endospermic.

cards.front: Fabaceae: name the sources of dye, fibre and medicine listed in NCERT.
cards.back: • Dye: Indigofera • Fibre: sunhemp • Medicine: muliathi

cards.front: Solanaceae: gynoecium and placentation?
cards.back: Bicarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary, bilocular; carpels obliquely placed; axile placentation on a swollen placenta.
cards.hint: Trap: Solanaceae is bicarpellary; Liliaceae is tricarpellary.

cards.front: Solanaceae: androecium, fruit and seed type?
cards.back: • Stamens 5, epipetalous • Fruit: berry or capsule • Seeds many, endospermous

cards.front: Solanaceae: give its uses as medicine, fumigatory and ornamental.
cards.back: • Medicine: belladonna, ashwagandha • Fumigatory: tobacco • Ornamental: petunia

cards.front: Liliaceae: describe the perianth and androecium.
cards.back: • Perianth: tepals six (3+3), often united into a tube; valvate • Stamens six (3+3), epitepalous
cards.hint: Epitepalous = stamens on tepals.

cards.front: Liliaceae: gynoecium and fruit?
cards.back: Tricarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary, trilocular, axile placentation. Fruit: capsule, rarely berry.

cards.front: Which plant of Liliaceae is the source of colchicine?
cards.back: Colchicum autumnale.

cards.front: Where are apical meristems located and what growth do they cause?
cards.back: At the tips of roots and shoots; they produce primary tissues (increase in length).

cards.front: What is intercalary meristem and where is it found?
cards.back: Meristem lying between mature tissues; found in grasses.

cards.front: What is the role of intercalary meristem in grasses?
cards.back: It helps regenerate parts removed by grazing herbivores.

cards.front: How are axillary buds formed?
cards.back: From cells left behind by the shoot apical meristem during leaf formation and stem elongation; they lie in the axils of leaves.

cards.front: Name 3 examples of lateral (secondary) meristems.
cards.back: • Fascicular vascular cambium • Interfascicular cambium • Cork cambium
cards.hint: Lateral meristems are cylindrical and increase girth.

cards.front: Primary vs secondary meristem: which appears early in plant life?
cards.back: • Primary (apical, intercalary): appear early and form the primary plant body • Secondary (lateral): appear later, cause increase in girth

cards.front: What is a permanent tissue?
cards.back: Cells that have become structurally and functionally specialised and lost the ability to divide.

cards.front: Simple vs complex permanent tissue?
cards.back: • Simple: one type of cell (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) • Complex: more than one type of cell (xylem, phloem)

cards.front: List 3 functions of parenchyma.
cards.back: • Photosynthesis • Storage • Secretion

cards.front: Where does collenchyma occur and why are its corners thick?
cards.back: In layers below the epidermis of dicots; corners thickened by deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin.
cards.hint: Trap: collenchyma walls are NOT lignified.

cards.front: What is the main function of collenchyma?
cards.back: Mechanical support to growing parts such as young stem and petiole of a leaf.

cards.front: Sclerenchyma: wall nature and state at maturity?
cards.back: Thick, lignified walls with few or numerous pits; cells usually dead and without protoplasts.

cards.front: Fibres vs sclereids: key difference in shape?
cards.back: • Fibres: elongated, pointed, generally in groups • Sclereids: spherical, oval or cylindrical, highly thickened, very narrow lumen
cards.hint: Sclereids = stone cells.

cards.front: Where are sclereids commonly found? Give 3 locations.
cards.back: • Fruit walls of nuts • Pulp of guava, pear, sapota • Seed coats of legumes; leaves of tea
cards.hint: Gritty feel of guava pulp = sclereids.

cards.front: Name the 4 elements of xylem.
cards.back: • Tracheids • Vessels • Xylem fibres • Xylem parenchyma

cards.front: Which xylem element is a characteristic feature of angiosperms?
cards.back: Vessels.

cards.front: Which is the only living element of xylem, and what does it store?
cards.back: Xylem parenchyma; stores food as starch or fat, and substances like tannins.

cards.front: Which cells carry out radial conduction of water in xylem?
cards.back: Ray parenchymatous cells.
cards.hint: Ray = radial.

cards.front: Protoxylem vs metaxylem?
cards.back: • Protoxylem: first-formed primary xylem • Metaxylem: later-formed primary xylem

cards.front: Endarch vs exarch xylem: arrangement and location?
cards.back: • Endarch (stems): protoxylem towards centre (pith) • Exarch (roots): protoxylem towards periphery
cards.hint: Exarch = protoxylem exterior, in roots.

cards.front: Name the 4 elements of phloem in angiosperms.
cards.back: • Sieve tube elements • Companion cells • Phloem parenchyma • Phloem fibres

cards.front: What replaces sieve tubes and companion cells in gymnosperm phloem?
cards.back: Sieve cells and albuminous cells.

cards.front: A mature sieve tube element lacks a nucleus. What controls its functions?
cards.back: The nucleus of the companion cell.
cards.hint: Sieve tube: no nucleus, but it is a living cell.

cards.front: What are the perforated end walls of sieve tube elements called?
cards.back: Sieve plates.

cards.front: How are companion cells connected to sieve tube elements?
cards.back: By pit fields in their common longitudinal walls; this helps maintain the pressure gradient in sieve tubes.

cards.front: Which phloem element is absent in most monocots?
cards.back: Phloem parenchyma.
cards.hint: Trap: monocots lack phloem parenchyma, not companion cells.

cards.front: What does phloem parenchyma store?
cards.back: Food material and substances like resins, latex and mucilage.

cards.front: What are bast fibres? Name 3 commercial sources.
cards.back: Phloem fibres, generally absent in primary phloem. • Jute, flax, hemp

cards.front: Name the 3 tissue systems of plants.
cards.back: • Epidermal • Ground (fundamental) • Vascular (conducting)

cards.front: In which organ is the cuticle absent?
cards.back: In roots.

cards.front: Shape of guard cells in dicots vs grasses?
cards.back: • Dicots: bean-shaped • Grasses: dumb-bell shaped
cards.hint: Grass = dumb-bell.

cards.front: What makes up the stomatal apparatus?
cards.back: Stomatal aperture, guard cells and surrounding subsidiary cells.

cards.front: Root hairs vs trichomes: cell number?
cards.back: • Root hairs: unicellular elongations of epidermal cells • Trichomes (on stem): usually multicellular, may be secretory

cards.front: What is the ground tissue in leaves called?
cards.back: Mesophyll; thin-walled, chloroplast-containing cells.

cards.front: Open vs closed vascular bundles: key difference and examples?
cards.back: • Open: cambium present between xylem and phloem (dicot stems) • Closed: no cambium (monocots)

cards.front: Radial vs conjoint vascular bundles: where is each found?
cards.back: • Radial (xylem and phloem on different radii): roots • Conjoint (on same radius): stems and leaves
cards.hint: In conjoint bundles, phloem lies on the outer side.

cards.front: What are Casparian strips made of and where are they found?
cards.back: Deposits of water-impermeable, waxy suberin on the tangential and radial walls of endodermal cells of root.

cards.front: What arises from the pericycle of a root?
cards.back: Lateral roots and the vascular cambium during secondary growth.

cards.front: How many xylem bundles does a dicot root usually have?
cards.back: Two to four xylem and phloem patches.
cards.hint: Diarch to tetrarch; monocot roots are polyarch.

cards.front: What is conjunctive tissue in a root?
cards.back: Parenchyma lying between the xylem and phloem patches.

cards.front: Monocot root vs dicot root: 2 key differences.
cards.back: • Monocot root has more than six xylem bundles (polyarch) • Monocot root has a large, well-developed pith; no secondary growth

cards.front: What is the hypodermis of a dicot stem made of?
cards.back: Collenchyma, a few layers below the epidermis, giving mechanical strength to the young stem.
cards.hint: Trap: monocot stem hypodermis is sclerenchymatous.

cards.front: Why is the endodermis of a dicot stem called the starch sheath?
cards.back: Its cells are rich in starch grains.

cards.front: Describe the pericycle of a dicot stem.
cards.back: On the inner side of endodermis, present as semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma.

cards.front: Describe the vascular bundles of a dicot stem.
cards.back: Arranged in a ring; conjoint, open, with endarch protoxylem.
cards.hint: Ring of bundles = dicot stem.

cards.front: Describe the vascular bundles of a monocot stem.
cards.back: Scattered, conjoint and closed, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath; peripheral bundles smaller than central ones.

cards.front: Name 2 features of monocot stem vascular bundles besides being closed.
cards.back: • Phloem parenchyma absent • Water-containing cavities present within the bundles

cards.front: In a dorsiventral leaf, which surface bears more stomata?
cards.back: The abaxial (lower) epidermis; the adaxial (upper) may even lack stomata.

cards.front: Palisade vs spongy parenchyma: position and cell shape?
cards.back: • Palisade: adaxial side, elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel • Spongy: below palisade, oval or round, loosely arranged with air spaces

cards.front: In a dicot leaf, what surrounds the vascular bundles?
cards.back: A layer of thick-walled bundle sheath cells.

cards.front: Isobilateral leaf: how does it differ from a dorsiventral leaf?
cards.back: • Stomata on both surfaces • Mesophyll not differentiated into palisade and spongy
cards.hint: Iso = equal on both sides.

cards.front: What are bulliform cells and what do they do?
cards.back: Large, empty, colourless adaxial epidermal cells in grasses; they become flaccid under water stress, rolling the leaf inward to reduce water loss.
cards.hint: Bulliform cells let grass leaves roll up in drought.

cards.front: How is parallel venation reflected in a monocot leaf section?
cards.back: Vascular bundles are of near-similar size, except in main veins.

cards.front: Name the 4 basic types of animal tissues.
cards.back: • Epithelial • Connective • Muscular • Neural

cards.front: What are the two types of epithelium based on number of cell layers?
cards.back: • Simple: single layer, lines body cavities, ducts, tubes • Compound: two or more layers, mainly protective

cards.front: Where is squamous epithelium found? Give 2 examples.
cards.back: Single thin layer of flattened cells. • Walls of blood vessels • Air sacs of lungs
cards.hint: Squamous = flat = good for diffusion.

cards.front: Where is cuboidal epithelium found and what are its main functions?
cards.back: In ducts of glands and tubular parts of nephrons; main functions are secretion and absorption.

cards.front: What is the brush border in the proximal convoluted tubule of nephron?
cards.back: Microvilli on cuboidal epithelial cells.
cards.hint: Brush border = microvilli, increases absorptive surface.

cards.front: Where is columnar epithelium found?
cards.back: Lining of stomach and intestine; helps in secretion and absorption. Microvilli present on free surface in intestine.

cards.front: Where is ciliated epithelium found and what does it do?
cards.back: Inner surface of hollow organs like bronchioles and fallopian tubes; cilia move particles or mucus in a specific direction.

cards.front: Give an example each of unicellular and multicellular glands.
cards.back: • Unicellular: goblet cells of alimentary canal • Multicellular: salivary gland

cards.front: Exocrine vs endocrine glands: key difference?
cards.back: • Exocrine: release products through ducts • Endocrine: ductless, secrete hormones directly into the fluid bathing the gland

cards.front: Name 4 products of exocrine glands listed in NCERT.
cards.back: Any four: mucus, saliva, earwax, oil, milk, digestive enzymes and other cell products.
cards.hint: Trap: hormones are endocrine products.

cards.front: Where is compound epithelium found? Give 3 locations.
cards.back: • Dry surface of skin • Moist surface of buccal cavity, pharynx • Inner lining of ducts of salivary glands and pancreas

cards.front: Name the 3 types of cell junctions and the role of each.
cards.back: • Tight: stop substances leaking across a tissue • Adhering: cement neighbouring cells together • Gap: connect cytoplasm for rapid transfer of ions, small molecules
cards.hint: Gap = gateway for communication.

cards.front: Which is the most abundant and widely distributed tissue in the body of complex animals?
cards.back: Connective tissue.

cards.front: Which connective tissue lacks fibres secreted by its cells?
cards.back: Blood. In all other connective tissues, cells secrete fibres of collagen or elastin.
cards.hint: Blood is the odd one out: fluid matrix, no secreted fibres.

cards.front: Name 3 cell types in areolar tissue. Where is it found?
cards.back: Fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells; found beneath the skin, serving as a support framework for epithelium.

cards.front: What is the function of adipose tissue and where is it located?
cards.back: Stores fats; located mainly beneath the skin. Excess nutrients are converted into fats and stored here.

cards.front: Tendons vs ligaments: what does each join?
cards.back: • Tendons: skeletal muscle to bone • Ligaments: bone to bone
cards.hint: Ligament = Link bone-bone.

cards.front: Tendons and ligaments are examples of which type of connective tissue?
cards.back: Dense regular connective tissue (collagen fibres in parallel rows).

cards.front: Give an example of dense irregular connective tissue.
cards.back: Skin: fibroblasts and fibres (mostly collagen) oriented differently.

cards.front: Where are chondrocytes found?
cards.back: In small cavities within the matrix secreted by them, in cartilage.

cards.front: Where is cartilage present in adult vertebrates? Give 3 sites.
cards.back: • Tip of nose • Outer ear joints • Between adjacent bones of vertebral column, limbs and hands
cards.hint: Most cartilage of the embryo is replaced by bone in adults.

cards.front: What makes the bone matrix hard and non-pliable?
cards.back: A ground substance rich in calcium salts and collagen fibres.

cards.front: Where are osteocytes located?
cards.back: In spaces called lacunae in the bone matrix.
cards.hint: Lacunae house both osteocytes (bone) and chondrocytes (cartilage).

cards.front: Skeletal muscle: appearance and an NCERT example?
cards.back: Striated, closely attached to bones. Example: biceps.

cards.front: Smooth muscle: shape, striations and location?
cards.back: Fusiform (tapering ends), no striations, involuntary. Found in walls of blood vessels, stomach, intestine.
cards.hint: Smooth = visceral = involuntary.

cards.front: What allows cardiac muscle cells to contract as a unit?
cards.back: Communication junctions (intercalated discs) at some fusion points of plasma membranes.

cards.front: Which muscle type is found only in the heart and has a branching pattern?
cards.back: Cardiac muscle: striated, involuntary, branched.
cards.hint: Trap: cardiac muscle is striated yet involuntary.

cards.front: What fraction of neural tissue volume is made up of neuroglia?
cards.back: More than one-half of the volume; neuroglia protect and support neurons.

cards.front: What is the scientific name of the common Indian frog given in NCERT?
cards.back: Rana tigrina.

cards.front: Frog: what are aestivation and hibernation?
cards.back: • Aestivation: summer sleep • Hibernation: winter sleep Both protect from extreme heat and cold.
cards.hint: Aestas = summer.

cards.front: Why is the skin of a frog slippery? How does a frog get water?
cards.back: Due to mucus; skin kept moist. Frog never drinks water but absorbs it through the skin.

cards.front: Which body parts are absent in an adult frog?
cards.back: Neck and tail; body has only head and trunk.

cards.front: What protects the frog's eyes in water?
cards.back: The nictitating membrane.

cards.front: Frog: how many digits on forelimbs vs hindlimbs?
cards.back: • Forelimbs: four digits • Hindlimbs: five digits, larger, muscular, webbed for swimming
cards.hint: Fore 4, hind 5.

cards.front: Name 2 features that distinguish a male frog from a female.
cards.back: • Vocal sacs for producing sound • Copulatory pad on the first digit of forelimbs

cards.front: Why is the alimentary canal of frog short?
cards.back: Frogs are carnivores, so the intestine is short.

cards.front: What is chyme in frog digestion?
cards.back: Partially digested food leaving the stomach (digested by HCl and gastric juices), passing to the duodenum.

cards.front: Frog respiration in water vs on land?
cards.back: • In water: through skin (cutaneous) • On land: buccal cavity, skin and lungs (pulmonary)
cards.hint: During aestivation and hibernation, exchange is through skin only.

cards.front: How many chambers does the frog heart have?
cards.back: Three: two atria and one ventricle; covered by pericardium.
cards.hint: Two atria + one ventricle; humans have four chambers.

cards.front: In the frog heart, what is the sinus venosus and where does it open?
cards.back: A triangular structure that joins the right atrium; it receives blood through the major veins called vena cava.

cards.front: The frog's ventricle opens into which structure?
cards.back: A sac-like conus arteriosus on the ventral side of the heart.

cards.front: Name the 2 special venous connections in frog circulation.
cards.back: • Hepatic portal system (liver–intestine) • Renal portal system (kidney–lower body)

cards.front: Frog RBCs: nucleated or not?
cards.back: Nucleated; contain the red pigment haemoglobin.
cards.hint: Trap: mammalian RBCs lack a nucleus; frog RBCs have one.

cards.front: What nitrogenous waste does a frog excrete?
cards.back: Urea; the frog is ureotelic.

cards.front: Frog: how do the ureters differ in males and females?
cards.back: • Male: ureters act as urinogenital ducts opening into cloaca • Female: ureters and oviducts open separately in the cloaca

cards.front: How many pairs of cranial nerves arise from the frog brain?
cards.back: Ten pairs.
cards.hint: Trap: humans have 12 pairs, frog 10.

cards.front: Frog brain: what does the forebrain include?
cards.back: Olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres and unpaired diencephalon.

cards.front: Through which opening does the medulla oblongata pass into the spinal cord in frog?
cards.back: Foramen magnum.

cards.front: Which sense organs of the frog are well organised (not just cellular aggregations)?
cards.back: Eyes and internal ears.

cards.front: What two functions do the ears of a frog serve?
cards.back: Hearing and balancing (equilibrium).

cards.front: What holds the testes of frog to the kidneys?
cards.back: A double fold of peritoneum called mesorchium, attaching the testes to the upper part of kidneys.

cards.front: In male frog, how many vasa efferentia arise from testes and where do they open?
cards.back: 10–12 vasa efferentia; they enter the kidneys and open into Bidder's canal.
cards.hint: Bidder's canal links to the urinogenital duct.

cards.front: How many ova can a mature female frog lay at a time?
Frog: type of fertilisation and name of the larval stage?
cards.back: External fertilisation in water; larva is the tadpole, which turns into adult by metamorphosis.

cards.front: Give 2 ways frogs are useful to humans.
cards.back: • Eat insects and protect crops • Help maintain ecological balance; legs eaten as food in some countries

cards.front: Which German botanist concluded in 1838 that plants are composed of different kinds of cells?
cards.back: Matthias Schleiden.

cards.front: Which scientist concluded that the presence of a cell wall is unique to plant cells?
cards.back: Theodore Schwann (1839), a zoologist; he also reported the thin outer layer of animal cells (plasma membrane).
cards.hint: Trap: Schwann was a zoologist, Schleiden a botanist.

cards.front: Who modified the cell theory by stating Omnis cellula-e cellula, and when?
cards.back: Rudolf Virchow in 1855: new cells arise from pre-existing cells.
cards.hint: Virchow 1855: cells from cells.

cards.front: State the two points of the cell theory as understood today.
cards.back: • All living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells • All cells arise from pre-existing cells

cards.front: Which cell organelle is NOT membrane-bound and is found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes?
cards.back: Ribosome.

cards.front: Which non-membrane-bound organelle is present in animal cells but absent in almost all plant cells?
cards.back: Centriole.

cards.front: Give the sizes of Mycoplasma, a typical bacterium and a human RBC.
cards.back: • Mycoplasma: 0.3 µm (smallest cell) • Bacteria: 3–5 µm • Human RBC: about 7.0 µm
cards.hint: Mycoplasma is the smallest cell; RBC about 7 µm.

cards.front: Which is the largest isolated single cell, and which cells are among the longest?
cards.back: • Largest: egg of ostrich • Longest: nerve cells

cards.front: Name the four groups of organisms with prokaryotic cells.
cards.back: Bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma and PPLO (pleuropneumonia-like organisms).

cards.front: What is a plasmid and what phenotype can it give to bacteria?
cards.back: Small circular DNA outside the genomic DNA; gives unique traits like resistance to antibiotics.
cards.hint: Plasmids are used to monitor bacterial transformation with foreign DNA.

cards.front: Name the three layers of the bacterial cell envelope from outside to inside.
cards.back: Glycocalyx → cell wall → plasma membrane.

cards.front: Slime layer vs capsule in bacteria?
cards.back: Both are forms of glycocalyx. • Slime layer: loose sheath • Capsule: thick and tough

cards.front: What is a mesosome and give 2 of its functions?
cards.back:
An infolding of the plasma membrane in prokaryotes (vesicles, tubules, lamellae).
• Cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells
• Respiration, secretion; increases surface area

cards.front: What are chromatophores in cyanobacteria?
cards.back: Membranous extensions into the cytoplasm containing pigments.

cards.front: Bacterial flagellum: name its 3 parts.
cards.back: • Filament (longest part) • Hook • Basal body

cards.front: Pili vs fimbriae: how do they differ in structure, and which helps attachment?
cards.back: • Pili: elongated tubular structures of special protein • Fimbriae: small bristle-like fibres; help attach bacteria to rocks in streams and to host tissues
cards.hint: Trap: pili and fimbriae do NOT play a role in motility.

cards.front: What are the subunits and size of the prokaryotic ribosome?
cards.back: 70S: 50S + 30S subunits; about 15 nm by 20 nm.
cards.hint: S values do not add: 50S + 30S = 70S.

cards.front: What is a polysome?
cards.back: Several ribosomes attached to a single mRNA, forming a chain; they translate the mRNA into proteins.

cards.front: Name 3 types of inclusion bodies in prokaryotes and the groups with gas vacuoles.
cards.back: • Phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules, glycogen granules • Gas vacuoles: blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria

cards.front: In human erythrocyte membrane, what are the proportions of protein and lipid?
cards.back: About 52% protein and 40% lipids.

cards.front: How are lipids arranged in the plasma membrane?
cards.back: As a bilayer: polar heads towards the outer sides, hydrophobic tails towards the inner part.

cards.front: Who proposed the fluid mosaic model and in which year?
cards.back: Singer and Nicolson, 1972.

cards.front: According to the fluid mosaic model, what allows lateral movement of proteins?
cards.back: The quasi-fluid nature of lipids in the bilayer.

cards.front: Passive vs active transport across the plasma membrane?
cards.back: • Passive: along concentration gradient, no energy (e.g. diffusion, osmosis) • Active: against gradient, uses ATP (e.g. Na+/K+ pump)

cards.front: Name 3 components of the algal cell wall.
cards.back: Cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals like calcium carbonate.

cards.front: What is the middle lamella made of?
cards.back: Mainly calcium pectate; it holds neighbouring plant cells together.
cards.hint: Calcium pectate is the cement between plant cells.

cards.front: Which organelles are included in the endomembrane system?
cards.back: ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes, vacuoles.
cards.hint: Trap: mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are NOT part of it.

cards.front: RER vs SER: main function of each?
cards.back: • RER: protein synthesis and secretion (ribosomes attached) • SER: major site of lipid synthesis; in animal cells, steroidal hormones
cards.hint: Rough = ribosomes = proteins; smooth = lipids.

cards.front: Who first observed the Golgi apparatus and when?
cards.back: Camillo Golgi in 1898, near the nucleus.

cards.front: Golgi cisternae: what are the cis and trans faces called?
cards.back: • Cis: forming face • Trans: maturing face
cards.hint: Cis faces the ER; trans faces the plasma membrane.

cards.front: Which molecules are formed in the Golgi apparatus?
cards.back: Glycoproteins and glycolipids.

cards.front: How are lysosomes formed and what is the pH of their interior?
cards.back: Formed by packaging in the Golgi apparatus; enzymes are active at acidic pH.

cards.front: What kinds of enzymes do lysosomes contain?
cards.back: Hydrolytic enzymes: lipases, proteases, carbohydrases (acid hydrolases).

cards.front: What is the tonoplast and how much of a plant cell can the vacuole occupy?
cards.back: The single membrane bounding the vacuole; the vacuole can occupy up to 90% of cell volume.

cards.front: Which vacuole is important for excretion and osmoregulation in Amoeba?
cards.back: Contractile vacuole.

cards.front: Give the diameter and length range of a mitochondrion.
cards.back: • Diameter: 0.2–1.0 µm (average 0.5 µm) • Length: 1.0–4.1 µm

cards.front: What does the mitochondrial matrix contain?
cards.back: A single circular DNA, a few RNA molecules, 70S ribosomes and components for protein synthesis.

cards.front: Amyloplasts, elaioplasts, aleuroplasts: what does each store?
cards.back: • Amyloplasts: starch (e.g. potato) • Elaioplasts: oils and fats • Aleuroplasts: proteins
cards.hint: Aleuro = protein, elaio = oil, amylo = starch.

cards.front: Which pigments give colour to chromoplasts?
cards.back: Fat-soluble carotenoid pigments like carotene and xanthophylls.

cards.front: How many chloroplasts per cell: Chlamydomonas vs mesophyll?
cards.back: • Chlamydomonas: 1 per cell • Mesophyll: 20–40 per cell

cards.front: Where are the enzymes for synthesis of sugar located in the chloroplast?
cards.back: In the stroma.
cards.hint: Trap: not in thylakoids.

cards.front: Who first observed ribosomes as dense particles, and when?
cards.back: George Palade in 1953, using the electron microscope.
cards.hint: Palade 1953; Golgi 1898; Brown 1831.

cards.front: What does S stand for in 70S and 80S ribosomes?
cards.back: Svedberg unit: sedimentation coefficient, an indirect measure of density and size.

cards.front: Name 3 functions of the cytoskeleton.
cards.back: • Mechanical support • Motility • Maintenance of cell shape

cards.front: Describe the arrangement of microtubules in the axoneme of cilia and flagella.
cards.back: 9+2 array: nine doublets of peripheral microtubules and a pair of centrally located microtubules.

cards.front: In a centriole, how are the peripheral fibrils arranged?
cards.back: Nine evenly spaced triplets of tubulin, in a cartwheel organisation.
cards.hint: Cilia: 9 doublets; centriole: 9 triplets.

cards.front: Who first described the nucleus and when?
cards.back: Robert Brown in 1831.

cards.front: Name 2 examples of cells that lack a nucleus.
cards.back: • Erythrocytes of many mammals • Sieve tube cells of vascular plants
cards.hint: Trap: frog RBCs do have a nucleus.

cards.front: What is the nucleolus the site of?
cards.back: Active ribosomal RNA (rRNA) synthesis.
cards.hint: Nucleolus is not membrane-bound.

cards.front: Who named the material of the nucleus stained by basic dyes as chromatin?
cards.back: Flemming.

cards.front: Where is the kinetochore located?
cards.back: On the sides of the centromere as disc-shaped structures.

cards.front: Classify chromosomes by centromere position.
cards.back: • Metacentric: middle • Sub-metacentric: slightly away from middle • Acrocentric: close to one end • Telocentric: terminal

cards.front: What is a satellite on a chromosome?
cards.back: A small fragment formed by a non-staining secondary constriction.

cards.front: What are microbodies and in which cells are they found?
cards.back: Many membrane-bound minute vesicles containing various enzymes, present in both plant and animal cells.

cards.front: Which acid is used to grind living tissue when analysing its organic compounds?
cards.back: Trichloroacetic acid (Cl3CCOOH); the tissue is ground in it with a mortar and pestle to get a thick slurry.

cards.front: When the tissue slurry is strained through cheesecloth, what are the filtrate and retentate called?
cards.back: • Filtrate: acid-soluble pool • Retentate: acid-insoluble fraction
cards.hint: Thousands of small organic compounds stay in the acid-soluble pool.

cards.front: What does the ash left after burning a living tissue contain?
cards.back: Inorganic elements (e.g. Ca, Mg) and inorganic compounds such as sulphate and phosphate.
cards.hint: All carbon compounds are oxidised to gas and lost; only inorganic matter remains.

cards.front: Per NCERT, what is the approximate percentage of carbon by weight in the human body vs Earth's crust?
cards.back: • Human body: 18.5% • Earth's crust: 0.03%

cards.front: Amino acids are substituted methanes. Which four groups occupy the four valencies of the alpha-carbon?
cards.back: • Hydrogen • Carboxyl group • Amino group • Variable R group
cards.hint: Since both amino and carboxyl are on the same (alpha) carbon, they are alpha-amino acids.

cards.front: What is the R group in glycine, alanine and serine?
cards.back: • Glycine: hydrogen • Alanine: methyl group • Serine: hydroxymethyl group

cards.front: Give one NCERT example each of an acidic, a basic and a neutral amino acid.
cards.back: • Acidic: glutamic acid • Basic: lysine • Neutral: valine
cards.hint: Based on the number of amino and carboxyl groups.

cards.front: Name the three aromatic amino acids mentioned in NCERT.
cards.back: Tyrosine, phenylalanine, tryptophan

cards.front: Which property of amino acids gives rise to the zwitterionic form?
cards.back: The ionizable nature of the -NH2 and -COOH groups; hence the structure of an amino acid changes in solutions of different pH.

cards.front: How many carbon atoms do palmitic acid and arachidonic acid have?
cards.back: • Palmitic acid: 16 • Arachidonic acid: 20 (both counts include the carboxyl carbon)
cards.hint: Trap: the count includes the carboxyl carbon.

cards.front: What are monoglycerides, diglycerides and triglycerides?
cards.back: Fatty acids esterified with glycerol; named by the number of fatty acids attached (one, two or three).

cards.front: Why do oils (e.g. gingelly oil) remain liquid in winter?
cards.back: Oils have a lower melting point than fats.

cards.front: Name a phospholipid found in the cell membrane.
cards.back: Lecithin

cards.front: Nucleoside vs nucleotide: what is the difference?
cards.back: • Nucleoside = nitrogen base + sugar • Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate group

cards.front: Give two examples each of nucleosides and nucleotides.
cards.back: • Nucleosides: adenosine, guanosine (also thymidine, uridine, cytidine) • Nucleotides: adenylic acid, thymidylic acid (also guanylic, uridylic, cytidylic acid)
cards.hint: -osine/-idine = nucleoside; -ylic acid = nucleotide.

cards.front: Primary vs secondary metabolites: key difference?
cards.back: • Primary: have identifiable functions in normal physiology • Secondary: role in host not fully known, but many are useful to human welfare

cards.front: Morphine and codeine belong to which class of secondary metabolites?
cards.back: Alkaloids

cards.front: Abrin and ricin are which type of secondary metabolites?
cards.back: Toxins

cards.front: Which secondary metabolite is given as an example of a lectin?
cards.back: Concanavalin A

cards.front: Vinblastin and curcumin are classified as which secondary metabolites?
cards.back: Drugs

cards.front: What molecular weight ranges separate biomicromolecules from biomacromolecules?
cards.back: • Micromolecules: 18 to around 800 daltons • Macromolecules: 10,000 daltons and above

cards.front: Why do lipids come in the acid-insoluble fraction though they are not macromolecules?
cards.back: On grinding, cell membranes break into vesicles that are not water soluble, so lipids separate with the macromolecules.
cards.hint: Lipid molecular weight does not exceed ~800 Da.

cards.front: Give NCERT's % of total cellular mass for proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids and ions.
cards.back: • Proteins: 10-15 • Nucleic acids: 5-7 • Carbohydrates: 3 • Lipids: 2 • Ions: 1
cards.hint: After water, proteins are the most abundant.

cards.front: Per NCERT's table, what is the function of collagen and of GLUT-4?
cards.back: • Collagen: intercellular ground substance • GLUT-4: enables glucose transport into cells

cards.front: Give the function of trypsin, insulin, antibody and receptor proteins.
cards.back: • Trypsin: enzyme • Insulin: hormone • Antibody: fights infectious agents • Receptor: sensory reception (smell, taste, hormone etc.)

cards.front: Which is the most abundant protein in the animal world and in the whole biosphere?
cards.back: • Animal world: collagen • Whole biosphere: RuBisCO
cards.hint: Trap: collagen is NOT the most abundant in the biosphere.

cards.front: Name the storage polysaccharide of plants and of animals.
cards.back: • Plants: starch • Animals: glycogen

cards.front: Inulin is a polymer of which sugar?
cards.back: Fructose
cards.hint: Trap: NOT glucose, unlike starch, glycogen and cellulose.

cards.front: In a polysaccharide chain like glycogen, which end is reducing and which is non-reducing?
cards.back: • Right end: reducing • Left end: non-reducing

cards.front: Why does starch give a blue colour with iodine while cellulose does not?
cards.back: Starch forms helical secondary structures that hold I2 (starch-I2 is blue); cellulose lacks complex helices, so it cannot hold I2.

cards.front: What is the exoskeleton of arthropods made of?
cards.back: Chitin, a complex polysaccharide.

cards.front: Per NCERT, what kinds of building blocks do complex polysaccharides have? Give two examples.
cards.back: Amino-sugars and chemically modified sugars, e.g. glucosamine and N-acetyl galactosamine.

cards.front: What are the three chemically distinct components of a nucleotide?
cards.back: • A heterocyclic compound (nitrogen base) • A monosaccharide (sugar) • Phosphoric acid (phosphate)

cards.front: Which nitrogen bases are substituted purines and which are substituted pyrimidines?
cards.back: • Purines: adenine, guanine • Pyrimidines: cytosine, uracil, thymine
cards.hint: Pure As Gold: purines = A, G.

cards.front: Which sugar is present in DNA and which in RNA?
cards.back: • DNA: 2'-deoxyribose • RNA: ribose

cards.front: What is the primary structure of a protein and what are its two ends called?
cards.back: The sequence of amino acids. First amino acid (left end) = N-terminal; last amino acid (right end) = C-terminal.

cards.front: In the secondary structure of proteins, what type of helix is observed?
cards.back: Only right-handed helices.
cards.hint: Trap: left-handed helices are NOT observed in proteins.

cards.front: NCERT compares the tertiary structure of a protein to what?
cards.back: A hollow woollen ball: the long chain folds upon itself, giving the 3-D view needed for biological activity.

cards.front: Describe the quaternary structure of adult human haemoglobin.
cards.back: 4 subunits: 2 alpha and 2 beta subunits.

cards.front: What are ribozymes?
cards.back: Nucleic acids that behave like enzymes.
cards.hint: Almost all enzymes are proteins; ribozymes are the exception.

cards.front: Up to what temperature are enzymes of thermophilic organisms (hot vents, sulphur springs) stable?
cards.hint: Most enzymes are damaged above about 40°C.

cards.front: How does the rate of a chemical reaction change for every 10°C change in temperature?
cards.back: It doubles (rise) or decreases by half (fall).

cards.front: Carbonic anhydrase: rate of H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> formation without vs with enzyme?
cards.back: • Without: about 200 molecules per hour • With: about 600,000 per second Rate is accelerated about 10 million times.

cards.front: Under anaerobic conditions, what does pyruvic acid form in skeletal muscle vs yeast?
cards.back: • Skeletal muscle: lactic acid • Yeast (fermentation): ethanol

cards.front: Give the sequence of steps in an enzyme's catalytic cycle.
cards.back: • Substrate binds active site • Enzyme changes shape, fitting substrate more tightly • Bonds broken; enzyme-product complex formed • Products released; enzyme free again

cards.front: Effect of low vs high temperature on enzymes?
cards.back: • Low: enzyme temporarily inactive (preserved) • High: enzyme denatured, activity destroyed

cards.front: Why does reaction velocity reach Vmax and not rise further with more substrate?
cards.back: Enzyme molecules are fewer than substrate molecules; after saturation there are no free enzyme molecules to bind extra substrate.

cards.front: Give NCERT's example of competitive inhibition.
cards.back: Malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase; it closely resembles the substrate succinate.
cards.hint: Competitive inhibitors are used to control bacterial pathogens.

cards.front: How many classes are enzymes divided into, and how are they named?
cards.back: 6 classes, each with 4-13 subclasses, named by a four-digit number.
cards.hint: Order: Oxidoreductases, Transferases, Hydrolases, Lyases, Isomerases, Ligases.

cards.front: What do lyases catalyse?
cards.back: Removal of groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds.

cards.front: What do isomerases and ligases catalyse?
cards.back: • Isomerases: interconversion of optical, geometric or positional isomers • Ligases: linking together of 2 compounds (C-O, C-S, C-N, P-O bonds)

cards.front: Name the three kinds of cofactors.
cards.back: • Prosthetic groups • Co-enzymes • Metal ions

cards.front: Which prosthetic group is present in peroxidase and catalase?
