cards.back: Haem; prosthetic groups are tightly bound to the apoenzyme.

cards.front: Which vitamin is contained in the co-enzymes NAD and NADP?
cards.back: Niacin; co-enzymes bind the apoenzyme only transiently.

cards.front: Which metal ion is the cofactor for carboxypeptidase?
cards.back: Zinc
cards.hint: Removing the cofactor makes the enzyme lose catalytic activity.

cards.front: What is the cell cycle?
cards.back: The sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and eventually divides into two daughter cells.

cards.front: Cell growth vs DNA synthesis during the cell cycle: which is continuous?
cards.back: • Cell growth (cytoplasmic increase): continuous • DNA synthesis: only in one specific stage (S phase)

cards.front: How long does a typical human cell in culture take to complete one cell cycle?
cards.back: About 24 hours

cards.front: How long does the yeast cell cycle take?
cards.back: About 90 minutes

cards.front: In a 24-hour human cell cycle, how long does M phase last?
cards.back: Only about 1 hour.

cards.front: What fraction of the cell cycle duration is spent in interphase?
cards.back: More than 95%

cards.front: Why is calling interphase the 'resting phase' misleading?
cards.back: During interphase the cell is preparing for division: it grows and replicates DNA in an orderly manner.

cards.front: Give the three sub-phases of interphase in order.
cards.hint: G = gap, S = synthesis.

cards.front: What happens in G1 phase?
cards.back: Cell is metabolically active and grows continuously, but does not replicate DNA.

cards.front: During S phase, what happens to DNA amount and chromosome number?
cards.back: • DNA: doubles, 2C → 4C • Chromosome number: no change (2n stays 2n)
cards.hint: Trap: DNA doubles, chromosome number does NOT.

cards.front: In animal cells, what event takes place in the cytoplasm during S phase?
cards.back: The centriole duplicates (while DNA replicates in the nucleus).

cards.front: What happens during G2 phase?
cards.back: Proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis while cell growth continues.

cards.front: What is the quiescent stage (G0)?
cards.back: A stage that cells enter on exiting G1; they remain metabolically active but do not proliferate unless called on to do so.

cards.front: Give NCERT's example of cells in adult animals that do not appear to divide.
cards.back: Heart cells

cards.front: In which cells is mitosis seen in animals vs plants?
cards.back: • Animals: only diploid somatic cells • Plants: both haploid and diploid cells
cards.hint: Trap: plants can divide mitotically even when haploid.

cards.front: Why is mitosis called equational division?
cards.back: The chromosome number in parent and progeny cells is the same.

cards.front: Give the four stages of karyokinesis in order.
cards.back: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase
cards.hint: PMAT

cards.front: Karyokinesis vs cytokinesis?
cards.back: • Karyokinesis: division of the nucleus • Cytokinesis: division of the cytoplasm

cards.front: Which mitotic stage begins with condensation of chromosomal material?
cards.back: Prophase

cards.front: What is the mitotic apparatus made of?
cards.back: Two asters together with the spindle fibres.
cards.hint: Asters = microtubules radiating from each centrosome.

cards.front: Which cell organelles are not seen at the end of prophase?
cards.back: Golgi complexes, ER, nucleolus and the nuclear envelope.

cards.front: Which stage of mitosis is best for studying chromosome morphology?
cards.back: Metaphase, when condensation of chromosomes is complete.

cards.front: What marks the start of metaphase?
cards.back: Complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope.

cards.front: What are kinetochores?
cards.back: Small disc-shaped structures on the surface of centromeres that serve as sites of attachment of spindle fibres.

cards.front: What is the metaphase plate?
cards.back: The plane of alignment of chromosomes at metaphase, at the equator of the spindle.

cards.front: What happens to centromeres and chromatids in mitotic anaphase?
cards.back: Centromeres split; chromatids separate as daughter chromosomes and move to opposite poles.

cards.front: During anaphase movement, which part of the chromosome leads?
cards.back: The centromere leads, with the arms trailing behind.

cards.front: What happens in telophase of mitosis?
cards.back: • Chromosomes cluster at poles and decondense, losing individuality • Nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi and ER reform

cards.front: How does cytokinesis occur in animal cells?
cards.back: By a furrow in the plasma membrane that deepens and joins at the centre, dividing the cytoplasm into two.

cards.front: How does cytokinesis occur in plant cells and in which direction does wall formation proceed?
cards.back: By cell plate formation; wall formation starts in the centre and grows outward to meet the lateral walls.
cards.hint: Trap: centrifugal (centre to periphery), unlike the animal furrow.

cards.front: The cell plate in plant cytokinesis represents which future structure?
cards.back: The middle lamella between the walls of two adjacent cells.

cards.front: What is a syncytium? Give NCERT's example.
cards.back: A multinucleate condition formed when karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis; e.g. liquid endosperm in coconut.

cards.front: Give two significances of mitosis.
cards.back: • Produces diploid daughter cells with identical genetic complement; aids growth • Restores the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio • Cell repair

cards.front: Give examples of cells continuously replaced by mitosis.
cards.back: Cells of the upper layer of epidermis, gut lining and blood cells.

cards.front: Which plant tissues show continuous mitotic growth throughout life?
cards.back: Meristematic tissues: apical and lateral cambium.

cards.front: How many DNA replications and nuclear divisions occur in meiosis?
cards.back: One DNA replication (S phase) and two sequential nuclear/cell divisions.

cards.front: Meiosis forms how many cells and with what ploidy?
cards.back: Four haploid cells.

cards.front: Give the five sub-stages of prophase I in order.
cards.back: Leptotene → Zygotene → Pachytene → Diplotene → Diakinesis
cards.hint: Lazy Zebra Plays Dirty Dance

cards.front: What happens in leptotene?
cards.back: Chromosomes become gradually visible under the light microscope; compaction continues.

cards.front: What is synapsis and in which stage does it occur?
cards.back: Pairing of homologous chromosomes; occurs in zygotene.

cards.front: What complex accompanies synapsis and what is the paired structure called?
cards.back: Synaptonemal complex; the pair of synapsed homologues is a bivalent or tetrad.

cards.front: What are recombination nodules and in which stage do they appear?
cards.back: Sites where crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids; they appear in pachytene.

cards.front: Which enzyme mediates crossing over?
cards.back: Recombinase

cards.front: Crossing over occurs between which chromatids?
cards.back: Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
cards.hint: Trap: NOT between sister chromatids.

cards.front: Which stage is marked by dissolution of the synaptonemal complex and appearance of chiasmata?
cards.back: Diplotene; chiasmata are X-shaped structures at sites of crossovers.

cards.front: In oocytes of some vertebrates, which meiotic stage can last for months or years?
cards.back: Diplotene

cards.front: What is terminalisation of chiasmata and in which stage does it occur?
cards.back: Movement of chiasmata towards chromosome ends; occurs in diakinesis.

cards.front: Which events of diakinesis mark the transition to metaphase I?
cards.back: Spindle is assembled; nucleolus disappears and nuclear envelope breaks down.

cards.front: What aligns on the equatorial plate in metaphase I?
cards.back: Bivalent chromosomes (homologous pairs).
cards.hint: In mitotic metaphase and metaphase II, single chromosomes align instead.

cards.front: Anaphase I vs anaphase II: what separates in each?
cards.back: • Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate; sister chromatids stay joined at centromere • Anaphase II: centromere splits, sister chromatids separate

cards.front: What is the product of telophase I and cytokinesis called?
cards.back: A dyad of cells.

cards.front: What is interkinesis and does DNA replicate during it?
cards.back: The short stage between meiosis I and meiosis II; there is no DNA replication.
cards.hint: Trap: interkinesis is NOT an interphase with S phase.

cards.front: When is prophase II initiated?
cards.back: Immediately after cytokinesis, usually before chromosomes have fully elongated.

cards.front: In metaphase II, spindle microtubules attach to what?
cards.back: Kinetochores of sister chromatids, from opposite poles.

cards.front: Give two significances of meiosis.
cards.back: • Conserves chromosome number across generations in sexually reproducing organisms • Increases genetic variability, important for evolution

cards.front: In the half-leaf experiment, what showed that CO<sub>2</sub> is needed for photosynthesis?
cards.back: The leaf part enclosed with KOH (which absorbs CO2) gave a negative starch test; the exposed part tested positive.

cards.front: What did Joseph Priestley's 1770 bell jar experiments show?
cards.back: A plant restores the air that a burning candle or a breathing mouse damages.
cards.hint: Priestley later discovered oxygen in 1774.

cards.front: Which scientist showed that sunlight is essential and only green parts release oxygen?
cards.back: Jan Ingenhousz

cards.front: What did Julius von Sachs (1854) show?
cards.back: Plants produce glucose, usually stored as starch; the green substance (chlorophyll) lies in chloroplasts.

cards.front: Which alga and organisms did T.W. Engelmann use to describe the first action spectrum?
cards.back: Green alga Cladophora with aerobic bacteria; bacteria gathered in blue and red light regions.

cards.front: Whose work on purple and green bacteria showed that O<sub>2</sub> released in photosynthesis comes from water?
cards.back: Cornelius van Niel
cards.hint: Trap: O<sub>2</sub> comes from H<sub>2</sub>O, NOT CO<sub>2</sub>.

cards.front: In van Niel's photosynthetic bacteria, what was the hydrogen donor and what was released instead of O<sub>2</sub>?
cards.back: Donor: H2S; oxidation product: sulphur or sulphate, not oxygen.

cards.front: Write the balanced equation of photosynthesis as given in NCERT.
cards.back: 6CO2 + 12H2O → C6H12O6 + 6H2O + 6O2 (in light)
cards.hint: 12 water used so that all O<sub>2</sub> released comes from water.

cards.front: In which leaf cells and organelle does photosynthesis mainly occur?
cards.back: Chloroplasts of mesophyll cells.

cards.front: Grana vs stroma: what happens in each?
cards.back: • Grana (membrane system): trap light, make ATP and NADPH • Stroma: enzymatic sugar synthesis (dark reactions)
cards.hint: Trap: 'dark reactions' do not occur in darkness; they depend on light-reaction products.

cards.front: Give the colour of each pigment on a paper chromatogram of leaf pigments.
cards.back: • Chlorophyll a: bright or blue green • Chlorophyll b: yellow green • Xanthophylls: yellow • Carotenoids: yellow to yellow-orange

cards.front: Which is the chief pigment of photosynthesis?
cards.back: Chlorophyll a

cards.front: In which regions of the spectrum does chlorophyll a show maximum absorption?
cards.back: Blue and red regions.

cards.front: What are the two roles of accessory pigments?
cards.back: • Absorb a wider range of wavelengths and pass energy to chlorophyll a • Protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation

cards.front: Name the events that make up the light reactions (photochemical phase).
cards.back: Light absorption, water splitting, oxygen release, and formation of ATP and NADPH.

cards.front: What makes up a light harvesting complex (LHC)?
cards.back: Hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins forming an antenna, around a reaction centre of one chlorophyll a molecule.

cards.front: Give the reaction centre and absorption peak of PS I and PS II.
cards.back: • PS I: P700, absorbs at 700 nm • PS II: P680, absorbs at 680 nm
cards.hint: PS I is numbered first because it was discovered first, NOT because it acts first.

cards.front: In non-cyclic electron flow, give the order of the electron path.
cards.back: PS II → acceptor → cytochromes (ETS) → PS I → acceptor → NADP+ → NADPH + H+
cards.hint: Drawn in a Z shape: the Z scheme.

cards.front: Why is non-cyclic electron transport called the Z scheme?
cards.back: Its shape arises when all carriers are placed in sequence on a redox potential scale.

cards.front: Water splitting is associated with which photosystem?
cards.back: PS II
cards.hint: Electrons from water replace those lost by PS II.

cards.front: Write the water-splitting reaction.
cards.back: 2H2O → 4H+ + O2 + 4e-

cards.front: On which side of the thylakoid membrane is the water-splitting complex located?
cards.back: The inner side (lumen side); H+ and O2 are formed in the lumen.

cards.front: Cyclic photophosphorylation involves which photosystem and makes what?
cards.back: Only PS I; makes only ATP, no NADPH + H+.

cards.front: Where does cyclic photophosphorylation occur and why there?
cards.back: In stroma lamellae, which lack PS II and the enzyme NADP reductase.

cards.front: Under what light condition does cyclic photophosphorylation occur?
cards.back: When only light of wavelengths beyond 680 nm is available for excitation.

cards.front: According to the chemiosmotic hypothesis, ATP synthesis is linked to what?
cards.back: A proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane, with protons accumulating in the lumen.

cards.front: Give the three causes of the proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane.
cards.back: • Water splitting on the inner side adds H+ to lumen • Primary acceptor passes on an H atom, removing H+ from stroma • NADP reductase uses stromal H+

cards.front: Where are the CF<sub>0</sub> and CF<sub>1</sub> parts of chloroplast ATP synthase located?
cards.back: • CF0: embedded in thylakoid membrane, forms a proton channel • CF1: protrudes on outer surface facing stroma; makes ATP

cards.front: What technique did Melvin Calvin use to find the first CO<sub>2</sub> fixation product?
cards.back: Radioactive 14C in algal photosynthesis studies.
cards.topic: Where are ATP and NADPH used?

cards.front: What is the first stable product of CO<sub>2</sub> fixation in C<sub>3</sub> vs C<sub>4</sub> plants?
cards.back: • C3: 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA), 3C • C4: oxaloacetic acid (OAA), 4C
cards.topic: Where are ATP and NADPH used?

cards.front: What is the primary CO<sub>2</sub> acceptor in the Calvin cycle?
cards.back: Ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP), a 5-carbon ketose sugar.

cards.front: Name the three stages of the Calvin cycle in order.
cards.back: Carboxylation → Reduction → Regeneration (of RuBP)

cards.front: What is the full name of RuBisCO?
cards.back: Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase
cards.hint: Most abundant enzyme in the world.

cards.front: How many ATP and NADPH are needed to fix one CO<sub>2</sub> in the Calvin cycle?
cards.back: 3 ATP and 2 NADPH
cards.hint: 2 ATP + 2 NADPH for reduction; 1 ATP for regeneration.

cards.front: How many Calvin cycle turns, ATP and NADPH are needed to make one glucose?
cards.back: 6 turns, 18 ATP, 12 NADPH

cards.front: Which Calvin cycle step uses ATP but not NADPH?
cards.back: Regeneration of RuBP (1 ATP per CO2).

cards.front: Give two NCERT examples of C<sub>4</sub> plants.
cards.back: Maize and sorghum

cards.front: What does 'Kranz' mean and what does Kranz anatomy refer to?
cards.back: Kranz = wreath; refers to the arrangement of large bundle sheath cells around the vascular bundles of C4 leaves.

cards.front: Give features of bundle sheath cells in C<sub>4</sub> plants.
cards.back: • Several layers, many chloroplasts • Thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange • No intercellular spaces

cards.front: By what other name is the C<sub>4</sub> pathway known?
cards.back: Hatch and Slack pathway

cards.front: In C<sub>4</sub> plants, what is the primary CO<sub>2</sub> acceptor, which enzyme fixes it, and where?
cards.back: Phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP), 3C; enzyme PEP carboxylase (PEPcase); in mesophyll cells.

cards.front: Which enzyme do C<sub>4</sub> mesophyll cells lack, and which do bundle sheath cells lack?
cards.back: • Mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO • Bundle sheath cells lack PEPcase

cards.front: In C<sub>4</sub> plants, OAA is converted to which 4C acids before moving to bundle sheath cells?
cards.back: Malic acid or aspartic acid

cards.front: In bundle sheath cells of C<sub>4</sub> plants, what happens to the C<sub>4</sub> acid?
cards.back: It is decarboxylated: CO2 enters the Calvin cycle; the 3C molecule returns to mesophyll to regenerate PEP.

cards.front: In photorespiration, what does RuBP + O<sub>2</sub> produce?
cards.back: One molecule of PGA and one of phosphoglycolate.

cards.front: Why is photorespiration considered wasteful?
cards.back: No sugar, ATP or NADPH is made; instead CO2 is released with use of ATP.

cards.front: Why do C<sub>4</sub> plants not show photorespiration?
cards.back: They increase CO2 concentration at the RuBisCO site in bundle sheath cells, so RuBisCO acts as a carboxylase.

cards.front: Who gave the Law of Limiting Factors and in which year?
cards.back: Blackman, 1905

cards.front: At what light intensity does light saturation of photosynthesis occur?
cards.back: At about 10% of full sunlight.
cards.hint: So light is rarely limiting, except for plants in shade or dense forests.

cards.front: What happens if light intensity rises far beyond saturation?
cards.back: Chlorophyll breaks down and photosynthesis decreases.

cards.front: What is the atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> concentration and up to what level does increase raise fixation?
cards.back: Atmosphere: 0.03-0.04%; increase up to 0.05% raises CO2 fixation (higher is damaging over long periods).

cards.front: At what CO<sub>2</sub> concentrations do C<sub>4</sub> and C<sub>3</sub> plants saturate?
cards.back: • C4: about 360 µlL-1 • C3: only beyond 450 µlL-1
cards.hint: So current CO<sub>2</sub> levels are limiting for C<sub>3</sub> plants.

cards.front: Which greenhouse crops are grown in CO<sub>2</sub>-enriched atmosphere for higher yield?
cards.back: Tomatoes and bell pepper

cards.front: C<sub>3</sub> vs C<sub>4</sub> plants: which has a higher temperature optimum?
cards.back: C4 plants; also tropical plants have a higher optimum than temperate plants.

cards.front: How does water stress reduce photosynthesis?
cards.back: Causes stomata to close, reducing CO2 availability; leaves wilt, lowering surface area and metabolic activity.
cards.hint: Its effect is indirect, through the plant rather than directly on the reaction.

cards.front: What is cellular respiration?
cards.back: The breaking of C-C bonds of complex compounds through oxidation within cells, releasing a considerable amount of energy.

cards.front: What are respiratory substrates? Name the usual one.
cards.back: Compounds oxidised during respiration; usually carbohydrates, but proteins, fats and even organic acids can be used.

cards.front: Why is ATP called the energy currency of the cell?
cards.back: Energy released by respiration is trapped as ATP, which is broken down wherever energy is needed.

cards.front: Through which structures do plants exchange gases for respiration?
cards.back: Stomata and lenticels
cards.hint: Plants have no specialised respiratory organs.

cards.front: Give reasons why plants can manage without specialised respiratory organs.
cards.back: • Each part handles its own gas exchange • Low demand for gas exchange • Short diffusion distances • Loosely packed parenchyma with connected air spaces

cards.front: Who worked out the scheme of glycolysis, and what is it also called?
cards.back: Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and J. Parnas; it is called the EMP pathway.

cards.front: Where does glycolysis occur, and in which organisms is it the only respiratory process?
cards.back: In the cytoplasm of all living organisms; it is the only process in anaerobic organisms.

cards.front: Which enzyme converts sucrose into glucose and fructose?
cards.back: Invertase

cards.front: Which enzyme phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate?
cards.back: Hexokinase

cards.front: At which two steps of glycolysis is ATP utilised?
cards.back: • Glucose → glucose-6-phosphate • Fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate

cards.front: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is split into which two triose phosphates?
cards.back: Dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL)

cards.front: At which glycolytic step is NADH + H<sup>+</sup> formed?
cards.back: PGAL → 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPGA)

cards.front: At which two glycolytic steps is ATP synthesised directly?
cards.back: • BPGA → 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA) • PEP → pyruvic acid
cards.hint: Each step occurs twice per glucose, so 4 ATP made directly.

cards.front: What is the key end product of glycolysis?
cards.back: Pyruvic acid (2 molecules per glucose).

cards.front: Name the three major fates of pyruvic acid.
cards.back: • Lactic acid fermentation • Alcoholic fermentation • Aerobic respiration

cards.front: Which two enzymes convert pyruvic acid to ethanol and CO<sub>2</sub> in yeast?
cards.back: Pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase

cards.front: Which enzyme reduces pyruvic acid to lactic acid in muscle and some bacteria?
cards.back: Lactate dehydrogenase; NADH + H+ is reoxidised to NAD+.

cards.front: What % of the energy in glucose is released in fermentation?
cards.back: Less than 7%, and not all of it is trapped as ATP.

cards.front: At what alcohol concentration do yeasts poison themselves to death?
cards.back: About 13%

cards.front: What are the two crucial events of aerobic respiration and where does each occur?
cards.back: • Complete oxidation of pyruvate releasing CO2: matrix of mitochondria • Electron transport and ATP synthesis: inner mitochondrial membrane

cards.front: Which enzyme catalyses oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate, and which coenzymes does it need?
cards.back: Pyruvic dehydrogenase; needs NAD+ and coenzyme A.

cards.front: Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate produces what?
cards.back: Acetyl CoA + CO2 + NADH + H+ (2 NADH from 2 pyruvates of one glucose).

cards.front: Who elucidated the TCA cycle?
cards.back: Hans Krebs

cards.front: What is the first reaction of the Krebs cycle and which enzyme catalyses it?
cards.back: Acetyl CoA + OAA + water → citric acid; enzyme citrate synthase; CoA is released.

cards.front: Citrate is first isomerised to what compound?
cards.back: Isocitrate

cards.front: The two successive decarboxylations after isocitrate form which compounds?
cards.back: α-ketoglutaric acid and then succinyl-CoA

cards.front: At which step of the Krebs cycle does substrate-level phosphorylation occur?
cards.back: Succinyl-CoA → succinic acid, forming GTP (which yields ATP in a coupled reaction).

cards.front: Per Krebs cycle turn, at how many points are NAD<sup>+</sup> and FAD reduced?
cards.back: • NAD+: 3 points • FAD: 1 point

cards.front: For one pyruvic acid fully oxidised in mitochondria, how many CO<sub>2</sub>, NADH, FADH<sub>2</sub> and ATP form?
cards.back: 3 CO2, 4 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 ATP
cards.hint: Includes the link reaction (pyruvate → acetyl CoA).

cards.front: Which molecule is regenerated in the Krebs cycle to accept acetyl CoA again?
cards.back: Oxaloacetic acid (OAA)

cards.front: Where is the electron transport system located?
cards.back: The inner mitochondrial membrane.

cards.front: Which complex oxidises NADH, and to which carrier are electrons passed?
cards.back: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase); electrons go to ubiquinone.

cards.front: Through which complex do electrons from FADH<sub>2</sub> enter the ETS?
cards.back: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), passing them to ubiquinone.
cards.hint: FADH<sub>2</sub> bypasses complex I, so it yields fewer ATP.

cards.front: Reduced ubiquinone (ubiquinol) passes electrons to cytochrome c through which complex?
cards.back: Complex III (cytochrome bc1 complex)

cards.front: What is cytochrome c and where is it located?
cards.back: A small protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane; a mobile carrier between complex III and IV.

cards.front: What does Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) contain?
cards.back: Cytochromes a and a3 and two copper centres.

cards.front: How many ATP are formed from oxidation of one NADH and one FADH<sub>2</sub> in the ETS?
cards.back: • NADH: 3 ATP • FADH2: 2 ATP

cards.front: What is the final hydrogen (electron) acceptor in aerobic respiration?
cards.back: Oxygen; it accepts electrons and H+ to form water.
cards.hint: Oxygen acts only at the end of the chain, but drives the whole process.

cards.front: Photophosphorylation vs oxidative phosphorylation: what provides energy for the proton gradient?
cards.back: • Photophosphorylation: light • Oxidative phosphorylation: oxidation-reduction energy

cards.front: Which complex is ATP synthase?
cards.back: Complex V

cards.front: F<sub>1</sub> vs F<sub>0</sub> of mitochondrial ATP synthase: role of each?
cards.back: • F1: peripheral headpiece, site of ATP synthesis • F0: integral membrane protein forming the proton channel

cards.front: Per NCERT, how many protons pass through F<sub>0</sub> for each ATP produced, and in which direction?
cards.back: 2 H+, from the intermembrane space to the matrix.

cards.front: What is the net ATP gain from aerobic respiration of one glucose per the respiratory balance sheet?
cards.back: 38 ATP
cards.hint: A theoretical value based on assumptions (sequential pathway, 3 ATP/NADH, no intermediates withdrawn).

cards.front: Fermentation vs aerobic respiration: net ATP per glucose?
cards.back: • Fermentation: 2 ATP • Aerobic respiration: 38 ATP

cards.front: Fermentation vs aerobic respiration: how fast is NADH oxidised in each?
cards.back: • Fermentation: NADH oxidised to NAD+ rather slowly • Aerobic: oxidation is very vigorous

cards.front: Why is the respiratory pathway called amphibolic?
cards.back: It is involved in both catabolism (breakdown) and anabolism (synthesis).

cards.front: Into what do fatty acids and glycerol enter the respiratory pathway?
cards.back: • Fatty acids: acetyl CoA • Glycerol: PGAL
cards.hint: Glycerol is converted to PGAL first.

cards.front: How do amino acids enter the respiratory pathway?
cards.back: After deamination, they enter at pyruvate, acetyl CoA or within the Krebs cycle, depending on structure.

cards.front: Define respiratory quotient (RQ).
cards.back: Ratio of volume of CO2 evolved to volume of O2 consumed in respiration.

cards.front: What is the RQ of carbohydrates, fats and proteins?
cards.back: • Carbohydrates: 1 • Fats: less than 1 (about 0.7) • Proteins: about 0.9

cards.front: Why is the RQ of carbohydrates exactly 1?
cards.back: Equal amounts (6 molecules each) of CO2 evolved and O2 consumed: 6CO2/6O2 = 1.

cards.front: Which fat does NCERT use to calculate RQ, and what is the value?
cards.back: Tripalmitin: 102 CO2 / 145 O2 = 0.7

cards.front: Do living organisms respire pure fats or pure proteins as substrates?
cards.back: No; they use mixtures of substrates, never pure proteins or fats.

cards.front: Why is plant growth described as 'open' or indeterminate?
cards.back: Meristems keep adding new cells throughout life, so the plant body is always growing.

cards.front: Primary vs secondary growth: which meristems cause each?
cards.back: • Primary (elongation): root and shoot apical meristems • Secondary (girth): lateral meristems (vascular and cork cambium) in dicots and gymnosperms

cards.front: Roughly how many new cells per hour does a single maize root apical meristem produce?
cards.back: More than 17,500 new cells per hour.

cards.front: Cells in a watermelon may increase in size by up to how many times?
cards.back: Up to about 3,50,000 times.
cards.hint: Example of growth measured as increase in cell size

cards.front: Which parameter is used to measure growth of a pollen tube?
cards.back: Increase in length.
cards.hint: Dorsiventral leaf growth is measured as increase in surface area

cards.front: Name the three phases of growth in order, as seen behind a root tip.
cards.back: • Meristematic • Elongation • Maturation

cards.front: Which feature marks cells of the meristematic phase of growth?
cards.back: Rich protoplasm, large conspicuous nuclei, thin primary cellulosic walls with abundant plasmodesmata.

cards.front: What features mark the zone of elongation?
cards.back: Increased vacuolation, cell enlargement and new cell wall deposition.

cards.front: Give the equation for arithmetic growth.
cards.back: Lt = L0 + rt Only one daughter cell keeps dividing; the other differentiates. Plot is linear.
cards.hint: Example: root elongating at a constant rate

cards.front: Give the exponential (geometric) growth equation.
cards.back: W1 = W0 ert W0 = initial size, r = relative growth rate, t = time, e = base of natural logarithms.

cards.front: In W<sub>1</sub> = W<sub>0</sub> e<sup>rt</sup>, what is 'r' also called?
cards.back: Relative growth rate, a measure of the plant's ability to produce new material: the efficiency index.

cards.front: What shape is the curve of geometric growth under limited nutrients, and its phases?
cards.back: Sigmoid (S-shaped) curve: • Lag phase • Log/exponential phase • Stationary phase

cards.front: Absolute vs relative growth rate: key difference?
cards.back: • Absolute: total growth per unit time • Relative: growth per unit time per unit initial size
cards.hint: Two leaves can show the same absolute growth but different relative growth

cards.front: List four conditions necessary for plant growth.
cards.back: • Water • Oxygen • Nutrients • Optimum temperature (plus light and gravity also influence some stages)

cards.front: Define differentiation in plants.
cards.back: The process by which cells from meristems mature to perform specific functions, with structural changes in walls and protoplasm.

cards.front: Which cells lose their protoplasm on differentiation, and why?
cards.back: Tracheary elements; they develop strong, elastic lignocellulosic secondary walls to carry water under extreme tension.

cards.front: What is dedifferentiation?
cards.back: Living differentiated cells that had lost the capacity to divide regain the ability to divide under certain conditions.

cards.front: Give two meristems formed by dedifferentiation of fully differentiated parenchyma.
cards.back: • Interfascicular cambium • Cork cambium

cards.front: What is redifferentiation?
cards.back: Cells produced by dedifferentiated tissue lose the capacity to divide again and mature to perform specific functions, i.e. they are redifferentiated.

cards.front: What does 'development' include in plants?
cards.back: All changes an organism goes through in its life cycle, from seed germination to senescence; it is growth + differentiation.

cards.front: What is plasticity in plants?
cards.back: Ability to follow different pathways and form different structures in response to environment or life phase.

cards.front: Name three plants showing heterophylly due to life phase (juvenile vs mature leaves).
cards.back: • Cotton • Coriander • Larkspur

cards.front: Which plant shows heterophylly due to environment (air vs water leaves)?
cards.back: Buttercup: leaves in air differ in shape from those under water.
cards.hint: Trap: cotton/coriander/larkspur are due to life phase, not environment

cards.front: Development in plants is under the control of which two kinds of factors?
cards.back: • Intrinsic: genetic and intercellular (PGRs) • Extrinsic: light, temperature, water, oxygen, nutrition

cards.front: Into which two groups are PGRs broadly divided by function?
cards.back: • Promoters: auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins • Inhibitors: abscisic acid Ethylene can fit either group but is largely an inhibitor.

cards.front: Match chemical nature: IAA, kinetin, ABA, gibberellic acid, ethylene?
cards.back: • IAA: indole compound • Kinetin: adenine derivative • ABA: carotenoid derivative • GA: terpene • Ethylene: gas

cards.front: Which observation by Charles Darwin and his son led to the discovery of auxin?
cards.back: Coleoptiles of canary grass bent towards unilateral light (phototropism); the tip was the site of the transmissible influence.

cards.front: Who isolated auxin and from which plant?
cards.back: F.W. Went, from coleoptile tips of oat seedlings.
cards.hint: Darwin = canary grass; Went = oat

cards.front: Bakanae (foolish seedling) disease of rice is caused by which fungus?
cards.back: Gibberella fujikuroi; its active substance was later identified as gibberellic acid.
cards.hint: Reported by E. Kurosawa

cards.front: From what did Skoog and Miller crystallise kinetin?
cards.back: From autoclaved herring sperm DNA; it promoted cytokinesis in tobacco callus.

cards.front: Which three inhibitors were found to be chemically identical in the mid-1960s?
cards.back: Inhibitor-B, abscisin II and dormin; together named abscisic acid (ABA).

cards.front: Who confirmed that ripened oranges release a volatile substance that hastens banana ripening?
cards.back: H.H. Cousins (1910); the substance was later identified as ethylene.

cards.front: Give the natural and synthetic auxins named in NCERT.
cards.back: • Natural: IAA, IBA • Synthetic: NAA, 2,4-D

cards.front: Which auxin is widely used as a weedicide, and what does it kill?
cards.back: 2,4-D; kills dicotyledonous weeds without affecting mature monocots.
cards.hint: Used to prepare weed-free lawns

cards.front: What is apical dominance, and which PGR causes it?
cards.back: Growing apical bud inhibits growth of lateral buds; caused by auxin. Removing the tip (decapitation) promotes lateral buds.
cards.hint: Applied in tea plantations and hedge-making

cards.front: List four practical uses of auxins.
cards.back: • Rooting in stem cuttings • Flowering in pineapple • Prevent early fruit and leaf drop • Induce parthenocarpy (e.g. tomato)

cards.front: Auxins promote abscission of which leaves and fruits?
cards.back: Older, mature leaves and fruits (they prevent early drop of young ones).

cards.front: Which gibberellin was one of the first discovered and remains the most intensively studied?
cards.back: GA3 (gibberellic acid). Over 100 gibberellins are known; all are acidic.

cards.front: How do gibberellins help grapes and apples?
cards.back: • Grapes: increase stalk length • Apples: elongate fruit and improve shape

cards.front: Why is sugarcane sprayed with gibberellins?
cards.back: Increases stem length, raising yield by as much as 20 tonnes per acre.

cards.front: Name three other uses of gibberellins (besides fruit and sugarcane).
cards.back: • Speed up malting in brewing • Hasten maturity of juvenile conifers for early seed production • Also delay senescence

cards.front: What is bolting, and which PGR promotes it?
cards.back: Internode elongation just before flowering in rosette plants (e.g. beet, cabbage); promoted by gibberellins.

cards.front: Name the natural cytokinin and two sources it was isolated from.
cards.back: Zeatin, from corn kernels and coconut milk.
cards.hint: Kinetin is NOT natural in plants

cards.front: Where are natural cytokinins synthesised in plants?
cards.back: Regions of rapid cell division: root apices, developing shoot buds, young fruits.

cards.front: Give the main functions of cytokinins.
cards.back: • New leaves, chloroplasts, lateral shoot growth, adventitious shoots • Overcome apical dominance • Nutrient mobilisation; delay leaf senescence

cards.front: Which tissues synthesise ethylene in large amounts?
cards.back: Tissues undergoing senescence and ripening fruits.

cards.front: What is respiratory climacteric?
cards.back: Rise in respiration rate during fruit ripening, enhanced by ethylene.

cards.front: Name ethylene's effects on seedlings.
cards.back: Horizontal growth, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation in dicot seedlings.

cards.front: Ethylene breaks dormancy/promotes growth in which NCERT examples?
cards.back: • Germination of peanut seeds • Sprouting of potato tubers • Internode/petiole elongation in deep water rice

cards.front: Which is the most widely used compound as a source of ethylene?
cards.back: Ethephon: absorbed in aqueous solution and slowly releases ethylene.

cards.front: Give three uses of ethephon.
cards.back: • Hastens ripening in tomatoes and apples • Fruit thinning by abscission (cotton, cherry, walnut) • Promotes female flowers in cucumber

cards.front: Which PGR induces flowering in pineapple and synchronises fruit-set?
cards.back: Ethylene.
cards.hint: Auxin is also listed as initiating flowering in pineapple

cards.front: Why is abscisic acid called the 'stress hormone'?
cards.back: It increases plant tolerance to various stresses.

cards.front: List the main functions of ABA.
cards.back: • Inhibits seed germination and plant metabolism • Stimulates stomatal closure • Seed development, maturation and dormancy

cards.front: ABA acts as an antagonist to which PGR in most situations?
cards.back: Gibberellins (GAs).

cards.front: How do sponges, coelenterates and flatworms exchange O<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub>?
cards.back: By simple diffusion over their entire body surface.

cards.front: Through which surface do earthworms respire?
cards.back: Their moist cuticle.

cards.front: Which respiratory structure do insects use?
cards.back: A network of tracheal tubes.

cards.front: Which animals use gills (branchial respiration) per NCERT?
cards.back: Most aquatic arthropods and molluscs; also fishes.

cards.front: Which vertebrate groups respire through lungs?
cards.back: Amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals (pulmonary respiration).
cards.hint: Fishes use gills

cards.front: Besides lungs, how can frogs respire?
cards.back: Through their moist skin (cutaneous respiration).

cards.front: Give the path of air from external nostrils to the trachea.
cards.back: External nostrils → nasal passage → nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx → trachea

cards.front: Why is the larynx called the sound box?
cards.back: It is a cartilaginous box that helps in sound production.

cards.front: What does the epiglottis do?
cards.back: Thin, elastic cartilaginous flap that covers the glottis during swallowing, preventing food entry into the larynx.

cards.front: At the level of which vertebra does the trachea divide into right and left primary bronchi?
cards.back: 5th thoracic vertebra (mid-thoracic cavity).
cards.hint: Trap: thoracic, not cervical

cards.front: Which airways are supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings?
cards.back: Trachea, primary, secondary and tertiary bronchi, and initial bronchioles.

cards.front: What are alveoli?
cards.back: Very thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like structures at the end of terminal bronchioles; site of gas exchange.

cards.front: What covers the lungs, and what is the role of the fluid inside it?
cards.back: Double-layered pleura with pleural fluid between; the fluid reduces friction on the lung surface.

cards.front: Outer vs inner pleural membrane: what does each contact?
cards.back: • Outer: close contact with thoracic lining • Inner: in contact with lung surface

cards.front: What does the conducting part of the respiratory system include?
cards.back: From external nostrils up to terminal bronchioles.
cards.hint: Respiratory/exchange part = alveoli and their ducts

cards.front: Give the functions of the conducting part besides transporting air.
cards.back: • Clears air of foreign particles • Humidifies it • Brings it to body temperature

cards.front: What bounds the thoracic chamber on each side?
cards.back: • Dorsal: vertebral column • Ventral: sternum • Lateral: ribs • Lower: dome-shaped diaphragm

cards.front: Why is the thoracic chamber called anatomically air-tight?
cards.back: Lungs are placed so that any change in thoracic cavity volume is reflected in the lung (pulmonary) cavity; this is essential for breathing.

cards.front: List the five steps of respiration in order.
cards.back: • Breathing (pulmonary ventilation) • Diffusion across alveolar membrane • Transport by blood • Diffusion between blood and tissues • Cellular respiration (O2 use)

cards.front: When does inspiration occur in terms of pressure?
cards.back: When intra-pulmonary pressure is less than atmospheric pressure (negative pressure in lungs).

cards.front: Contraction of the diaphragm increases thoracic volume along which axis?
cards.back: Antero-posterior axis.
cards.hint: Diaphragm = antero-posterior; intercostals = dorso-ventral

cards.front: Which muscles lift the ribs and sternum during inspiration, and which axis do they expand?
cards.back: External intercostal muscles; they increase volume in the dorso-ventral axis.

cards.front: What causes normal expiration?
cards.back: Relaxation of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles; thoracic volume falls and intra-pulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric.

cards.front: How can the strength of inspiration and expiration be increased?
cards.back: With the help of additional muscles in the abdomen.

cards.front: How many times per minute does a healthy human breathe?
cards.back: 12–16 times per minute.

cards.front: Which instrument estimates the volume of air in breathing movements?
cards.back: Spirometer.

cards.front: What is tidal volume, and its value?
cards.back: Air inspired or expired during a normal breath: about 500 mL.
cards.hint: So a healthy person moves about 6000–8000 mL air per minute

cards.front: Give NCERT values of IRV, ERV and RV.
Define residual volume.
cards.back: Air remaining in the lungs even after a forcible expiration.

cards.front: Inspiratory capacity equals which volumes?
cards.back: TV + IRV

cards.front: Expiratory capacity equals which volumes?
cards.back: TV + ERV

cards.front: Functional residual capacity equals which volumes?
cards.back: ERV + RV: air remaining in lungs after a normal expiration.

cards.front: What is vital capacity?
cards.back: Maximum air breathed out after a forced inspiration (or in after forced expiration): ERV + TV + IRV.

cards.front: What is total lung capacity?
cards.back: Total air in lungs at the end of a forced inspiration: VC + RV (= RV + ERV + TV + IRV).

cards.front: What is the primary site of gas exchange in humans?
cards.back: Alveoli; exchange also occurs between blood and tissues.

cards.front: Name factors affecting rate of gas diffusion across the membrane.
cards.back: Pressure/concentration gradient, solubility of gases and thickness of membranes.

cards.front: How many times more soluble is CO<sub>2</sub> than O<sub>2</sub>?
cards.back: 20–25 times higher solubility.
cards.hint: So more CO<sub>2</sub> diffuses per unit partial pressure difference

cards.front: Give pO<sub>2</sub> and pCO<sub>2</sub> (mm Hg) in alveoli.
cards.back: pO2 104; pCO2 40
cards.hint: Atmospheric air: pO<sub>2</sub> 159, pCO<sub>2</sub> 0.3

cards.front: Give pO<sub>2</sub> and pCO<sub>2</sub> (mm Hg) in deoxygenated and oxygenated blood.
cards.back: • Deoxygenated: pO2 40, pCO2 45 • Oxygenated: pO2 95, pCO2 40
cards.hint: Tissues: pO<sub>2</sub> 40, pCO<sub>2</sub> 45

cards.front: Name the three layers of the diffusion membrane in lungs.
cards.back: • Thin squamous epithelium of alveoli • Endothelium of alveolar capillaries • Basement substance in between Total thickness much less than a millimetre.

cards.front: What percent of O<sub>2</sub> is carried by RBCs vs dissolved in plasma?
cards.back: • RBCs: about 97% • Plasma (dissolved): about 3%

cards.front: What percentages of CO<sub>2</sub> are carried in each form?
cards.back: • 20–25% by RBCs (carbamino-haemoglobin) • 70% as bicarbonate • 7% dissolved in plasma

cards.front: How many O<sub>2</sub> molecules can one haemoglobin molecule carry at most?
cards.back: Four.

cards.front: What is the shape of the oxygen dissociation curve?
cards.back: Sigmoid: % saturation of Hb with O2 plotted against pO2.

cards.front: Which alveolar conditions favour oxyhaemoglobin formation?
cards.back: High pO2, low pCO2, lesser H+ concentration and lower temperature.
cards.hint: Tissues have the opposite conditions, favouring dissociation

cards.front: Under normal conditions, how much O<sub>2</sub> does 100 mL of oxygenated blood deliver to tissues?
cards.back: Around 5 mL of O2.
cards.hint: Deoxygenated blood delivers ~4 mL CO<sub>2</sub> per 100 mL to alveoli

cards.front: Which two factors affect CO<sub>2</sub> binding to haemoglobin as carbamino-haemoglobin?
cards.back: pCO2 and pO2 (pO2 is a major factor). • Tissues (high pCO2, low pO2): binding • Alveoli (low pCO2, high pO2): dissociation

cards.front: Which enzyme speeds up CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, and where is it?
cards.back: Carbonic anhydrase: very high in RBCs, minute amounts in plasma.

cards.front: Write the reaction catalysed by carbonic anhydrase leading to bicarbonate.
cards.back: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ HCO3- + H+ Forward in tissues; reverse at alveoli releases CO2.

cards.front: What proportion of blood is plasma, and what does it look like?
cards.back: About 55%; a straw-coloured, viscous fluid.

cards.front: What percentage of plasma is water and what percentage proteins?
cards.back: • Water: 90–92% • Proteins: 6–8%

cards.front: Match plasma proteins to function: fibrinogen, globulins, albumins?
cards.back: • Fibrinogen: clotting/coagulation • Globulins: defence mechanisms • Albumins: osmotic balance

cards.front: What is serum?
cards.back: Plasma without clotting factors.

cards.front: What is the RBC count in a healthy adult man?
cards.back: 5–5.5 million RBCs per mm3 of blood.

cards.front: Where are RBCs formed in adults?
cards.back: Red bone marrow.

cards.front: What is the normal haemoglobin content of blood?
cards.back: 12–16 g per 100 mL of blood.

cards.front: What is the average lifespan of RBCs and where are they destroyed?
cards.back: About 120 days; destroyed in the spleen (graveyard of RBCs).

cards.front: What is the normal WBC count?
cards.back: 6000–8000 per mm3 of blood. WBCs are nucleated and generally short-lived.

cards.front: Name the granulocytes and agranulocytes.
cards.back: • Granulocytes: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils • Agranulocytes: lymphocytes, monocytes

cards.front: Which WBC is most abundant and which is least abundant?
cards.back: • Most: neutrophils (60–65%) • Least: basophils (0.5–1%)

cards.front: Which two WBCs are phagocytic?
cards.back: Neutrophils (60–65%) and monocytes (6–8%).

cards.front: Which substances do basophils secrete?
cards.back: Histamine, serotonin, heparin; involved in inflammatory reactions.

cards.front: Eosinophils: percentage and role?
cards.back: 2–3%; resist infections and are associated with allergic reactions.

cards.front: What percentage of WBCs are lymphocytes, and what are their two major types?
cards.back: 20–25%; B and T lymphocytes, responsible for immune responses.

cards.front: Platelets are fragments of which cells?
cards.back: Megakaryocytes (special cells in bone marrow).

cards.front: What is the normal platelet count, and what happens if it falls?
cards.back: 1,50,000–3,50,000 per mm3; reduction causes clotting disorders and excess blood loss.

cards.front: ABO grouping is based on which antigens, and where are they?
cards.back: Antigens A and B on the surface of RBCs.

cards.front: Which antibodies are present in plasma of blood group A?
cards.back: Anti-B.
cards.hint: Group B has anti-A

cards.front: Which group is the universal donor, and why?
cards.back: Group O: RBCs have no A or B antigens.
cards.hint: Trap: O plasma has both anti-A and anti-B

cards.front: Which group is the universal recipient?
cards.back: Group AB: plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies.

cards.front: Roughly what percentage of humans are Rh positive?
cards.back: Nearly 80%.
cards.hint: Rh antigen is similar to one in Rhesus monkeys

cards.front: What is erythroblastosis foetalis?
cards.back: Destruction of foetal RBCs by the Rh-ve mother's anti-Rh antibodies in a later Rh+ve pregnancy; causes severe anaemia and jaundice.

cards.front: Why is the first Rh+ve pregnancy of an Rh-ve mother usually unaffected?
cards.back: The placenta keeps the two bloods separate; the mother is exposed to small foetal blood mainly at delivery, then makes antibodies.

cards.front: How can erythroblastosis foetalis be avoided?
cards.back: Give anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after delivery of the first child.

cards.front: What is a blood clot made of?
cards.back: A network of fibrin threads trapping dead and damaged formed elements of blood.

cards.front: Give the sequence of key steps in blood clotting.
cards.back: Thrombokinase converts prothrombin → thrombin; thrombin converts fibrinogen → fibrin.

cards.front: Which ion plays a very important role in blood clotting?
cards.back: Calcium ions (Ca2+).

cards.front: Which nutrient is absorbed through lymph in the intestinal villi, and via what?
cards.back: Fats, through lacteals.

cards.front: Open vs closed circulatory system: give the animal groups.
cards.back: • Open: arthropods, molluscs • Closed: annelids, chordates

cards.front: How many heart chambers do fishes, amphibians, crocodiles and birds have?
cards.back: • Fishes: 2 • Amphibians and most reptiles: 3 • Crocodiles, birds, mammals: 4
cards.hint: Crocodile = the 4-chambered reptile exception

cards.front: Which vertebrates show incomplete double circulation?
cards.back: Amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles): the single ventricle pumps out mixed blood.
cards.hint: Fishes: single circulation

cards.front: Which valve guards the right atrio-ventricular opening, and which the left?
cards.back: • Right: tricuspid • Left: bicuspid (mitral)

cards.front: Where are semilunar valves located?
cards.back: At openings of the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery and left ventricle into the aorta.

cards.front: Where exactly is the SA node located?
cards.back: Right upper corner of the right atrium.

cards.front: Where exactly is the AV node located?
cards.back: Lower left corner of the right atrium, close to the atrio-ventricular septum.
cards.hint: Trap: AVN is in the right atrium, not the left

cards.front: Give the conduction path from AV node to ventricular walls.
cards.back: AVN → AV bundle (bundle of His) → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres

cards.front: Why is the SA node called the pacemaker?
cards.back: It generates the maximum number of action potentials (70–75/min), initiating and maintaining rhythmic contraction.

cards.front: What is the duration of one cardiac cycle?
cards.back: 0.8 seconds (at ~72 beats per minute).

cards.front: Atrial systole increases flow of blood into ventricles by about how much?
cards.back: About 30%.

cards.front: What are the stroke volume and cardiac output of a healthy person?
cards.back: • Stroke volume: about 70 mL • Cardiac output: about 5000 mL (5 L) per minute
cards.hint: Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate

cards.front: Which valve closures produce the 'lub' and 'dub' sounds?
cards.back: • Lub: closure of tricuspid and bicuspid valves • Dub: closure of semilunar valves

cards.front: What does each ECG wave represent: P, QRS, T?
cards.back: • P: atrial depolarisation • QRS: ventricular depolarisation • T: ventricular repolarisation

cards.front: Which ECG event marks the end of systole?
cards.back: The end of the T-wave.

cards.front: Counting which ECG complex gives the heart beat rate?
cards.back: Number of QRS complexes in a given time.

cards.front: Give the path of pulmonary circulation.
cards.back: Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium

cards.front: What is the hepatic portal system?
cards.back: Hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver before it reaches systemic circulation.

cards.front: What supplies blood exclusively to cardiac musculature?
cards.back: The coronary system of blood vessels.

cards.front: Why is the human heart called myogenic?
cards.back: Its normal activity is auto-regulated by specialised muscles (nodal tissue).

cards.front: Where is the neural centre that moderates cardiac function?
cards.back: Medulla oblongata.

cards.front: Sympathetic vs parasympathetic effect on the heart?
cards.back: • Sympathetic: increases rate, strength of contraction, cardiac output • Parasympathetic: decreases them
cards.hint: Adrenal medullary hormones also increase cardiac output

cards.front: What blood pressure reading indicates hypertension?
cards.back: 140/90 mm Hg or higher, repeatedly. Normal is 120/80.

cards.front: What deposits narrow arteries in coronary artery disease (atherosclerosis)?
cards.back: Calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue.

cards.front: What causes angina pectoris?
cards.back: Not enough oxygen reaching heart muscle, causing acute chest pain. More common in middle-aged and elderly.

cards.front: Heart failure vs cardiac arrest vs heart attack: key difference?
cards.back: • Heart failure: heart pumps ineffectively (lung congestion) • Cardiac arrest: heart stops beating • Heart attack: muscle damaged by inadequate blood supply

cards.front: Which nitrogenous waste is most toxic and needs the most water for elimination?
cards.back: Ammonia.
cards.hint: Uric acid is least toxic, needs least water

cards.front: What is ammonotelism? Give examples.
cards.back: Excretion of ammonia: many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects.

cards.front: How is ammonia removed in ammonotelic animals?
cards.back: As ammonium ions by diffusion across body surfaces or gill surfaces; kidneys play no significant role.

cards.front: Name ureotelic animals given in NCERT.
cards.back: Mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes.
cards.hint: Trap: aquatic amphibians are ammonotelic; terrestrial amphibians are ureotelic

cards.front: Why do some animals retain urea in the kidney matrix?
cards.back: To maintain a desired osmolarity.

cards.front: Name uricotelic animals.
cards.back: Reptiles, birds, land snails, insects; uric acid excreted as pellet or paste with minimum water loss.

cards.front: Which animals have protonephridia (flame cells)?
cards.back: Platyhelminthes (e.g. Planaria), rotifers, some annelids and the cephalochordate Amphioxus.

cards.front: Primary function of protonephridia?
cards.back: Ionic and fluid volume regulation (osmoregulation).

cards.front: Match excretory structures: earthworm, cockroach, prawn?
cards.back: • Earthworm: nephridia • Cockroach: Malpighian tubules • Prawn: antennal/green glands

cards.front: Kidneys lie between which vertebrae?
cards.back: Between the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebra, close to the dorsal inner abdominal wall.

cards.front: Give the dimensions and weight of an adult human kidney.
cards.back: • Length 10–12 cm, width 5–7 cm, thickness 2–3 cm • Weight 120–170 g

cards.front: What is the hilum of the kidney?
cards.back: Notch on the inner concave surface through which ureter, blood vessels and nerves enter.

cards.front: What lies just inner to the hilum?
cards.back: Broad funnel-shaped renal pelvis with projections called calyces.

cards.front: What are columns of Bertini?
cards.back: Extensions of the cortex between the medullary pyramids (renal columns).

cards.front: Approximately how many nephrons does each kidney have?
cards.back: About one million.

cards.front: What is the Malpighian body (renal corpuscle)?
cards.back: Glomerulus + Bowman's capsule.

cards.front: Which parts of the nephron lie in the cortex?
cards.back: Malpighian corpuscle, PCT and DCT; Henle's loop dips into the medulla.

cards.front: Cortical vs juxtamedullary nephron: key difference?
cards.back: • Cortical: short loop, extends only a little into medulla (majority) • Juxtamedullary: very long loop running deep into medulla

cards.front: What is the vasa recta, and in which nephrons is it reduced or absent?
cards.back: U-shaped vessel from peritubular capillaries running parallel to Henle's loop; absent or highly reduced in cortical nephrons.

cards.front: How much blood do kidneys filter per minute on average?
cards.back: 1100–1200 mL per minute, about 1/5th of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute.

cards.front: Name the three layers of the glomerular filtration membrane.
cards.back: • Endothelium of glomerular blood vessels • Epithelium of Bowman's capsule • Basement membrane between them

cards.front: What are podocytes?
cards.back: Epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule arranged intricately, leaving minute spaces called filtration slits (slit pores).

cards.front: Which plasma component does NOT pass into the filtrate?
cards.back: Proteins; almost all other constituents pass, so it is called ultrafiltration.

cards.front: What is the GFR of a healthy person?
cards.back: About 125 mL/minute, i.e. 180 L per day.

cards.front: What is the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)?
cards.back: Sensitive region formed by cellular modifications in the DCT and afferent arteriole where they contact.

cards.front: How does the JGA respond to a fall in GFR?
cards.back: JG cells release renin, which stimulates glomerular blood flow and brings GFR back to normal.

cards.front: Which substances are reabsorbed actively vs passively in tubules?
cards.back: • Active: glucose, amino acids, Na+ • Passive: nitrogenous wastes; water also passively in initial segments

cards.front: Which ions/substances are secreted into the filtrate, and why?
cards.back: H+, K+ and ammonia; to maintain ionic and acid-base balance.

cards.front: What epithelium lines the PCT?
cards.back: Simple cuboidal brush border epithelium, which increases reabsorption surface.

cards.front: What fraction of electrolytes and water is reabsorbed in the PCT?
cards.back: 70–80% of electrolytes and water, plus nearly all essential nutrients.

cards.front: In which segment of Henle's loop is reabsorption minimum?
cards.back: Ascending limb.

cards.front: Descending vs ascending limb of Henle's loop: permeability?
cards.back: • Descending: permeable to water, almost impermeable to electrolytes (filtrate concentrates) • Ascending: impermeable to water, transports electrolytes (filtrate dilutes)
cards.hint: Descending limb loses water; ascending limb loses salts

cards.front: What is conditional reabsorption, and where does it occur?
cards.back: Reabsorption of Na+ and water as per need; occurs in the DCT.

cards.front: Role of the collecting duct in urine concentration?
cards.back: Reabsorbs large amounts of water to make concentrated urine, and lets small amounts of urea into medullary interstitium.

cards.front: Which two structures form counter-current patterns in the kidney?
cards.back: Henle's loop and vasa recta: flow in their two limbs is in opposite directions.

cards.front: Medullary interstitial osmolarity rises from what to what?
cards.back: From 300 mOsmol/L in cortex to about 1200 mOsmol/L in inner medulla.

cards.front: Which two solutes mainly cause the medullary osmotic gradient?
cards.back: NaCl and urea.

cards.front: How is urea recycled to maintain the medullary gradient?
cards.back: Urea enters the thin ascending limb of Henle's loop and is transported back to interstitium by the collecting tubule.

cards.front: Human kidneys can make urine how concentrated relative to initial filtrate?
cards.back: Nearly four times as concentrated.

cards.front: What triggers ADH release, and from where is it released?
cards.back: Excess fluid loss activates osmoreceptors, stimulating the hypothalamus; ADH (vasopressin) is released from the neurohypophysis.

cards.front: Give the two effects of ADH.
cards.back: • Increases water reabsorption from later parts of tubule • Constricts blood vessels, raising BP and GFR

cards.front: Give the sequence of the renin–angiotensin pathway.
cards.back: Renin converts angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → angiotensin II (powerful vasoconstrictor).

cards.front: How does aldosterone act on the kidney, and what releases it?
cards.back: Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which increases Na+ and water reabsorption from distal tubule.

cards.front: Where is ANF released from, and what are its effects?
cards.back: Atrial walls of the heart, when blood flow to the atria increases; ANF causes vasodilation, lowers BP and checks the renin-angiotensin mechanism.

cards.front: What happens in the micturition reflex?
cards.back: Stretch receptors signal CNS; motor messages cause bladder smooth muscle contraction and simultaneous urethral sphincter relaxation.

cards.front: Give the normal daily urine output, pH and urea content in an adult.
cards.back: • 1–1.5 L per day • Slightly acidic, pH about 6.0 • 25–30 g urea per day

cards.front: Presence of glucose and ketone bodies in urine indicates what?
cards.back: Glycosuria and ketonuria: indicative of diabetes mellitus.

cards.front: Approximately how much CO<sub>2</sub> do lungs remove per minute?
cards.back: About 200 mL/minute.
cards.topic: Role of other organs in excretion

cards.front: Which substances does the liver excrete via bile?
cards.back: Bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs.
cards.topic: Role of other organs in excretion

cards.front: Sweat vs sebum: what does each eliminate, and main role?
cards.back: • Sweat: NaCl, small urea, lactic acid; main role cooling • Sebum: sterols, hydrocarbons, waxes; protective oily skin covering
cards.topic: Role of other organs in excretion

cards.front: What is uremia, and how is it treated?
cards.back: Accumulation of urea in blood due to kidney malfunction; managed by haemodialysis.

cards.front: In haemodialysis, which anticoagulant is added before and what after?
cards.back: Heparin added before dialysis; anti-heparin added before return to the body.

cards.front: How does dialysing fluid differ from plasma?
cards.back: Same composition as plasma except the nitrogenous wastes.

cards.front: What are renal calculi?
cards.back: Stones or insoluble masses of crystallised salts (oxalates, etc.) formed in the kidney.

cards.front: What is glomerulonephritis?
cards.back: Inflammation of glomeruli of the kidney.

cards.front: Which three main types of movement are shown by cells of the human body?
cards.back: • Amoeboid • Ciliary • Muscular

cards.front: Which structures serve both feeding and locomotion in Paramecium and in Hydra?
cards.back: • Paramecium: cilia move food through the cytopharynx and aid locomotion • Hydra: tentacles capture prey and aid locomotion

cards.front: Which human cells show amoeboid movement?
cards.back: Specialised cells such as macrophages and leucocytes in blood.

cards.front: How is amoeboid movement brought about?
cards.back: By pseudopodia formed by streaming of protoplasm; cytoskeletal elements like microfilaments are also involved.

cards.front: Give two examples of ciliary movement in the human body?
cards.back: • Removal of dust particles by ciliated epithelium of the trachea • Passage of ova through the female reproductive tract

cards.front: What fraction of an adult human's body weight is contributed by muscles?
Name the four special properties of muscle?
cards.back: • Excitability • Contractility • Extensibility • Elasticity

cards.front: Which muscle type is striated and voluntary?
cards.back: Skeletal muscle – closely associated with skeletal components; shows a striped appearance.

cards.front: Where are visceral muscles found, and what are their features?
cards.back: Inner walls of hollow visceral organs (alimentary canal, reproductive tract). They are smooth (non-striated) and involuntary.

cards.front: Which muscle is striated yet involuntary?
cards.back: Cardiac muscle – its cells assemble in a branching pattern.
cards.hint: Trap: striated does not always mean voluntary.

cards.front: Why is a skeletal muscle fibre called a syncytium?
cards.back: Its sarcoplasm contains many nuclei.

cards.front: What is the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and which ion does it store?
cards.back: The endoplasmic reticulum of a muscle fibre; store house of Ca2+.

cards.front: Which protein makes up the light (I) band and which the dark (A) band?
cards.back: • I band (isotropic): actin • A band (anisotropic): myosin
cards.hint: I = Isotropic = light; A = Anisotropic = dark.

cards.front: Which line bisects each I band?
cards.back: The Z line; thin (actin) filaments are firmly attached to it.

cards.front: What is a sarcomere?
cards.back: The portion of a myofibril between two successive Z lines; the functional unit of contraction.
cards.hint: Z line to Z line = one sarcomere.

cards.front: What is the H zone?
cards.back: The central part of the thick filaments not overlapped by thin filaments in a resting muscle.
cards.hint: During contraction the H zone and I band shrink; the A band does not.

cards.front: What is the structure of a thin (actin) filament?
cards.back: Two F (filamentous) actins helically wound; each F-actin is a polymer of monomeric G (globular) actins.

cards.front: Besides actin, which two proteins are part of the thin filament?
cards.back: • Tropomyosin: two filaments running along the F-actin • Troponin: complex at regular intervals on tropomyosin

cards.front: In a resting muscle, what masks the myosin-binding active sites on actin?
cards.back: A subunit of troponin.
cards.hint: Trap: it is troponin, not tropomyosin, per NCERT.

cards.front: Each meromyosin of the thick filament has which two parts?
cards.back: • Heavy meromyosin (HMM): globular head with short arm • Light meromyosin (LMM): tail

cards.front: What enzymatic activity and binding sites does the myosin head have?
cards.back: It is an active ATPase, with binding sites for ATP and active sites for actin.

cards.front: Which theory explains muscle contraction?
cards.back: Sliding filament theory: thin filaments slide over thick filaments.

cards.front: What is a motor unit?
cards.back: A motor neuron along with the muscle fibres connected to it.

cards.front: Which neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction (motor end plate)?
cards.back: Acetylcholine – it generates an action potential in the sarcolemma.

cards.front: Which ion released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum starts contraction, and what does it bind?
cards.back: Ca2+ binds a subunit of troponin, unmasking active sites on actin for myosin.

cards.front: During contraction, which band shortens and which keeps its length?
cards.back: • I band gets reduced • A band retains its length Sarcomere shortens as Z lines are pulled inward.
cards.hint: Trap: A band length does NOT change.

cards.front: What breaks the cross bridge after a power stroke?
cards.back: Binding of a new ATP to the myosin head (after ADP and Pi are released).

cards.front: What brings about muscle relaxation?
cards.back: Ca2+ is pumped back to the sarcoplasmic cisternae, so actin sites are masked again and Z lines return to their original position.

cards.front: What causes muscle fatigue?
cards.back: Accumulation of lactic acid from anaerobic breakdown of glycogen during repeated activation.

cards.front: Red vs white muscle fibres: key differences?
cards.back: • Red: high myoglobin, many mitochondria, aerobic • White: less myoglobin, few mitochondria, more sarcoplasmic reticulum, anaerobic

cards.front: How many bones are in the human skeleton, and how many are axial vs appendicular?
cards.back: 206 bones: axial 80, appendicular 126.
cards.hint: Axial 80 = skull 22 + hyoid 1 + ossicles 6 + vertebrae 26 + sternum 1 + ribs 24.

cards.front: How many cranial and facial bones together make up the skull (excluding hyoid and ear ossicles)?
cards.back: 22: 8 cranial + 14 facial.
cards.hint: Add hyoid (1) and ear ossicles (6) to get 29.

cards.front: Which U-shaped bone lies at the base of the buccal cavity?
cards.back: The hyoid bone (included in the skull).

cards.front: Name the three ear ossicles of each middle ear, from outside inwards?
cards.back: Malleus → Incus → Stapes

cards.front: Why is the human skull called dicondylic?
cards.back: It articulates with the first vertebra, the atlas, by two occipital condyles.

cards.front: How many vertebrae form the human vertebral column, region-wise?
cards.back: 26: cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacral 1 (fused), coccygeal 1 (fused).
cards.hint: C7 T12 L5 S1 C1

cards.front: How many cervical vertebrae do almost all mammals have?
cards.back: Seven, including humans.

cards.front: How many pairs of ribs do humans have, and why are ribs called bicephalic?
cards.back: 12 pairs; each rib has two articulation surfaces on its dorsal end.

cards.front: How are the 12 pairs of human ribs classified?
cards.back: • 1st–7th: true ribs (joined to sternum) • 8th–10th: vertebrochondral (false), join 7th rib by hyaline cartilage • 11th–12th: floating ribs
cards.hint: 7 true + 3 false + 2 floating = 12 pairs.

cards.front: Give the number of carpals, metacarpals and phalanges in each hand?
cards.back: • Carpals: 8 • Metacarpals: 5 • Phalanges: 14
cards.hint: Each limb has 30 bones.

cards.front: How many tarsals are present in each foot, and which is the longest bone?
cards.back: 7 tarsals; the femur (thigh bone) is the longest bone.

cards.front: Where is the scapula located?
cards.back: Dorsal part of the thorax, between the 2nd and 7th ribs; a large triangular flat bone.

cards.front: What is the acromion?
cards.back: The flat expanded process of the spine of the scapula; the clavicle articulates with it.

cards.front: Which cavity of the scapula articulates with the head of the humerus?
cards.back: The glenoid cavity, forming the shoulder joint.

cards.front: Each coxal bone of the pelvic girdle is formed by fusion of which bones?
cards.back: Ilium, ischium and pubis.
cards.hint: Hip bone = I-I-P: ilium, ischium, pubis.

cards.front: Give an example of a fibrous joint?
cards.back: Sutures between flat skull bones forming the cranium; no movement possible.

cards.front: Where are cartilaginous joints found, and how much movement do they allow?
cards.back: Between adjacent vertebrae; they allow limited movement.

cards.front: Which feature defines a synovial joint?
cards.back: A fluid-filled synovial cavity between articulating surfaces; allows considerable movement.

cards.front: Match the joints: atlas–axis, knee, humerus–pectoral girdle?
cards.back: • Atlas–axis: pivot • Knee: hinge • Humerus–pectoral girdle: ball and socket

cards.front: Which synovial joint lies between carpals, and which between carpal and metacarpal of thumb?
cards.back: • Between carpals: gliding • Carpal–metacarpal of thumb: saddle
cards.hint: Trap: thumb joint is saddle, not gliding.

cards.front: What is myasthenia gravis?
cards.back: An autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction causing fatigue, weakening and paralysis of skeletal muscle.
cards.hint: Trap: autoimmune, not genetic (that is muscular dystrophy).
cards.topic: Disorders of muscular and skeletal system

cards.front: What is muscular dystrophy?
cards.back: Progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle, mostly due to a genetic disorder.
cards.hint: Trap: genetic, not autoimmune (that is myasthenia gravis).
cards.topic: Disorders of muscular and skeletal system

cards.front: What causes tetany?
cards.back: Rapid spasms (wild contractions) of muscle due to low Ca2+ in body fluid.
cards.hint: Low Ca<sup>2+</sup> → tetany; low estrogen → osteoporosis.
cards.topic: Disorders of muscular and skeletal system

cards.front: What is osteoporosis, and what is a common cause?
cards.back: Age-related decrease in bone mass raising fracture risk; decreased estrogen is a common cause.
cards.topic: Disorders of muscular and skeletal system

cards.front: Which joint disorder is caused by accumulation of uric acid crystals?
cards.back: Gout.
cards.hint: Arthritis = inflammation of joints in general.
cards.topic: Disorders of muscular and skeletal system

cards.front: Which system provides an organised network of point-to-point connections for quick coordination?
cards.back: The neural system; the endocrine system gives chemical integration through hormones.

cards.front: What type of neural system is found in Hydra?
cards.back: A network of neurons (lower invertebrates).

cards.front: What does the neural system of insects consist of?
cards.back: A brain along with a number of ganglia and neural tissues.

cards.front: What are the two main divisions of the human neural system?
cards.back: • CNS: brain and spinal cord • PNS: all nerves associated with the CNS

cards.front: Afferent vs efferent nerve fibres: what is the difference?
cards.back: • Afferent: tissues/organs → CNS • Efferent: CNS → peripheral tissues/organs
cards.hint: Afferent = Arrives at CNS; Efferent = Exits CNS.

cards.front: Into which two divisions is the PNS divided?
cards.back: • Somatic: CNS → skeletal muscles • Autonomic: CNS → involuntary organs and smooth muscles

cards.front: Into which two parts is the autonomic neural system further classified?
cards.back: Sympathetic and parasympathetic neural systems.

cards.front: What is the visceral nervous system?
cards.back: Part of the PNS: the nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses carrying impulses from CNS to viscera and viscera to CNS.

cards.front: What are the three major parts of a neuron?
cards.back: • Cell body • Dendrites • Axon

cards.front: Where are Nissl's granules found in a neuron?
cards.back: In the cell body and the dendrites.
cards.hint: Trap: not in the axon.

cards.front: In which direction do dendrites transmit impulses?
cards.back: Towards the cell body; they are short, repeatedly branched fibres.

cards.front: In which direction does an axon transmit impulses?
cards.back: Away from the cell body, to a synapse or a neuromuscular junction.

cards.front: What is a synaptic knob?
cards.back: The bulb-like ending of each axon branch; contains synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitters.

cards.front: What is a multipolar neuron, and where is it found?
cards.back: One axon and two or more dendrites; found in the cerebral cortex.

cards.front: What is a bipolar neuron, and where is it found?
cards.back: One axon and one dendrite; found in the retina of the eye.
cards.hint: Multi → cortex; Bi → retina; Uni → embryo.

cards.front: What is a unipolar neuron, and where is it usually found?
cards.back: A cell body with one axon only; usually found in the embryonic stage.

cards.front: Which cells form the myelin sheath around myelinated nerve fibres?
cards.back: Schwann cells.

cards.front: What are nodes of Ranvier?
cards.back: Gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths.

cards.front: Where are myelinated nerve fibres found?
cards.back: In spinal and cranial nerves.

cards.front: How is an unmyelinated nerve fibre enclosed, and where is it common?
cards.back: By a Schwann cell that does not form a myelin sheath; common in autonomous and somatic neural systems.
cards.hint: Myelinated → spinal and cranial nerves.

cards.front: Why are neurons called excitable cells?
cards.back: Their membranes are in a polarised state.
cards.topic: Generation and conduction of nerve impulse

cards.front: At rest, the axonal membrane is more permeable to which ion?
cards.back: K+; it is nearly impermeable to Na+ and impermeable to negatively charged proteins of the axoplasm.
cards.topic: Generation and conduction of nerve impulse

cards.front: How do ion concentrations differ inside and outside a resting axon?
cards.back: • Axoplasm: high K+ and negative proteins, low Na+ • Outside fluid: high Na+, low K+
cards.topic: Generation and conduction of nerve impulse

cards.front: How many Na<sup>+</sup> and K<sup>+</sup> ions does the sodium-potassium pump move per cycle?
cards.back: 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in, by active transport.
cards.hint: 3 out, 2 in.
cards.topic: Generation and conduction of nerve impulse

cards.front: What is the resting potential?
cards.back: The electrical potential difference across a resting (polarised) membrane: outside positive, inside negative.
cards.hint: Polarised = positive outside, negative inside.
cards.topic: Generation and conduction of nerve impulse

cards.front: What happens at the membrane site where a stimulus is applied?
cards.back: It becomes freely permeable to Na+; rapid Na+ influx reverses polarity (outside negative, inside positive) – depolarisation.
cards.hint: Na<sup>+</sup> in = depolarise; K<sup>+</sup> out = repolarise.
cards.topic: Generation and conduction of nerve impulse

cards.front: How is the resting potential restored after an action potential?
cards.back: The rise in Na+ permeability is short-lived; it is followed by a rise in K+ permeability, and K+ diffuses outside.
cards.hint: Repolarisation = K<sup>+</sup> moving out.
cards.topic: Generation and conduction of nerve impulse

cards.front: What is a synapse?
cards.back: A junction formed by membranes of a pre-synaptic and a post-synaptic neuron, which may or may not be separated by a synaptic cleft.

cards.front: What are the two types of synapse?
cards.back: Electrical and chemical synapses.

cards.front: What are the key features of an electrical synapse?
cards.back: Membranes in very close proximity; current flows directly; transmission is faster than chemical synapses but rare in our system.
cards.hint: Trap: faster, yet rare in humans.

cards.front: What is the synaptic cleft?
cards.back: The fluid-filled space separating pre- and post-synaptic membranes at a chemical synapse.

cards.front: What is the sequence of events at a chemical synapse?
cards.back: Impulse reaches axon terminal → vesicles fuse with membrane → neurotransmitter released into cleft → binds receptors on post-synaptic membrane → ion channels open

cards.front: Where are the receptors for neurotransmitters located?
cards.back: On the post-synaptic membrane.

cards.front: What kind of potential can be generated in the post-synaptic neuron?
cards.back: Either excitatory or inhibitory.

cards.front: Name the three cranial meninges from outer to inner?
cards.back: Dura mater → Arachnoid → Pia mater
cards.hint: D-A-P from outside in.

cards.front: Which cranial meninx is in contact with the brain tissue?
cards.back: Pia mater (inner layer); the arachnoid is the very thin middle layer.

cards.front: What are the three major parts of the human brain?
cards.back: Forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.

cards.front: What does the forebrain consist of?
cards.back: Cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus.

cards.front: Which tract of nerve fibres connects the two cerebral hemispheres?
cards.back: The corpus callosum.

cards.front: Why is the cerebral cortex called grey matter?
cards.back: Neuron cell bodies are concentrated there, giving a greyish appearance.

cards.front: What forms the white matter of the cerebral hemispheres?
cards.back: Fibre tracts covered with myelin sheath, forming the inner part; they look opaque white.

cards.front: What are association areas of the cerebral cortex responsible for?
cards.back: Regions neither clearly sensory nor motor; handle complex functions like intersensory associations, memory and communication.

cards.front: Which structure is the major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling?
cards.back: The thalamus, around which the cerebrum wraps.

cards.front: Which centres does the hypothalamus contain?
cards.back: Centres controlling body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking.
cards.hint: Hypothalamus = thermostat plus hunger and thirst centre.

cards.front: Besides its control centres, what does the hypothalamus secrete?
cards.back: Hypothalamic hormones, from groups of neurosecretory cells.
