cards.front: What makes up the limbic system?
cards.back: Inner parts of the cerebral hemispheres with deep structures like the amygdala and hippocampus.

cards.front: Along with the hypothalamus, what does the limbic system regulate?
cards.back: • Sexual behaviour • Emotional reactions (excitement, pleasure, rage, fear) • Motivation

cards.front: Where is the midbrain located?
cards.back: Between the thalamus/hypothalamus of the forebrain and the pons of the hindbrain.

cards.front: Which canal passes through the midbrain?
cards.back: The cerebral aqueduct.

cards.front: What are corpora quadrigemina?
cards.back: Four round swellings (lobes) forming the dorsal portion of the midbrain.
cards.hint: Quadri = four.

cards.front: What are the parts of the hindbrain?
cards.back: Pons, cerebellum and medulla oblongata.

cards.front: What does the pons consist of?
cards.back: Fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain.
cards.hint: Pons = 'bridge' of fibre tracts.

cards.front: Why does the cerebellum have a very convoluted surface?
cards.back: To provide additional space for many more neurons.

cards.front: Which centres are present in the medulla?
cards.back: Centres controlling respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions.
cards.hint: Medulla = vital centres (breathing, heart, gastric).

cards.front: Which parts form the brain stem?
cards.back: Midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata; it connects the brain and spinal cord.
cards.hint: Trap: cerebellum is NOT part of the brain stem.

cards.front: Why are endocrine glands called ductless glands?
cards.back: They lack ducts; their secretions (hormones) are released into the blood.

cards.front: What is the current scientific definition of a hormone?
cards.back: Non-nutrient chemicals that act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts.
cards.hint: Classical definition: made by endocrine glands, carried by blood to a distant target.

cards.front: Where is the hypothalamus located?
cards.back: In the basal part of the diencephalon (forebrain).

cards.front: What are the two types of hypothalamic hormones?
cards.back: Releasing hormones (stimulate pituitary secretion) and inhibiting hormones (inhibit it).

cards.front: Which hypothalamic hormone inhibits release of growth hormone from the pituitary?
cards.back: Somatostatin.

cards.front: How do hypothalamic hormones reach the anterior pituitary?
cards.back: Through a portal circulatory system; the posterior pituitary is under direct neural control.

cards.front: Where is the pituitary gland located?
cards.back: In a bony cavity, the sella turcica, attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk.

cards.front: What are the two parts of the adenohypophysis?
cards.back: Pars distalis and pars intermedia.

cards.front: Which hormones are produced by the pars distalis (anterior pituitary)?
cards.back: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH
cards.hint: Mnemonic FLAT PiG: FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, PRL, GH.

cards.front: Which hormone does the pars intermedia secrete?
cards.back: Only MSH; in humans the pars intermedia is almost merged with the pars distalis.

cards.front: Which hormones does the neurohypophysis store and release, and where are they made?
cards.back: Oxytocin and vasopressin; synthesised by the hypothalamus and transported axonally.
cards.hint: Trap: posterior pituitary does not synthesise them.

cards.front: What do over-secretion and low secretion of GH in childhood cause?
cards.back: • Excess: gigantism • Low: stunted growth – pituitary dwarfism
cards.hint: Same excess in adults → acromegaly.

cards.front: What is acromegaly?
cards.back: Excess GH in adults, especially middle age; severe disfigurement, especially of the face; often goes undetected for years.

cards.front: What are the roles of LH and FSH in males?
cards.back: • LH: synthesis and secretion of androgens from testis • FSH with androgens: regulates spermatogenesis

cards.front: What are the roles of LH and FSH in females?
cards.back: • LH: induces ovulation of Graafian follicles; maintains the corpus luteum • FSH: growth and development of ovarian follicles

cards.front: What are the actions of oxytocin?
cards.back: Contraction of uterus at childbirth and milk ejection from mammary glands.

cards.front: Why is vasopressin called anti-diuretic hormone (ADH)?
cards.back: It acts on distal tubules of the kidney to resorb water and electrolytes, reducing water loss in urine (diuresis).

cards.front: What causes diabetes insipidus?
cards.back: Impaired synthesis or release of ADH, so kidneys cannot conserve water → water loss and dehydration.
cards.hint: Trap: NOT related to insulin.

cards.front: Where is the pineal gland located, and which hormone does it secrete?
cards.back: On the dorsal side of the forebrain; secretes melatonin.

cards.front: What are the roles of melatonin?
cards.back: Regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm – sleep-wake cycle, body temperature; also influences metabolism, pigmentation, menstrual cycle and defence.

cards.front: What connects the two lobes of the thyroid gland?
cards.back: The isthmus, a thin flap of connective tissue; the lobes lie on either side of the trachea.

cards.front: Which thyroid cells synthesise T<sub>4</sub> and T<sub>3</sub>, and what are their full names?
cards.back: Follicular cells: T4 = tetraiodothyronine (thyroxine); T3 = triiodothyronine.

cards.front: What does iodine deficiency in diet cause?
cards.back: Hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland – goitre.

cards.front: What is the effect of hypothyroidism during pregnancy on the baby?
cards.back: Cretinism: stunted growth, mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin, deaf-mutism.

cards.front: What does hypothyroidism cause in adult women?
cards.back: Irregular menstrual cycle.

cards.front: What are the features of exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease)?
cards.back: A form of hyperthyroidism: enlarged thyroid, protruding eyeballs, increased BMR, weight loss.
cards.hint: Exophthalmos = protruding eyeballs.

cards.front: Which conditions of the thyroid lead to hyperthyroidism, per NCERT?
cards.back: Cancer of the thyroid or development of nodules.

cards.front: What are the functions of thyroid hormones?
cards.back: • Regulate BMR • Support RBC formation • Control carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism; water and electrolyte balance

cards.front: Which thyroid hormone regulates blood calcium level?
cards.back: Thyrocalcitonin (TCT), a protein hormone.
cards.hint: TCT and PTH together maintain Ca<sup>2+</sup> balance.

cards.front: How many parathyroid glands are there, and where?
cards.back: Four, on the back side of the thyroid – one pair in each lobe.

cards.front: How does PTH raise blood Ca<sup>2+</sup>?
cards.back: • Stimulates bone resorption (demineralisation) • Ca2+ reabsorption by renal tubules • Ca2+ absorption from digested food
cards.hint: PTH is a hypercalcemic hormone.

cards.front: Where is the thymus located?
cards.back: Between the lungs, behind the sternum, on the ventral side of the aorta.

cards.front: What is the role of thymosins?
cards.back: Differentiation of T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity); also promote antibody production (humoral immunity).
cards.hint: Thymus degenerates with age → fewer thymosins → weaker immunity.

cards.front: Which hormones does the adrenal medulla secrete?
cards.back: Adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine) – the catecholamines.

cards.front: Give the effects of catecholamines?
cards.back: Alertness, pupil dilation, piloerection, sweating; raise heart beat, heart contraction and respiration; glycogen breakdown raises blood glucose.
cards.hint: Fight-or-flight hormones, rapidly released in stress.

cards.front: Name the layers of the adrenal cortex from inner to outer?
cards.back: Zona reticularis → Zona fasciculata → Zona glomerulosa
cards.hint: Outer to inner: GFR – glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis.

cards.front: What are the metabolic actions of glucocorticoids?
cards.back: Stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, proteolysis; inhibit cellular uptake and use of amino acids.

cards.front: Besides metabolism, what are the actions of cortisol?
cards.back: Maintains cardiovascular and kidney functions; anti-inflammatory; suppresses immune response; stimulates RBC production.

cards.front: What is the main mineralocorticoid, and how does it act?
cards.back: Aldosterone: at renal tubules, reabsorption of Na+ and water; excretion of K+ and phosphate.
cards.hint: Aldosterone: Na<sup>+</sup> kept, K<sup>+</sup> lost.

cards.front: What role do adrenal androgens play?
cards.back: Growth of axial, pubic and facial hair during puberty.

cards.front: How many Islets of Langerhans are there in the human pancreas?
cards.back: About 1 to 2 million, forming 1–2% of pancreatic tissue.

cards.front: Which hormones do α-cells and β-cells of the islets secrete?
cards.back: • α-cells: glucagon • β-cells: insulin

cards.front: How does glucagon cause hyperglycemia?
cards.back: Acts mainly on hepatocytes: stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; reduces cellular glucose uptake.
cards.hint: Glucagon = hyperglycemic; insulin = hypoglycemic.

cards.front: On which cells does insulin mainly act, and with what effect?
cards.back: Hepatocytes and adipocytes: increases glucose uptake and use, and glycogenesis → hypoglycemia.

cards.front: What is diabetes mellitus associated with?
cards.back: Prolonged hyperglycemia, loss of glucose in urine and formation of ketone bodies; treated with insulin therapy.
cards.hint: Trap: diabetes insipidus is due to ADH, not insulin.

cards.front: Which testis cells produce androgens, and where are they?
cards.back: Leydig (interstitial) cells in the intertubular spaces; mainly testosterone.

cards.front: Which ovarian structures secrete estrogen and progesterone?
cards.back: • Estrogen: mainly growing ovarian follicles • Progesterone: corpus luteum

cards.front: What does progesterone do in the mammary glands?
cards.back: Stimulates formation of alveoli (milk-storing sacs) and milk secretion; also supports pregnancy.

cards.front: Which heart hormone lowers blood pressure, and how?
cards.back: Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF) from atrial walls causes dilation of blood vessels.
cards.topic: Hormones of heart, kidney and GI tract

cards.front: Which kidney cells secrete erythropoietin, and what does it do?
cards.back: Juxtaglomerular cells; stimulates erythropoiesis (RBC formation).
cards.topic: Hormones of heart, kidney and GI tract

cards.front: Match the GI hormones with their actions: gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP?
cards.back: • Gastrin: HCl and pepsinogen • Secretin: water and HCO3– from pancreas • CCK: pancreatic enzymes and bile • GIP: inhibits gastric secretion and motility
cards.topic: Hormones of heart, kidney and GI tract

cards.front: Hormones acting through membrane-bound receptors use which messengers?
cards.back: Second messengers such as cyclic AMP, IP3, Ca2+; the hormone usually does not enter the cell.

cards.front: Which hormones act through intracellular receptors, and what do they regulate?
cards.back: Steroid hormones and iodothyronines; they mostly regulate gene expression or chromosome function.

cards.front: Classify chemically: insulin, cortisol, thyroxine, epinephrine?
cards.back: • Insulin: peptide • Cortisol: steroid • Thyroxine: iodothyronine • Epinephrine: amino-acid derivative

cards.front: Why is a typical angiosperm anther called dithecous?
cards.back: It is bilobed and each lobe has two theca.
cards.hint: 2 lobes × 2 theca = 4 microsporangia.

cards.front: How many microsporangia does a typical anther have?
cards.back: Four, at the corners – two in each lobe; they become pollen sacs.

cards.front: Name the four wall layers of a microsporangium from outer to inner?
cards.back: Epidermis → Endothecium → Middle layers → Tapetum

cards.front: What is the function of the tapetum?
cards.back: Nourishes the developing pollen grains.
cards.hint: Its cells have dense cytoplasm and often more than one nucleus.

cards.front: What is microsporogenesis?
cards.back: Formation of microspores from a pollen mother cell by meiosis; they form a microspore tetrad.

cards.front: What is the exine made of, and why is it remarkable?
cards.back: Sporopollenin – one of the most resistant organic materials; withstands high temperature, strong acids and alkali; no enzyme degrades it.
cards.hint: Sporopollenin is why pollen is well preserved as fossils.

cards.front: What are germ pores?
cards.back: Apertures on the exine where sporopollenin is absent; the pollen tube emerges through one of them.

cards.front: What is the intine made of?
cards.back: Cellulose and pectin; it is thin and continuous.

cards.front: Vegetative cell vs generative cell of a pollen grain: how do they differ?
cards.back: • Vegetative: bigger, abundant food, large irregular nucleus • Generative: small, spindle-shaped, floats in vegetative cell cytoplasm

cards.front: What percentage of angiosperms shed pollen at the 2-celled stage?
cards.back: Over 60%; in the rest the generative cell divides into two male gametes before shedding (3-celled stage).

cards.front: Which weed causes pollen allergy and how did it reach India?
cards.back: Parthenium (carrot grass); came as a contaminant with imported wheat.

cards.front: How long do pollen grains of rice and wheat stay viable?
cards.back: They lose viability within 30 minutes of release.
cards.hint: Contrast: some Rosaceae, Leguminosae, Solanaceae – months.

cards.front: Members of which families keep pollen viable for months?
cards.back: Some members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae.

cards.front: Give examples of ovaries with one ovule and with many ovules?
cards.back: • One: wheat, paddy, mango • Many: papaya, water melon, orchids

cards.front: What are the funicle and the hilum of an ovule?
cards.back: • Funicle: stalk attaching ovule to placenta • Hilum: junction of ovule and funicle

cards.front: Micropyle vs chalaza: what is each?
cards.back: • Micropyle: small opening at the tip where integuments are absent • Chalaza: basal part, opposite the micropylar end

cards.front: In which region of the nucellus does the megaspore mother cell differentiate?
cards.back: The micropylar region.

cards.front: What happens to the four megaspores in most flowering plants?
cards.back: One is functional; the other three degenerate.
cards.hint: Monosporic: only one megaspore forms the embryo sac.

cards.front: How many mitotic divisions form the embryo sac, and what is special about them?
cards.back: Three, strictly free nuclear – walls form only after the 8-nucleate stage.

cards.front: How many nuclei and cells does a typical mature embryo sac have?
cards.back: 8-nucleate, 7-celled.
cards.hint: Central cell has 2 polar nuclei, so 8 nuclei but 7 cells.

cards.front: What does the egg apparatus consist of?
cards.back: Two synergids and one egg cell, at the micropylar end.

cards.front: What is the filiform apparatus and its role?
cards.back: Cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip of synergids; guide the pollen tube into the synergid.
cards.hint: Trap: belongs to synergids, not the egg cell.

cards.front: Autogamy, geitonogamy, xenogamy: define each?
cards.back: • Autogamy: same flower • Geitonogamy: another flower, same plant • Xenogamy: flower of a different plant

cards.front: What are cleistogamous flowers?
cards.back: Flowers that never open; anthers and stigma lie close, so they are invariably autogamous with assured seed-set.
cards.hint: Cleisto = closed; chasmo = open.

cards.front: Name plants that bear both chasmogamous and cleistogamous flowers?
cards.back: Viola (common pansy), Oxalis, Commelina.

cards.front: What are the features of wind-pollinated flowers?
cards.back: • Light, non-sticky pollen • Well-exposed stamens • Large, often feathery stigma • Single ovule per ovary; many flowers in an inflorescence

cards.front: Water pollination is limited to about how many genera, mostly of which group?
cards.back: About 30 genera, mostly monocotyledons.

cards.front: Give examples of water-pollinated plants?
cards.back: • Fresh water: Vallisneria, Hydrilla • Marine sea-grass: Zostera

cards.front: Which aquatic plants are NOT water-pollinated?
cards.back: Water hyacinth and water lily – flowers emerge above water; pollinated by insects or wind.
cards.hint: Trap: aquatic does not mean water-pollinated.

cards.front: How does pollination occur in Vallisneria?
cards.back: Female flower reaches the surface by a long stalk; male flowers/pollen released on the surface are carried passively by water currents.

cards.front: How does pollination occur in sea-grasses?
cards.back: Female flowers stay submerged; long, ribbon-like pollen is released inside the water and carried passively.

cards.front: Besides insects, birds and bats, which animals are reported as pollinators?
cards.back: • Primates: lemurs • Arboreal rodents • Reptiles: gecko lizard, garden lizard

cards.front: Which plant has the tallest flower, and what reward does it offer insects?
cards.back: Amorphophallus (about 6 feet); gives a safe place to lay eggs.

cards.front: Describe the relationship between Yucca and its moth?
cards.back: The moth lays eggs in the locule of the ovary and pollinates the flower; larvae emerge as seeds develop. Neither completes its life cycle without the other.

cards.front: List the outbreeding devices in flowering plants?
cards.back: • Pollen release and stigma receptivity not synchronised • Anther and stigma at different positions • Self-incompatibility • Unisexual flowers

cards.front: What is self-incompatibility?
cards.back: A genetic mechanism preventing self-pollen from fertilising ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or tube growth in the pistil.

cards.front: Monoecious vs dioecious plants: which pollination does each prevent?
cards.back: • Monoecious (castor, maize): prevents autogamy, NOT geitonogamy • Dioecious (papaya): prevents both

cards.front: What path does the pollen tube take inside the ovule?
cards.back: Enters through the micropyle, then into one synergid through the filiform apparatus.

cards.front: What is emasculation, and when is it needed?
cards.back: Removal of anthers from a flower bud before dehiscence, using forceps; needed if the female parent has bisexual flowers.

cards.front: What is bagging in artificial hybridisation?
cards.back: Covering the emasculated flower with a bag, usually of butter paper, to prevent contamination by unwanted pollen.

cards.front: Syngamy vs triple fusion: what fuses in each?
cards.back: • Syngamy: male gamete + egg → diploid zygote • Triple fusion: male gamete + 2 polar nuclei → triploid PEN
cards.hint: PEN is 3n: one male gamete + two polar nuclei.

cards.front: Why is fertilisation in angiosperms called double fertilisation?
cards.back: Two fusions – syngamy and triple fusion – occur in one embryo sac; unique to flowering plants.

cards.front: Coconut water and white kernel are which types of endosperm?
cards.back: • Water: free-nuclear endosperm • White kernel: cellular endosperm
cards.hint: Trap: coconut water is NOT cellular.

cards.front: Give examples where endosperm is consumed before seed maturation and where it persists?
cards.back: • Consumed: pea, groundnut, beans • Persists: castor, coconut

cards.front: What is the sequence of stages in embryo development?
cards.back: Zygote → proembryo → globular → heart-shaped → mature embryo

cards.front: In a dicot embryo, what do the epicotyl and hypocotyl end in?
cards.back: • Epicotyl: plumule (stem tip) • Hypocotyl: radicle (root tip, covered by root cap)

cards.front: Coleorhiza vs coleoptile: what does each enclose?
cards.back: • Coleorhiza: radicle and root cap • Coleoptile: shoot apex and leaf primordia
cards.hint: Rhiza = root, so coleorhiza covers the root end; coleoptile covers the shoot end.

cards.front: Albuminous vs non-albuminous seeds: give examples?
cards.back: • Non-albuminous: pea, groundnut • Albuminous: wheat, maize, barley, castor

cards.front: What is perisperm, and give examples?
cards.back: Residual persistent nucellus in seeds, e.g. black pepper and beet.
cards.hint: Trap: perisperm is nucellus, not endosperm.

cards.front: What are false fruits? Give examples?
cards.back: Fruits where the thalamus also contributes, e.g. apple, strawberry, cashew.

cards.front: What are parthenocarpic fruits?
cards.back: Fruits formed without fertilisation, e.g. banana; can be induced by growth hormones and are seedless.
cards.hint: Trap: parthenocarpy = seedless fruit; apomixis = seed without fertilisation.

cards.front: Which is the oldest viable seed recorded, and how old?
cards.back: Lupinus arcticus (lupine) from the Arctic Tundra; germinated after about 10,000 years.
cards.hint: Also: 2000-year-old date palm seed from near the Dead Sea.

cards.front: What is apomixis?
cards.back: Production of seeds without fertilisation – asexual reproduction mimicking sexual; seen in Asteraceae and grasses.
cards.hint: Apomictic hybrids show no segregation, so seed need not be bought every year.

cards.front: How do embryos form in apomictic Citrus and mango varieties?
cards.back: Nucellar cells around the embryo sac divide, protrude into it and develop into embryos.

cards.front: What is polyembryony?
cards.back: Occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed, e.g. in Citrus.

cards.front: Why are the human testes located outside the abdominal cavity, in the scrotum?
cards.back: The scrotum keeps the testes about 2–2.5 °C lower than normal body temperature, which is needed for spermatogenesis.

cards.front: Approximately how many testicular lobules are present in each human testis?
cards.back: About 250 compartments called testicular lobules.

cards.front: How many seminiferous tubules does each testicular lobule contain?
cards.back: One to three highly coiled seminiferous tubules.

cards.front: Which two types of cells line the inside of a seminiferous tubule?
cards.back: • Male germ cells (spermatogonia) • Sertoli cells (provide nutrition to germ cells)

cards.front: Which cells, found in the interstitial spaces outside seminiferous tubules, synthesise androgens?
cards.back: Leydig cells (interstitial cells)
cards.hint: Trap: Sertoli cells nourish germ cells; Leydig cells make testosterone.

cards.front: Give the correct order of male accessory ducts carrying sperm out of the testis.
cards.back: Seminiferous tubules → rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra
cards.hint: Rete–Efferentia–Epididymis–Deferens

cards.front: The vas deferens joins the duct of which gland to form the ejaculatory duct?
cards.back: The duct of the seminal vesicle.

cards.front: Name the male accessory glands. Which are paired?
cards.back: • Seminal vesicles – paired • Bulbourethral glands – paired • Prostate – single

cards.front: Seminal plasma is rich in which substances?
cards.back: Fructose, calcium and certain enzymes.

cards.front: What is the function of bulbourethral gland secretion?
cards.back: It helps in lubrication of the penis.

cards.front: What is the approximate length of a human ovary?
cards.back: About 2–4 cm in length.

cards.front: Name the three parts of the fallopian tube from ovary to uterus.
cards.back: Infundibulum (with fimbriae) → ampulla (wider part) → isthmus (narrow lumen, joins uterus)
cards.hint: I-A-I: Infundibulum, Ampulla, Isthmus

cards.front: What are fimbriae and what is their role?
cards.back: Finger-like projections at the edge of the infundibulum that help collect the ovum after ovulation.

cards.front: Which structures together form the birth canal?
cards.back: The cervical canal along with the vagina.

cards.front: Name the three layers of the uterine wall from outside to inside.
cards.back: • Perimetrium – thin outer membrane • Myometrium – thick smooth muscle • Endometrium – inner glandular layer

cards.front: Which uterine layer shows strong contractions during delivery, and which undergoes cyclical changes?
cards.back: • Myometrium – strong contractions at delivery • Endometrium – cyclical changes in menstrual cycle

cards.front: Name the parts of the female external genitalia.
cards.back: Mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, hymen and clitoris.
cards.hint: Trap: an intact hymen is not a reliable indicator of virginity.

cards.front: How many mammary lobes are present in each mammary gland?
cards.back: 15–20 mammary lobes, containing clusters of cells called alveoli.

cards.front: Give the path of milk from mammary alveoli to the outside.
cards.back: Alveoli → mammary tubules → mammary duct → mammary ampulla → lactiferous duct

cards.front: When does spermatogenesis begin in human males?
cards.back: At puberty.
cards.hint: Contrast: oogenesis begins in the embryonic stage.

cards.front: Give the ploidy of spermatogonia, primary spermatocytes, secondary spermatocytes and spermatids.
cards.back: • Spermatogonia – 2n (46) • Primary spermatocyte – 2n (46) • Secondary spermatocyte – n (23) • Spermatid – n (23)
cards.hint: Meiosis I halves the number; secondary onward are haploid.

cards.front: Spermiogenesis vs spermiation: key difference?
cards.back: • Spermiogenesis: transformation of spermatids into spermatozoa • Spermiation: release of sperms from seminiferous tubules

cards.front: During spermatogenesis, LH and FSH act on which cells respectively?
cards.back: • LH → Leydig cells (androgen secretion) • FSH → Sertoli cells (factors for spermiogenesis)
cards.hint: Trap: LH acts on Leydig, not Sertoli.

cards.front: What is the acrosome and what does it contain?
cards.back: A cap-like structure covering the anterior part of the sperm head, filled with enzymes that help in fertilisation of the ovum.

cards.front: Which part of the sperm contains numerous mitochondria, and why?
cards.back: The middle piece; mitochondria provide energy for sperm motility.

cards.front: How many sperms does a human male ejaculate at a time?
cards.back: About 200 to 300 million sperms.

cards.front: For normal fertility, what percentage of sperms must show normal shape/size and vigorous motility?
cards.back: • At least 60% with normal shape and size • At least 40% with vigorous motility
cards.hint: 60 for shape, 40 for motion.

cards.front: When is oogenesis initiated in the human female?
cards.back: During the embryonic (fetal) stage, when a couple of million oogonia form in each fetal ovary; no more are formed after birth.

cards.front: At which stage do primary oocytes remain temporarily arrested?
cards.back: Prophase I of meiosis I.

cards.front: How many primary follicles remain in each ovary at puberty?
cards.back: Only about 60,000–80,000; a large number degenerate between birth and puberty.

cards.front: Which ovarian follicle is characterised by a fluid-filled cavity called the antrum?
cards.back: The tertiary follicle.

cards.front: In which follicle does the primary oocyte complete meiosis I, and what are the products?
cards.back: In the tertiary follicle; products are a large haploid secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body.
cards.hint: Unequal division: the oocyte keeps most cytoplasm.

cards.front: What is the new membrane formed around the secondary oocyte in a Graafian follicle?
cards.back: Zona pellucida.

cards.front: What are menarche and menopause?
cards.back: • Menarche: first menstruation, at puberty • Menopause: cessation of the cycle, around 50 years

cards.front: What is the average duration of a human menstrual cycle, and how long does the menstrual flow last?
cards.back: Cycle: about 28/29 days; menstrual flow: 3–5 days.

cards.front: What causes the menstrual flow?
cards.back: Breakdown of the endometrial lining and its blood vessels when the released ovum is not fertilised.

cards.front: Which hormonal event induces ovulation, and around which day of the cycle?
cards.back: The LH surge (rapid secretion of LH reaching maximum at mid-cycle), around the 14th day.

cards.front: Which hormone is secreted in large amounts by the corpus luteum, and what does it do?
cards.back: Progesterone; it is essential for maintaining the endometrium for implantation and pregnancy.

cards.front: The follicular phase is also called which phase with respect to the uterus?
cards.back: Proliferative phase – the endometrium regenerates through proliferation.
cards.hint: Luteal phase = secretory phase.

cards.front: In which region of the fallopian tube does fertilisation occur?
cards.back: Ampullary region (ampulla) of the fallopian tube.
cards.hint: Trap: NOT isthmus or uterus.

cards.front: What prevents polyspermy in humans?
cards.back: Sperm contact with the zona pellucida induces changes in the membrane that block entry of additional sperms.

cards.front: Entry of sperm triggers completion of meiosis II in the secondary oocyte. What are the products?
cards.back: A haploid ootid (ovum) and a second polar body.

cards.front: Whose gamete determines the sex of a human baby?
cards.back: The father's sperm (X or Y); all ova carry X.

cards.front: What is a morula?
cards.back: An embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres formed by mitotic cleavage of the zygote.

cards.front: Name the two parts of a blastocyst and what each forms.
cards.back: • Trophoblast – outer layer; attaches to endometrium • Inner cell mass – differentiates into the embryo

cards.front: What is implantation?
cards.back: Embedding of the blastocyst in the endometrium of the uterus after the trophoblast attaches to it.

cards.front: Which hormones are produced by the human placenta?
cards.back: hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestogens.
cards.hint: Trap: relaxin is secreted by the ovary in later pregnancy.

cards.front: The placenta is formed by interdigitation of which two tissues?
cards.back: Chorionic villi and the uterine tissue.

cards.front: Which three germ layers develop from the inner cell mass after implantation?
cards.back: Ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.

cards.front: Which cells of the inner cell mass can give rise to all tissues and organs?
cards.back: Stem cells.

cards.front: Match the month of pregnancy: heart forms; limbs and digits form; first movements and head hair appear.
cards.back: • After 1 month – heart • End of 2nd month – limbs and digits • During 5th month – first movements, hair on head

cards.front: By the end of which period are most major organ systems formed in the human fetus?
cards.back: By the end of 12 weeks (first trimester).

cards.front: By the end of 24 weeks (second trimester), what changes are seen in the fetus?
cards.back: Body covered with fine hair, eyelids separate and eyelashes are formed.

cards.front: What signal triggers parturition, and which hormone does it release?
cards.back: Signals from the fully developed foetus and placenta cause mild uterine contractions (foetal ejection reflex), which trigger release of oxytocin from the maternal pituitary.

cards.front: What is colostrum and why is it important?
cards.back: Milk produced in the initial few days of lactation; it contains antibodies (IgA) that give the newborn resistance.

cards.front: According to WHO, what does reproductive health mean?
cards.back: A total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social.
cards.hint: Trap: it is NOT just absence of reproductive disease.

cards.front: In which year did India initiate its national 'family planning' programme?
cards.back: 1951; India was among the first countries in the world to do so.
cards.hint: Trap: 1951 is family planning; MTP was legalised in 1971.

cards.front: What is the improved, wider programme covering reproduction-related areas in India called?
cards.back: Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes.

cards.front: Why has a statutory ban been imposed on amniocentesis in India?
cards.back: To prevent its misuse for sex determination, which leads to female foeticide.

cards.front: Amniocentesis is a foetal test based on what?
cards.back: Analysing the chromosomal pattern of cells in the amniotic fluid around the developing embryo.

cards.front: Name two reasons NCERT gives for the population explosion.
cards.back: • Rapid decline in death rate, MMR and IMR • Increase in number of people in reproducible age
cards.hint: MMR = maternal mortality rate; IMR = infant mortality rate.

cards.front: What was India's approximate population at Independence, and what mark did it approach by 2000?
cards.back: About 350 million at Independence; it reached close to the billion mark by 2000.

cards.front: India's population crossed which figure in May 2011?
cards.back: 1.2 billion.

cards.front: What are the legal marriageable ages in India for females and males?
cards.back: 18 years for females and 21 years for males.
cards.hint: Girls 18, boys 21.

cards.front: List the characteristics of an ideal contraceptive.
cards.back: User-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible, with no or least side-effects, and not interfering with sexual drive or the act.

cards.front: Periodic abstinence: avoiding coitus during which days of the menstrual cycle?
cards.back: From day 10 to day 17, the fertile period when ovulation is expected.
cards.hint: Ovulation expected around day 14, so avoid days 10–17.

cards.front: What is coitus interruptus?
cards.back: The withdrawal method: the male withdraws the penis from the vagina just before ejaculation to avoid insemination.

cards.front: Lactational amenorrhea is effective as a contraceptive for how long after parturition?
cards.back: Up to a maximum of six months, while the mother breastfeeds fully (no ovulation and no menstruation).
cards.hint: Amenorrhea = absence of menstruation.

cards.front: Why are natural methods of contraception considered to have few side-effects but a high failure rate?
cards.back: No medicines or devices are used, so side-effects are almost nil, but chances of failure are high.

cards.front: Name the popular brand of condom for males in India.
cards.back: 'Nirodh'.

cards.front: Besides preventing conception, what extra benefit do condoms provide?
cards.back: Protection from STIs and AIDS.
cards.hint: Only barrier method NCERT credits with STI protection.

cards.front: Name the female barrier devices made of rubber that cover the cervix.
cards.back: Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults; they are reusable.

cards.front: Why are spermicidal creams, jellies and foams used with barrier devices?
cards.back: To increase contraceptive efficiency of barriers.

cards.front: Classify IUDs into three types with one example each.
cards.back: • Non-medicated – Lippes loop • Copper-releasing – CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375 • Hormone-releasing – Progestasert, LNG-20

cards.front: Odd one out: CuT, Multiload 375, LNG-20, Cu7?
cards.back: LNG-20 – it is a hormone-releasing IUD; others are copper-releasing.

cards.front: How do IUDs prevent pregnancy?
cards.back: They increase phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus; Cu ions suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity.

cards.front: How do hormone-releasing IUDs act?
cards.back: They make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms.

cards.front: IUDs are ideal for which group of women?
cards.back: Females who want to delay pregnancy and/or space children.

cards.front: Oral contraceptive pills contain which hormones?
cards.back: Progestogens alone or progestogen–estrogen combinations.

cards.front: How are combined oral pills taken?
cards.back: Daily for 21 days, starting preferably within the first five days of the cycle; repeated after 7 days gap.

cards.front: How do oral contraceptive pills prevent conception?
cards.back: • Inhibit ovulation and implantation • Alter quality of cervical mucus to retard sperm entry

cards.front: What is 'Saheli', and who developed it?
cards.back: A new oral contraceptive for females developed by CDRI, Lucknow.

cards.front: Saheli: how often is it taken, and is it steroidal?
cards.back: Once a week; it is a non-steroidal preparation with very few side effects and high contraceptive value.
cards.hint: Trap: Saheli is NOT a daily pill.

cards.front: Within what time after coitus must emergency contraceptives be used?
cards.back: Within 72 hours of coitus (rape or casual unprotected intercourse).
cards.hint: 72 hours = 3 days.

cards.front: Name methods of emergency contraception.
cards.back: Administration of progestogens or progestogen–estrogen combinations, or IUDs, within 72 hours.

cards.front: Vasectomy vs tubectomy?
cards.back: • Vasectomy: small part of vas deferens removed or tied (males) • Tubectomy: small part of fallopian tube removed or tied (females)

cards.front: What is the main drawback of surgical methods (sterilisation)?
cards.back: Reversibility is very poor; they are a terminal method.

cards.front: In which year did the Government of India legalise MTP?
cards.back: 1971, with strict conditions to avoid misuse.
cards.hint: Trap: NOT 1951 (family planning).

cards.front: Roughly how many MTPs are performed worldwide each year, and what fraction of conceptions is this?
cards.back: About 45 to 50 million per year, nearly 1/5th of total conceived pregnancies.

cards.front: During which period are MTPs considered relatively safe?
cards.back: During the first trimester, i.e. up to 12 weeks of pregnancy.

cards.front: Why is MTP during the second trimester risky?
cards.back: Second-trimester abortions are much riskier for the mother, and many are done illegally by unqualified quacks, which can be fatal.

cards.front: Give 4 examples of sexually transmitted infections (STIs).
cards.back: Gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B, HIV (any 4).

cards.front: Which STIs are NOT completely curable?
cards.back: Hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV infections.
cards.hint: B-H-H: hepatitis-B, herpes, HIV.

cards.front: Hepatitis-B and HIV can be transmitted by which routes besides sexual contact?
cards.back: Sharing injection needles, surgical instruments, blood transfusion, or from infected mother to foetus.

cards.front: Which age group is most vulnerable to STIs?
cards.back: People in the 15–24 years age group.

cards.front: Name early symptoms of STIs.
cards.back: Itching, fluid discharge, slight pain and swellings in the genital region.

cards.front: Name complications of untreated STIs.
cards.back: Pelvic inflammatory diseases (PID), abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancies, infertility or cancer of the reproductive tract.

cards.front: What simple principles help a person avoid contracting STIs?
cards.back: • Avoid sex with unknown or multiple partners • Always use condoms during coitus • Consult a doctor early if in doubt

cards.front: What is IVF–ET popularly called?
cards.back: Test tube baby programme: in vitro fertilisation followed by embryo transfer.

cards.front: ZIFT vs IUT: what is transferred, and where?
cards.back: • ZIFT: zygote or early embryo (up to 8 blastomeres) into the fallopian tube • IUT: embryo with more than 8 blastomeres into the uterus
cards.hint: Up to 8 → tube; more than 8 → uterus.

cards.front: What is GIFT and for whom is it used?
cards.back: Gamete intra fallopian transfer: transfer of an ovum from a donor into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment.
cards.hint: GIFT moves a gamete; ZIFT moves a zygote.

cards.front: What is ICSI?
cards.back: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection: a sperm is directly injected into the ovum in the laboratory to form an embryo.

cards.front: Artificial insemination (AI) is used when the male partner has which problem?
cards.back: Inability to inseminate the female or very low sperm counts; semen is introduced into the vagina or uterus (IUI).
cards.hint: IUI = intra-uterine insemination.

cards.front: Name a social alternative NCERT suggests for childless couples besides ART.
cards.back: Legal adoption of orphaned and destitute children.

cards.front: During which years did Gregor Mendel conduct his hybridisation experiments on garden peas?
cards.back: For seven years, 1856–1863.

cards.front: How many pairs of contrasting traits of garden pea did Mendel study?
cards.back: Seven pairs of contrasting traits.

cards.front: How many true-breeding pea varieties did Mendel select?
cards.back: 14 true-breeding pea plant varieties (pairs differing in one character).
cards.hint: 7 traits × 2 contrasting forms = 14

cards.front: What is a true-breeding line?
cards.back: A line that, having undergone continuous self-pollination, shows stable trait inheritance and expression for several generations.

cards.front: In pea, which are dominant: green or yellow seed; green or yellow pod?
cards.back: • Seed colour: yellow dominant • Pod colour: green dominant
cards.hint: Trap: yellow wins in seeds, green wins in pods.

cards.front: Which flower position and pod shape are dominant in Mendel's pea traits?
cards.back: • Flower position: axial (over terminal) • Pod shape: inflated (over constricted)

cards.front: What did Mendel call the units that pass from parent to offspring through gametes?
cards.back: 'Factors'; now called genes.

cards.front: What are alleles?
cards.back: Slightly different forms of the same gene coding for a pair of contrasting traits.

cards.front: Monohybrid cross: give the F2 phenotypic and genotypic ratios.
cards.back: • Phenotypic: 3 : 1 • Genotypic: 1 : 2 : 1

cards.front: Who developed the Punnett square?
cards.back: British geneticist Reginald C. Punnett.

cards.front: What is a test cross?
cards.back: Crossing an organism of dominant phenotype (unknown genotype) with a recessive parent to determine its genotype.

cards.front: Monohybrid test cross of a heterozygous tall plant (Tt × tt): give the ratio.
cards.back: 1 : 1 (tall : dwarf).
cards.hint: Homozygous TT × tt gives all tall.

cards.front: State the Law of Segregation.
cards.back: Alleles do not blend; the two alleles of a parent segregate during gamete formation so each gamete receives only one of them.

cards.front: Give the NCERT example of incomplete dominance and its F2 ratio.
cards.back: Flower colour in dog flower (snapdragon, Antirrhinum sp.); F2 phenotypic ratio = genotypic ratio = 1 : 2 : 1 (red : pink : white).

cards.front: Why is the recessive allele often not expressed in a heterozygote?
cards.back: It usually produces a non-functional or less efficient enzyme (or none), so the phenotype depends only on the functional (dominant) allele.

cards.front: In co-dominance, how does the F1 phenotype differ from incomplete dominance?
cards.back: In co-dominance the F1 resembles both parents; in incomplete dominance it is intermediate.

cards.front: Which gene controls the human ABO blood group, and how many alleles does it have?
cards.back: Gene I, with three alleles: IA, IB and i.

cards.front: In the ABO system, how many genotypes and phenotypes are possible?
cards.back: Six genotypes and four phenotypes.

cards.front: Which ABO genotype shows co-dominance, and what blood group results?
cards.back: IAIB – both sugars expressed, giving blood group AB.

cards.front: Which ABO genotypes give blood group A?
cards.back: IAIA and IAi.

cards.front: ABO blood group is an example of which two phenomena?
cards.back: Co-dominance and multiple alleles.

cards.front: Why can multiple alleles be detected only in a population, not in an individual?
cards.back: An individual (diploid) carries only two alleles of a gene.

cards.front: Pea starch grain size (gene B): seed shape shows dominance, but grain size shows what?
cards.back: Incomplete dominance – Bb seeds have intermediate-sized starch grains (BB large, bb small).
cards.hint: Same gene: round/wrinkled shape is dominant–recessive.

cards.front: Dihybrid cross (RRYY × rryy): give the F2 phenotypic ratio.
cards.back: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (round yellow : wrinkled yellow : round green : wrinkled green).

cards.front: What is the phenotypic ratio of a dihybrid test cross (RrYy × rryy)?
State the Law of Independent Assortment.
cards.back: When two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair.

cards.front: Which law did Mendel derive from the dihybrid cross that cannot come from a monohybrid cross?
cards.back: The Law of Independent Assortment.

cards.front: In which year was Mendel's work rediscovered, and by whom?
cards.back: 1900, independently by de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak.

cards.front: Who proposed the chromosomal theory of inheritance?
cards.back: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri (1902).

cards.front: Who experimentally verified the chromosomal theory of inheritance, and using which organism?
cards.back: Thomas Hunt Morgan, using fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster.

cards.front: Give 3 reasons why Drosophila is suitable for genetic studies.
cards.back: • Grows on simple synthetic medium • Completes life cycle in about two weeks • Many progeny per mating; clear sexual dimorphism; many visible hereditary variations

cards.front: Linkage vs recombination: define.
cards.back: • Linkage: physical association of genes on a chromosome • Recombination: generation of non-parental gene combinations
cards.hint: Term 'linkage' coined by Morgan.

cards.front: In Morgan's crosses, what recombination frequencies were found for white–yellow and white–miniature?
cards.back: • White eye–yellow body: 1.3% • White eye–miniature wing: 37.2%
cards.hint: Higher % = genes farther apart.

cards.front: Who used recombination frequency between gene pairs to map gene positions on chromosomes?
cards.back: Alfred Sturtevant, Morgan's student.

cards.front: What is polygenic inheritance? Give the NCERT human example.
cards.back: A trait controlled by three or more genes, with the effect of each allele being additive; e.g. human skin colour.

cards.front: What is pleiotropy? Give the NCERT example.
cards.back: A single gene showing multiple phenotypic effects; e.g. phenylketonuria in humans.
cards.hint: Polygenic = many genes, one trait; pleiotropy = one gene, many traits.

cards.front: Who first observed the 'X body' in insects, and in which year?
cards.back: Henking, in 1891.

cards.front: Which insect shows XO type of sex determination?
cards.back: Grasshopper: males XO (one X), females XX.

cards.front: In which organisms does female heterogamety (ZW) occur, per NCERT?
cards.back: In birds: females ZW, males ZZ.
cards.hint: Trap: in humans, the male is heterogametic.

cards.front: Name two organisms with XY type of male heterogamety.
cards.back: Humans and Drosophila.

cards.front: How is sex determined in honey bee?
cards.back: Haplodiploid system: fertilised eggs → females (diploid, 32 chromosomes); unfertilised eggs → males (haploid, 16 chromosomes) by parthenogenesis.
cards.hint: Male bee: no father, cannot have sons.

cards.front: What is a point mutation? Give the NCERT example.
cards.back: Mutation from change in a single base pair of DNA; e.g. sickle-cell anaemia.

cards.front: In pedigree symbols, what do a square and a circle represent?
cards.back: Square = male; circle = female.

cards.front: Haemophilia: pattern of inheritance and the famous royal carrier?
cards.back: Sex-linked recessive; Queen Victoria was a carrier, and many of her descendants were haemophilic.

cards.front: Why is haemophilia rare in females?
cards.back: A female is affected only if her mother is at least a carrier and her father is haemophilic, which is rare.

cards.front: In sickle-cell anaemia, which amino acid substitution occurs, and where?
cards.back: Glutamic acid (Glu) → valine (Val) at the sixth position of the β-globin chain.
cards.hint: Trap: 6th position of beta chain, NOT alpha.

cards.front: What codon change causes sickle-cell anaemia?
cards.back: GAG → GUG (single base substitution in the β-globin gene).

cards.front: Phenylketonuria: inheritance pattern and missing enzyme?
cards.back: Autosomal recessive; lacks the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine.

cards.front: Thalassemia: which chromosomes carry the α and β globin genes?
cards.back: • α thalassemia – chromosome 16 (HBA1, HBA2) • β thalassemia – chromosome 11 (HBB)

cards.front: Thalassemia vs sickle-cell anaemia: key difference?
cards.back: Thalassemia is a quantitative problem (too few globin molecules); sickle-cell is a qualitative problem (incorrectly functioning globin).

cards.front: Colour blindness: inheritance type and approximate frequency in males and females?
cards.back: Sex-linked recessive (red/green); about 8% of males and only 0.4% of females.

cards.front: Aneuploidy vs polyploidy?
cards.back: • Aneuploidy: gain or loss of one or more chromosomes (failure of chromatid segregation) • Polyploidy: increase in whole chromosome sets; often seen in plants

cards.front: Down's syndrome: cause and who first described it?
cards.back: Trisomy of chromosome 21; first described by Langdon Down (1866).

cards.front: Name 2 features of Down's syndrome individuals.
cards.back: Short stature with small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, palm crease, retarded physical, psychomotor and mental development.

cards.front: Klinefelter's vs Turner's syndrome: karyotypes?
cards.back: • Klinefelter's: 47, XXY (male, gynaecomastia, sterile) • Turner's: 45, X0 (female, rudimentary ovaries, sterile)

cards.front: Give the size of the genome of bacteriophage φX174 and bacteriophage lambda.
cards.back: • φX174: 5386 nucleotides • Lambda: 48502 base pairs

cards.front: What are the genome sizes of E. coli and the haploid human genome?
cards.back: • E. coli: 4.6 × 106 bp • Human haploid: 3.3 × 109 bp

cards.front: Which bond links a nitrogenous base to the pentose sugar in a nucleoside?
cards.back: N-glycosidic linkage (to the 1' C of the sugar).

cards.front: Which bond links two nucleotides in a polynucleotide chain?
cards.back: 3'-5' phosphodiester linkage.

cards.front: Who first identified DNA as an acidic substance in the nucleus, and what did he call it?
cards.back: Friedrich Miescher (spelt 'Meischer' in NCERT), in 1869; he named it 'Nuclein'.

cards.front: The double helix model of DNA (Watson and Crick, 1953) was based on whose X-ray diffraction data?
cards.back: Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin.

cards.front: State Chargaff's rule for double-stranded DNA.
cards.back: Ratio of A to T and G to C is constant and equals one.
cards.hint: A = T and G = C, so purines = pyrimidines.

cards.front: Give the pitch of the DNA helix, bp per turn, and distance between adjacent bp.
cards.back: Pitch 3.4 nm; about 10 bp per turn; 0.34 nm between bp.
cards.hint: 10 bp × 0.34 nm = 3.4 nm per turn.

cards.front: What is the length of DNA in a typical mammalian (human diploid) cell?
cards.back: About 2.2 metres (6.6 × 109 bp × 0.34 nm).

cards.front: Why are histones positively charged?
cards.back: They are rich in basic amino acids lysine and arginine, with positively charged side chains.

cards.front: What is a nucleosome made of?
cards.back: Negatively charged DNA wrapped around a positively charged histone octamer; a typical nucleosome has about 200 bp of DNA.

cards.front: Euchromatin vs heterochromatin?
cards.back: • Euchromatin: loosely packed, light-stained, transcriptionally active • Heterochromatin: densely packed, dark-stained, inactive

cards.front: Which bacterium did Griffith use in 1928, and which strain was virulent?
cards.back: Streptococcus pneumoniae; the S strain (smooth, with capsule) was virulent; R strain was not.
cards.hint: S = smooth (capsule) = killer.

cards.front: What result in Griffith's experiment showed 'transformation'?
cards.back: Mice injected with heat-killed S + live R strain died, and living S bacteria were recovered from them.

cards.front: Who showed that the transforming principle was DNA?
cards.back: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty (1933–44).
cards.hint: Proteases and RNases did not stop transformation; DNase did.

cards.front: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, which radioactive isotopes labelled DNA and protein?
cards.back: • DNA: 32P (radioactive phosphorus) • Protein: 35S (radioactive sulphur)
cards.hint: DNA has P but no S; protein has S but no P.

cards.front: Give the criteria a molecule must fulfil to act as genetic material.
cards.back: • Able to replicate • Chemically and structurally stable • Scope for slow mutation • Express itself as Mendelian characters

cards.front: Why is RNA more reactive and less stable than DNA?
cards.back: The 2'-OH group on every ribose makes RNA labile and easily degradable.

cards.front: Which was the first genetic material, and why?
cards.back: RNA; it could act both as genetic material and as a catalyst, and essential life processes evolved around it.

cards.front: Who proved semiconservative DNA replication, and in which organism?
cards.back: Meselson and Stahl (1958), in E. coli.
cards.hint: Taylor (1958) did it in Vicia faba using radioactive thymidine.

cards.front: In Meselson–Stahl's experiment, what was the nitrogen source and how were DNAs separated?
cards.back: 15NH4Cl as sole N source; DNAs separated by CsCl density gradient centrifugation.

cards.front: Meselson–Stahl: DNA composition after 20 min and 40 min in <sup>14</sup>N medium?
cards.back: • 20 min (1 generation): all hybrid • 40 min (2 generations): equal hybrid and light

cards.front: Which enzyme catalyses polymerisation of deoxynucleotides during replication?
cards.back: DNA-dependent DNA polymerase.

cards.front: DNA polymerase can polymerise nucleotides only in which direction?
cards.back: 5' → 3' direction.

cards.front: On which template strand is replication discontinuous, and which enzyme joins the fragments?
cards.back: On the 5'→3' template (lagging strand); the fragments are joined by DNA ligase.

cards.front: Name the three regions of a transcription unit.
cards.back: Promoter, structural gene and terminator.

cards.front: Template strand vs coding strand?
cards.back: • Template: 3'→5' polarity, used to make RNA • Coding: 5'→3', same sequence as RNA (T instead of U), does not code anything

cards.front: Where is the promoter located relative to the structural gene?
cards.back: Towards the 5'-end (upstream) of the structural gene, with respect to the coding strand.

cards.front: Exons vs introns?
cards.back: • Exons: coding sequences that appear in mature RNA • Introns: intervening sequences absent in mature RNA

cards.front: In bacteria, which factors help RNA polymerase in initiation and termination?
cards.back: • Initiation: sigma (σ) factor • Termination: rho (ρ) factor

cards.front: Match eukaryotic RNA polymerases I, II and III to their products.
cards.back: • Pol I: rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S) • Pol II: hnRNA (precursor of mRNA) • Pol III: tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNAs
cards.hint: Trap: 5S rRNA is made by Pol III, not Pol I.

cards.front: What are capping and tailing of hnRNA?
cards.back: • Capping: methyl guanosine triphosphate added at 5'-end • Tailing: 200–300 adenylate residues added at 3'-end

cards.front: Who suggested that the genetic code should be a triplet, and why?
cards.back: George Gamow; 4 bases must code for 20 amino acids, and 43 = 64 combinations suffice.

cards.front: Match the scientist to contribution in cracking the genetic code: Khorana, Nirenberg, Severo Ochoa.
cards.back: • Khorana: chemical synthesis of RNA with defined base combinations • Nirenberg: cell-free system for protein synthesis • Ochoa: enzyme (polynucleotide phosphorylase) to polymerise RNA

cards.front: Of 64 codons, how many code for amino acids? Name the stop codons.
cards.back: 61 code for amino acids; stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA.
cards.hint: Stop codons: U Are Away, U Are Gone, U Go Away.

cards.front: Which codon has a dual function?
cards.back: AUG – codes for methionine and acts as the initiator codon.

cards.front: What does it mean that the genetic code is 'degenerate'?
cards.back: Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon.
cards.hint: Trap: unambiguous = one codon codes only one amino acid.

cards.front: The genetic code is nearly universal. Give the NCERT exceptions.
cards.back: Mitochondrial codons and codons in some protozoans.

cards.front: What are frameshift mutations?
cards.back: Insertion or deletion of one or two bases that changes the reading frame from the point of change.
cards.hint: Inserting/deleting three bases adds/removes one amino acid; frame is kept.

cards.front: Why is tRNA called an adapter molecule?
cards.back: It has an anticodon loop that reads the codon and an amino acid acceptor end that binds the amino acid.

cards.front: Secondary vs actual 3D structure of tRNA?
cards.back: Secondary: clover-leaf; actual 3D: compact inverted L-shape.

cards.front: What is charging (aminoacylation) of tRNA?
cards.back: Activation of amino acids in presence of ATP and their linking to their cognate tRNA.

cards.front: Which molecule acts as the ribozyme catalysing peptide bond formation in bacteria?
cards.back: 23S rRNA.
cards.hint: Trap: it is an RNA, not a protein enzyme.

cards.front: What are UTRs and where are they located on mRNA?
cards.back: Untranslated regions present at both 5'-end (before start codon) and 3'-end (after stop codon); needed for efficient translation.

cards.front: Who first elucidated the transcriptionally regulated lac operon?
cards.back: Francois Jacob and Jacque Monod.

cards.front: Match lac operon genes z, y and a with their enzymes.
cards.back: • z: β-galactosidase (hydrolyses lactose) • y: permease (increases cell permeability to lactose) • a: transacetylase
cards.hint: Order on DNA: i-p-o-z-y-a.

cards.front: What does the i gene of the lac operon code for, and is it constitutive?
cards.back: The repressor of the lac operon; yes, it is expressed constitutively.
cards.hint: 'i' is derived from the word inhibitor.

cards.front: What is the inducer of the lac operon, and how does it switch the operon on?
cards.back: Lactose (or allolactose); it binds and inactivates the repressor so it cannot bind the operator.

cards.front: Regulation of the lac operon by the repressor is called what kind of regulation?
cards.back: Negative regulation.

cards.front: When was the Human Genome Project launched and completed?
cards.back: Launched in 1990, completed in 2003.

cards.front: Which chromosome has the most genes and which has the fewest?
cards.back: • Most: chromosome 1 (2968 genes) • Fewest: Y chromosome (231 genes)

cards.front: Give 3 salient features of the human genome from HGP.
cards.back: • 3164.7 million bp • About 30,000 genes; largest gene dystrophin (2.4 million bases) • 99.9% of bases same in all humans; less than 2% codes for proteins

cards.front: Who developed the DNA fingerprinting technique, and which sequences are used as markers?
cards.back: Alec Jeffreys; VNTRs (variable number tandem repeats) as probes.

cards.front: Which blotting technique is used in DNA fingerprinting?
cards.back: Southern blot hybridisation using labelled VNTR probe.

cards.front: When is an inheritable mutation called a DNA polymorphism?
cards.back: When it is observed in a population at a frequency greater than 0.01.

cards.front: Which theory explains the origin of the universe?
cards.back: Big Bang theory: a single huge explosion, after which the universe expanded and temperature came down.

cards.front: According to NCERT, roughly how old is the universe?
cards.back: Almost 20 billion years old.
cards.hint: Trap: Earth is 4.5 billion years, universe is 20 billion years.

cards.front: About when was the Earth formed?
cards.back: About 4.5 billion years back.

cards.front: Which gases were released from the molten mass of early Earth to form its atmosphere?
cards.back: • Water vapour • Methane • CO2 • Ammonia

cards.front: On early Earth, what did UV rays do to water?
cards.back: Broke water into H2 and O2; the lighter H2 escaped and O2 combined with ammonia and methane to form water, CO2 and others.

cards.front: When did life appear on Earth, per NCERT?
cards.back: About 500 million years after Earth formed, i.e. almost four billion years back.

cards.front: What is panspermia?
cards.back: Idea that units of life called spores were transferred to Earth from other planets.

cards.front: Who disproved spontaneous generation, and how?
cards.back: Louis Pasteur: in pre-sterilised flasks no life arose from killed yeast, but in a flask open to air new organisms arose.
cards.hint: Life comes only from pre-existing life.

cards.front: Which two scientists proposed that the first life arose from pre-existing non-living organic molecules?
cards.back: Oparin (Russia) and Haldane (England); formation of life preceded by chemical evolution.

cards.front: In Miller's 1953 experiment, which gases were in the closed flask, at what temperature?
cards.back: CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800°C, with electric discharge.
cards.hint: Trap: no O<sub>2</sub> in the flask.

cards.front: What did S.L. Miller observe forming in his experiment?
cards.back: Amino acids. Similar experiments by others gave sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats.

cards.front: When could the first non-cellular forms of life have originated, and what were they?
cards.back: About 3 billion years back; giant molecules such as RNA, protein, polysaccharides.

cards.front: When did the first cellular forms of life originate?
cards.back: About 2000 million years ago; probably single cells, formed in water.
cards.hint: Non-cellular ~3 billion yrs; cellular ~2000 mya.

cards.front: Give the three connotations of the theory of special creation.
cards.back: • All living organisms were created as such • Diversity was always the same since creation • Earth is about 4000 years old
cards.topic: Evolution of life forms - a theory

cards.front: On which voyage did Charles Darwin base his observations?
cards.back: The sea voyage around the world on the ship H.M.S. Beagle.
cards.topic: Evolution of life forms - a theory

cards.front: In Darwin's theory, what does 'fitness' ultimately mean?
cards.back: Reproductive fitness: those better fit leave more progeny and are selected by nature.
cards.hint: Trap: not physical strength.
cards.topic: Evolution of life forms - a theory

cards.front: Which naturalist, working in the Malay Archipelago, reached conclusions similar to Darwin's?
cards.back: Alfred Wallace.
cards.topic: Evolution of life forms - a theory

cards.front: How do fossils give evidence for evolution?
cards.back: Rock layers (sediments) of different ages contain different life forms; age of fossils is found by radioactive dating.

cards.front: Homologous organs indicate which type of evolution?
cards.back: Divergent evolution: same structure (common ancestry) developed along different directions for different needs.
cards.hint: Homologous = same origin, different function.

cards.front: Give animal examples of homologous organs from NCERT.
cards.back: Forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetah and human (same bones: humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges); also vertebrate hearts and brains.

cards.front: Give the plant example of homology given in NCERT.
cards.back: Thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita.
cards.hint: Trap: sweet potato vs potato is analogy, not homology.

cards.front: Analogous organs indicate which type of evolution?
cards.back: Convergent evolution: different structures evolving for the same function due to similar habitat.
cards.hint: Analogous = same function, different origin.

cards.front: Give NCERT examples of analogous structures.
cards.back: • Wings of butterfly and birds • Eye of octopus and mammals • Flippers of penguins and dolphins • Sweet potato (root) and potato (stem)

cards.front: Odd one out (type of organ pair): bat wing-whale flipper, Bougainvillea thorn-Cucurbita tendril, octopus eye-mammal eye.
cards.back: Octopus eye-mammal eye: analogous (convergent). The others are homologous.

cards.front: In the English moth study, how did moth populations differ in 1850 vs 1920?
cards.back: Before industrialisation (1850): more white-winged moths. After industrialisation (1920): more dark-winged moths in the same area.

cards.front: Why did dark-winged moths survive better after industrialisation in England?
cards.back: Tree trunks became dark with smoke/soot and lichens did not grow, so dark moths were camouflaged from predators.
cards.hint: Lichens are industrial pollution indicators.

cards.front: Give examples of evolution by anthropogenic action from NCERT.
cards.back: Excess use of herbicides, pesticides, antibiotics and drugs selects resistant varieties of weeds, pests, microbes in a short time.

cards.front: What is adaptive radiation?
cards.back: Evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from a point and radiating to other habitats.

cards.front: Where did Darwin observe the finches that show adaptive radiation?
cards.back: Galapagos Islands; from original seed-eating finches, forms with altered beaks became insectivorous and vegetarian.

cards.front: Which Australian group is a classic example of adaptive radiation?
cards.back: Australian marsupials, evolved from an ancestral stock within the Australian island continent.

cards.front: Placental wolf and Tasmanian wolf (marsupial) resemble each other. This illustrates what?
cards.back: Convergent evolution: more than one adaptive radiation in an isolated area.

cards.front: How did Lamarck explain the long neck of the giraffe?
cards.back: By use and disuse of organs: necks elongated while reaching leaves on tall trees and the acquired character passed on. Not accepted now.

cards.front: Two key concepts of Darwinian theory of evolution?
cards.back: Branching descent and natural selection.

cards.front: Hugo de Vries proposed mutation theory from work on which plant?
cards.back: Evening primrose, Oenothera lamarckiana.
cards.hint: Trap: de Vries = mutation; Darwin = natural selection.

cards.front: What term did de Vries use for single-step large mutation?
cards.back: Saltation.

cards.front: Darwinian variations vs de Vries mutations: key difference?
cards.back: Darwin: small, directional variations. de Vries: mutations are random and directionless, causing speciation.

cards.front: What does the Hardy-Weinberg principle state?
cards.back: Allele frequencies in a population are stable and constant from generation to generation (genetic equilibrium).
cards.hint: Disturbance of equilibrium = evolution.

cards.front: Write the Hardy-Weinberg equation and what each term represents.
cards.back: p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1 p2 = AA, 2pq = Aa, q2 = aa frequency.

cards.front: Name the five factors that affect Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
cards.back: • Gene migration (gene flow) • Genetic drift • Mutation • Genetic recombination • Natural selection

cards.front: What is genetic drift?
cards.back: Change in allele frequency that occurs by chance.
cards.hint: Gene flow = movement; drift = chance.

cards.front: What is the founder effect?
cards.back: Allele frequency in a new sample population changes so much by drift that it becomes a different species; the original drifted population are the founders.

cards.front: Three outcomes of natural selection on a character, per NCERT?
cards.back: • Stabilisation: more individuals at mean value • Directional: more at a value other than mean • Disruption: more at both peripheral ends

cards.front: By about when had invertebrates formed and become active?
cards.back: About 500 mya.

cards.front: What fish was caught in South Africa in 1938, thought to be extinct?
cards.back: Coelacanth, a lobefin; lobefins evolved into the first amphibians.

cards.front: Which group were the first organisms to invade land?
cards.back: Plants.
cards.hint: Trap: not animals or amphibians.

cards.front: Ichthyosaurs, which appeared about 200 mya, were what?
cards.back: Fish-like reptiles: land reptiles that went back into water.

cards.front: Biggest dinosaur per NCERT, and when did dinosaurs disappear?
cards.back: Tyrannosaurus rex, about 20 feet tall; dinosaurs disappeared about 65 mya.

cards.front: Dryopithecus vs Ramapithecus (about 15 mya): which was more man-like?
cards.back: Ramapithecus was more man-like; Dryopithecus was more ape-like. Both were hairy and walked like gorillas/chimpanzees.
cards.hint: Rama = man.

cards.front: Where did Australopithecines live about 2 mya, and what did they do?
cards.back: East African grasslands; hunted with stone weapons, essentially ate fruit.

cards.front: Which was the first human-like being, and its brain capacity?
cards.back: Homo habilis; brain 650-800 cc; probably did not eat meat.

cards.front: Brain capacity of Homo erectus and when did it live?
cards.back: About 900 cc; about 1.5 mya (fossils from Java, 1891); probably ate meat.
cards.hint: Trap: H. habilis did not eat meat; H. erectus probably did.

cards.front: Neanderthal man: brain capacity, region and time span?
cards.back: 1400 cc; near east and central Asia, between 1,00,000-40,000 years back. Used hides and buried their dead.

cards.front: Arrange by brain size: Homo erectus, Neanderthal, Homo habilis.
cards.back: H. habilis (650-800 cc) < H. erectus (900 cc) < Neanderthal (1400 cc)

cards.front: Where did Homo sapiens arise?
cards.back: In Africa, then moved across continents and developed into distinct races.
cards.hint: Trap: not Asia; Africa.

cards.front: When did prehistoric cave art and agriculture begin, per NCERT?
cards.back: Cave art: about 18,000 years ago. Agriculture: around 10,000 years back.

cards.front: How is health defined in NCERT?
cards.back: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being.

cards.front: Causative agent of typhoid?
cards.back: Salmonella typhi, a bacterium.
cards.hint: Typhi = typhoid.

cards.front: How does Salmonella typhi enter the body and spread?
cards.back: Through contaminated food and water into the small intestine, then migrates to other organs via blood.

cards.front: Which test confirms typhoid fever?
cards.back: Widal test.
cards.hint: W for Widal, typhoid; ELISA for AIDS.

cards.front: Who was 'Typhoid Mary'?
cards.back: Mary Mallon, a cook and typhoid carrier who spread typhoid for years through the food she prepared.

cards.front: Name the bacteria responsible for pneumonia in humans.
cards.back: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae.
cards.hint: Trap: H. influenzae is a bacterium, not the flu virus.

cards.front: Which part of the lungs does pneumonia infect, and with what result?
cards.back: Alveoli (air-filled sacs) fill with fluid, causing severe problems in respiration.

cards.front: In severe pneumonia, what colour change occurs in lips and finger nails?
cards.back: They may turn gray to bluish.

cards.front: Which viruses cause common cold, and do they infect the lungs?
cards.back: Rhinoviruses; they infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs.
cards.hint: Rhino = nose.

cards.front: Name the Plasmodium species causing malaria; which is most serious?
cards.back: P. vivax, P. malariae, P. falciparum. P. falciparum causes malignant malaria, which is most serious and can be fatal.

cards.front: In which form does Plasmodium enter the human body?
cards.back: As sporozoites (infectious form), through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.

cards.front: Sequence of Plasmodium in humans after a mosquito bite?
cards.back: Sporozoites → multiply in liver cells → attack RBCs and multiply → RBCs rupture → gametocytes develop in RBCs.

cards.front: Which toxin causes the chill and high fever of malaria, and how often does fever recur?
cards.back: Haemozoin, released when RBCs rupture; fever recurs every 3-4 days.

cards.front: Where does fertilisation of Plasmodium gametes occur, and where are sporozoites stored?
cards.back: Fertilisation in the mosquito's stomach (gut); sporozoites stored in the mosquito's salivary glands.

cards.front: Causative agent and site of infection in amoebiasis?
cards.back: Entamoeba histolytica, a protozoan, in the large intestine.
cards.hint: Trap: large intestine, not small (typhoid is small).

cards.front: Ascaris causes which disease, and how is it transmitted?
cards.back: Ascariasis; eggs passed in faeces contaminate soil, water, plants; infection via contaminated water, vegetables, fruits.

cards.front: Which helminth causes elephantiasis (filariasis)?
cards.back: Wuchereria (W. bancrofti and W. malayi).
cards.hint: Wuchereria lives in lymphatics.

cards.front: Where do filarial worms live, and what is the effect?
cards.back: In lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs; chronic inflammation; genital organs may also be deformed. Spread by bite of female mosquito vectors.

cards.front: Name three fungal genera that cause ringworm.
cards.back: Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton.
cards.hint: MTE: My Tiny Enemies.

cards.front: Which mosquito transmits dengue and chikungunya?
cards.back: Aedes mosquitoes.
cards.hint: Trap: malaria = Anopheles.

cards.front: Name the four types of barriers of innate immunity with one example each.
cards.back: • Physical: skin, mucus coating • Physiological: stomach acid, saliva, tears • Cellular: neutrophils (PMNL), monocytes, NK cells, macrophages • Cytokine: interferons

cards.front: Acid in stomach and tears belong to which type of innate barrier?
cards.back: Physiological barriers.
cards.hint: Trap: skin and mucus are physical barriers.

cards.front: Which cells secrete interferons, and what do they do?
cards.back: Virus-infected cells; interferons protect non-infected cells from further viral infection (cytokine barrier).

cards.front: Primary vs secondary (anamnestic) immune response?
cards.back: Primary: first encounter, low intensity. Secondary: subsequent encounter, highly intensified due to memory.

cards.front: Which lymphocytes give humoral immunity and which give cell-mediated immunity?
cards.back: B-lymphocytes: antibodies in blood (humoral). T-lymphocytes: cell-mediated immunity (CMI); T cells also help B cells.

cards.front: How many polypeptide chains does an antibody have?
cards.back: Four: two light and two heavy chains, represented as H2L2.

cards.front: Which type of immunity is responsible for graft rejection?
cards.back: Cell-mediated immunity; hence tissue/blood group matching and lifelong immuno-suppressants are needed.

cards.front: Active vs passive immunity: key difference?
cards.back: Active: host produces its own antibodies on antigen exposure; slow. Passive: ready-made antibodies given; quick.

cards.front: Which antibody is abundant in colostrum, and what immunity does it give the infant?
cards.back: IgA; gives passive immunity.
cards.hint: Colostrum = IgA (A for Amma's milk).

cards.front: Injection given for snakebite or tetanus provides which immunity?
cards.back: Passive immunisation: preformed antibodies or antitoxin for a quick response.

cards.front: Which antibody is produced in allergy, and which chemicals cause the symptoms?
cards.back: IgE; mast cells release histamine and serotonin.
cards.hint: IgE = Excess response.

cards.front: What is autoimmunity? Give the NCERT example.
cards.back: Body attacks self-cells; e.g. rheumatoid arthritis.

cards.front: Name the primary lymphoid organs.
cards.back: Bone marrow and thymus: immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes here.
cards.hint: Primary = where lymphocytes are made/matured.

cards.front: Odd one out: spleen, lymph nodes, thymus, Peyer's patches, tonsils.
cards.back: Thymus: primary lymphoid organ. Others are secondary lymphoid organs.

cards.front: Which lymphoid organ acts as a reservoir of erythrocytes?
cards.back: Spleen: large bean-shaped organ with lymphocytes and phagocytes; filters blood.

cards.front: What is MALT and what share of lymphoid tissue does it form?
cards.back: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, lining respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts; about 50% of lymphoid tissue.

cards.front: When was AIDS first reported, and what type of virus is HIV?
cards.back: First reported in 1981; HIV is a retrovirus with an RNA genome.

cards.front: Give the modes of HIV transmission.
cards.back: • Sexual contact with infected person • Contaminated blood transfusion • Sharing infected needles • Infected mother to child via placenta

cards.front: Which enzyme copies HIV RNA into viral DNA in the host cell?
cards.back: Reverse transcriptase.

cards.front: Which cell acts as the 'HIV factory'?
cards.back: Macrophage: keeps producing virus while infected. HIV then attacks helper T-lymphocytes (TH), reducing their number.
cards.hint: Trap: factory = macrophage, not T<sub>H</sub> cell.

cards.front: Widely used diagnostic test for AIDS?
cards.back: ELISA (enzyme linked immuno-sorbent assay).

cards.front: Which loss of property of normal cells leads to cancer?
cards.back: Contact inhibition: cancer cells keep dividing, forming tumours.

cards.front: Benign vs malignant tumour?
cards.back: Benign: stays confined to its location, little damage. Malignant: proliferating neoplastic cells invade and spread (metastasis).

cards.front: Give examples of carcinogens per NCERT.
cards.back: • Ionising: X-rays, gamma rays • Non-ionising: UV • Chemical: tobacco smoke (lung cancer) • Oncogenic viruses

cards.front: What are proto-oncogenes (c-onc)?
cards.back: Cellular oncogenes in normal cells that, when activated under certain conditions, cause oncogenic transformation.

cards.front: Which biological response modifier is used in cancer immunotherapy?
cards.back: α-interferon: activates the immune system to destroy the tumour.

cards.front: Name the three classes of commonly abused drugs in NCERT.
cards.back: Opioids, cannabinoids and coca alkaloids.

cards.front: How is heroin (smack) obtained chemically?
cards.back: By acetylation of morphine (diacetylmorphine); morphine comes from latex of poppy, Papaver somniferum.
cards.hint: Trap: acetylation, not methylation.

cards.front: Where are opioid receptors present?
cards.back: In the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract. Heroin is a depressant.

cards.front: Cannabinoids are obtained from which plant, and which body system do they mainly affect?
cards.back: Inflorescences of Cannabis sativa (marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja); affect the cardiovascular system.

cards.front: Source of cocaine and its action?
cards.back: Erythroxylum coca (South America); interferes with dopamine transport; stimulates CNS, causing euphoria.
cards.hint: Coca alkaloid = dopamine transport blocker.

cards.front: Name two plants with hallucinogenic properties per NCERT.
cards.back: Atropa belladona and Datura.

cards.front: How does nicotine raise blood pressure and heart rate?
cards.back: Stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and nor-adrenaline.
cards.hint: Trap: acts via adrenal gland, not thyroid.

cards.front: Give side effects of anabolic steroids in females.
cards.back: Masculinisation, aggressiveness, mood swings, depression, abnormal menstrual cycles, facial hair, clitoris enlargement, deepening of voice.

cards.front: Which microbe converts milk into curd?
cards.back: Lactobacillus and other lactic acid bacteria (LAB).

cards.front: How do LAB convert milk to curd?
cards.back: They produce acids that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins.

cards.front: What is the starter or inoculum in curd making?
cards.back: A small amount of curd added to fresh milk; it contains millions of LAB that multiply.

cards.front: Which vitamin is increased in curd by LAB?
cards.back: Vitamin B12.
cards.hint: LAB also check disease-causing microbes in the stomach.

cards.front: Why do dosa and idli dough look puffed-up?
cards.back: Bacterial fermentation produces CO2 gas.

cards.front: Which microbe is used to make bread dough rise?
cards.back: Baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
cards.hint: Same species is brewer's yeast for beverages.

cards.front: What is toddy?
